topics.name: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem: Decision Variables, Objective Function, and Constraints
topics.summary: Every Linear Programming Problem (LPP) begins with formulation: identifying the decision variables (usually \(x\) and \(y\)) that represent the quantities to be decided, writing the objective function \(Z=ax+by\) that is to be maximised or minimised, and translating every real-world restriction into a linear constraint (\(\le\), \(\ge\), or \(=\)). Non-negativity (\(x\ge0,\ y\ge0\)) is included whenever the variables represent physical quantities like units produced or money invested. Getting the direction of each inequality right — a capacity is \(\le\), a minimum requirement is \(\ge\) — is the single most important formulation skill, since a correctly solved but wrongly formulated LPP gives a meaningless answer.
key_formulas: Objective function: \(Z=ax+by\) (to be maximised or minimised)
General linear constraint: \(px+qy\le c\), \(px+qy\ge c\), or \(px+qy=c\)
Non-negativity restrictions: \(x\ge0,\ y\ge0\)
A "maximum of" / "cannot exceed" / "capacity" phrase \(\Rightarrow\) \(\le\) constraint
A "minimum of" / "at least" / "must meet" phrase \(\Rightarrow\) \(\ge\) constraint
topics.worked_example: A carpenter makes tables (\(x\)) and chairs (\(y\)). Each table needs \(4\) hours of labour and each chair needs \(2\) hours, with \(60\) labour-hours available: \(4x+2y\le60\). Wood available limits production to \(x+y\le20\). Profit is \(\textrm{\textrupee}300\) per table and \(\textrm{\textrupee}150\) per chair. The complete formulation is: Maximise \(Z=300x+150y\) subject to \(4x+2y\le60,\ x+y\le20,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\).
common_mistakes: Reversing the inequality direction — writing \(\ge\) for a capacity limit or \(\le\) for a minimum requirement
Forgetting non-negativity constraints when the variables clearly represent physical, non-negative quantities
Mixing up which coefficient belongs to which variable when translating word-problem numbers into the objective function or a constraint
Treating a per-unit rate (e.g. hours per table) as if it were a total, instead of multiplying it by the decision variable

topics.name: Graphical Solution: Feasible Region and Corner Points
topics.summary: The feasible region is the set of all points \((x,y)\) that satisfy every constraint of the LPP simultaneously, including non-negativity. It is found by shading, for each constraint, the half-plane it represents, and taking the region common to all of them; this common region is always a convex polygon (or an unbounded convex area). Its corner points (vertices) are the points where two boundary lines meet, and by the Corner Point Theorem, the optimal value of any linear objective function over this region — when it exists — always occurs at one of these corner points, never at an interior point.
key_formulas: A point lies on the boundary line \(px+qy=c\) when equality holds exactly
Corner points are found by solving pairs of boundary-line equations simultaneously (including the axes \(x=0\) and \(y=0\) from non-negativity)
A candidate intersection point is a genuine corner only if it also satisfies every OTHER constraint of the problem
Convexity: the feasible region always has straight edges and no indentations
topics.worked_example: For \(x+y\le9\) and \(2x+y\le14\) (with \(x,y\ge0\)), the boundary lines meet the axes at \((0,9)\), \((9,0)\), \((0,14)\), \((7,0)\); solving the two lines together gives \((5,4)\). Checking each candidate against the other constraint, the true corner points are \((0,0)\), \((0,9)\), \((5,4)\), and \((7,0)\) — note that \((0,14)\) and \((9,0)\) are excluded because they fail the other constraint.
common_mistakes: Listing an axis intercept without checking it against every OTHER constraint, which can make it infeasible
Skipping the intersection of two non-axis constraint lines, which is very often a genuine corner
Forgetting that the origin is a corner point whenever both non-negativity constraints are active there
Assuming a region is a simple shape (triangle, rectangle) without actually verifying every candidate corner point

topics.name: Corner Point Method: Finding the Optimal (Maximum or Minimum) Value
topics.summary: The Corner Point Method finds the optimal value of \(Z\) by evaluating the objective function at every corner point of the feasible region and comparing the results: for a BOUNDED region, the Corner Point Theorem guarantees that the largest value is the maximum and the smallest is the minimum. Every single corner point must be evaluated — skipping even one can silently miss the true optimum — and the correct extreme (largest for maximisation, smallest for minimisation) must be selected, since mixing these up gives exactly the wrong answer even when every \(Z\)-value was computed correctly.
key_formulas: Evaluate \(Z=ax+by\) at each corner point \((x_i,y_i)\)
Maximisation: optimal \(Z=\max_i\{Z(x_i,y_i)\}\)
Minimisation: optimal \(Z=\min_i\{Z(x_i,y_i)\}\)
For an UNBOUNDED region: extra check needed — see Topic 4
topics.worked_example: For Maximise \(Z=3x+2y\) subject to \(x\le6,\ y\le6,\ x+y\le9,\ 2x+y\le14\ (x,y\ge0)\), the corner points are \((0,0)\), \((0,6)\), \((3,6)\), \((5,4)\), \((6,2)\), \((6,0)\), giving \(Z=0,\ 12,\ 21,\ 23,\ 22,\ 18\). Since the region is bounded, the largest value, \(23\) at \((5,4)\), is the guaranteed maximum.
common_mistakes: Trap A: computing every \(Z\)-value correctly but then picking the maximum when a minimum was asked for, or vice versa
Trap B: missing a genuine corner point (often an intersection of two non-axis lines), which can hide the true optimum
Trap C: trusting a corner-point value as final for an UNBOUNDED region without the extra half-plane verification
Assuming the optimum is always at the corner with the largest (or smallest) \(x\)- or \(y\)-coordinate, instead of actually computing every \(Z\)-value

topics.name: Bounded and Unbounded Feasible Regions
topics.summary: A feasible region is bounded if it can be enclosed within some large enough circle — every constraint eventually caps the region in every direction. It is unbounded if it stretches to infinity in at least one direction, which typically happens when one or more constraints are \(\ge\)-type lower bounds with nothing capping the variables from above. For a bounded region, the Corner Point Theorem guarantees both a maximum and minimum exist among the corners. For an UNBOUNDED region, a corner-point value is only a CANDIDATE optimum: it must be verified by checking whether the open half-plane \(ax+by>M\) (for a maximum candidate \(M\)) or \(ax+by<m\) (for a minimum candidate \(m\)) shares any point with the feasible region — if it does not, the candidate is confirmed genuine; if it does, no finite optimum of that kind exists.
key_formulas: Half-plane test for a MAX candidate \(M\): check whether \(ax+by>M\) has any point in common with the feasible region
Half-plane test for a MIN candidate \(m\): check whether \(ax+by<m\) has any point in common with the feasible region
No shared point \(\Rightarrow\) candidate is the genuine optimum
Shared point(s) exist \(\Rightarrow\) no finite optimum of that kind (unbounded optimal value)
topics.worked_example: For Minimise \(Z=3x+5y\) subject to \(x+3y\ge3,\ x+y\ge2\ (x,y\ge0)\), the region is unbounded with corner points \((0,2)\), \(\left(\tfrac32,\tfrac12\right)\), \((3,0)\), giving \(Z=10,\ 7,\ 9\). The smallest, \(7\), is only a candidate; checking confirms that \(3x+5y<7\) shares no point with the feasible region, so \(Z=7\) is genuinely the minimum.
common_mistakes: Assuming any \(\ge\) constraint automatically makes the whole region unbounded, without checking whether other \(\le\) constraints already close it off
Trusting a corner-point value as the final optimum for an unbounded region without performing the half-plane check
Confusing "region is unbounded" with "optimal value is unbounded" — many unbounded regions still have a perfectly finite optimum
Believing a single corner point rules out an unbounded region, when in fact it is often a sign of one

topics.name: Special Cases: Multiple Optimal Solutions, Infeasible Problems, and Unbounded Optimal Values
topics.summary: Beyond the ordinary case of a single unique optimal solution, an LPP can fall into one of three special cases. Infeasibility: the constraints are mutually contradictory, so the feasible region is empty and no solution exists at all. Multiple optimal solutions: the optimal VALUE of \(Z\) (still a single number) is achieved at more than one point — typically along an entire edge — because the objective function's direction is parallel to that edge. Unbounded optimal value: the feasible region is unbounded and \(Z\) itself can be made arbitrarily large (or small) within it, so no finite optimum exists. Recognising which (if any) special case applies, rather than defaulting to "ordinary unique solution", is the key skill this topic tests.
key_formulas: Infeasible: feasible region is empty (zero corner points, contradictory constraints)
Multiple optimal solutions: two or more corner points tie at the OPTIMAL value, and lie on the same edge with the objective's coefficients matching that edge's direction
Unbounded optimal value: region unbounded AND the half-plane test finds points beating any proposed candidate, without limit
Ordinary unique solution: none of the above — a single corner point strictly beats all others, verified if the region is unbounded
topics.worked_example: For Maximise \(Z=4x+4y\) subject to \(x+y\le50,\ 3x+y\le90\ (x,y\ge0)\), the corners \((20,30)\) and \((30,20)\) both lie on the edge \(x+y=50\), and since the objective \((4,4)\) is proportional to that edge's own coefficients \((1,1)\), both give the same maximum \(Z=200\) — the entire edge between them is optimal, a genuine case of multiple optimal solutions.
common_mistakes: Mistaking a coincidental tie between two NON-optimal corner values for the genuine multiple-optimal-solutions special case
Assuming an unbounded feasible region automatically means an unbounded optimal value, without actually performing the half-plane verification
Treating a genuinely infeasible LPP (zero corner points from contradictory constraints) as simply "needing more searching"
Believing that multiple optimal SOLUTIONS means multiple different optimal VALUES, rather than one value shared by more than one point

questions.topic: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem: Decision Variables, Objective Function, and Constraints
questions.question: In a Linear Programming Problem (LPP), what does a \(\textbf{decision variable}\) represent?
options: The maximum value that the objective function can ever reach
The final numerical answer of the optimisation problem
A fixed resource limit stated in the problem, such as available hours
The quantity to be determined, whose values the decision-maker controls (e.g. the number of units to produce)
questions.explanation: A decision variable (such as \(x\) and \(y\)) is an unknown quantity that the LPP is solved for — for example, the number of units of two products to manufacture. The values chosen for these variables are what the decision-maker actually controls; everything else (constraints, objective) is built around them.
questions.hint: Ask: which quantity in the problem is actually being chosen/decided by the manufacturer?
distractor_logic: This describes the optimal value of Z, not a decision variable — confuses the answer of the LPP with its unknowns.
This describes the solution/output of the LPP, not the variable itself — confuses what is asked for with what is found.
This describes a constraint constant (a resource limit), not a decision variable — mixes up the given data with the unknowns being solved for.

questions.topic: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem: Decision Variables, Objective Function, and Constraints
questions.question: In the general form \(Z = ax + by\), which is to be maximised or minimised, what is \(Z\) called?
options: The objective function
A decision variable
The feasible region
A constraint
questions.explanation: \(Z = ax + by\) is the linear function that expresses the quantity to be optimised (such as profit or cost) in terms of the decision variables \(x\) and \(y\); this is called the objective function.
questions.hint: This is the expression the problem asks you to maximise or minimise — that naming is the giveaway.
distractor_logic: \(x\) and \(y\) themselves are the decision variables; \(Z\) is built from them, not one of them.
The feasible region is the set of points satisfying all constraints, not the function \(Z\) itself.
A constraint is an inequality restricting \(x\) and \(y\), not the function being optimised.

questions.topic: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem: Decision Variables, Objective Function, and Constraints
questions.question: What mathematical form must both the objective function and every constraint of an LPP take?
options: Exponential functions of the decision variables
Linear (first-degree) functions of the decision variables
Quadratic functions of the decision variables
Any continuous function, linear or non-linear
questions.explanation: The word \(\textit{linear}\) in \(\textit{Linear Programming}\) refers to the requirement that the objective function \(Z=ax+by\) and every constraint are first-degree (linear) expressions in the decision variables — no squares, products of variables, or other non-linear terms are allowed.
questions.hint: The name of the technique itself describes the required form of every function involved.
distractor_logic: Exponential functions are non-linear and are excluded by definition from a Linear Programming Problem.
Quadratic terms would make the problem non-linear, which standard LPP theory (and the corner-point method) does not cover.
Allowing any non-linear function would break the straight-line/half-plane geometry that the graphical method relies on.

questions.topic: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem: Decision Variables, Objective Function, and Constraints
questions.question: What do the non-negativity restrictions \(x \ge 0,\ y \ge 0\) express in an LPP?
options: That the feasible region must always be bounded
That the objective function value can never be negative
That the decision variables, representing quantities like units produced, cannot be negative in a real-world sense
That the LPP always has a unique optimal solution
questions.explanation: Decision variables in most LPPs represent physical quantities such as the number of items manufactured, hours of labour used, or amount invested — none of which can meaningfully be negative. The restrictions \(x \ge 0, y \ge 0\) build this real-world fact into the mathematical model.
questions.hint: Think about what \(x\) and \(y\) usually stand for in these problems (units produced, quantity used) and whether a negative amount would make sense.
distractor_logic: Non-negativity alone does not guarantee boundedness — a region can be unbounded even with \(x,y \ge 0\), as with an unbounded feasible region.
\(Z\) can be negative in general (e.g. a cost/loss context); non-negativity restricts \(x\) and \(y\), not \(Z\) itself.
Non-negativity says nothing about uniqueness — an LPP can still have multiple optimal solutions or no solution at all.

questions.topic: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem: Decision Variables, Objective Function, and Constraints
questions.question: A point \((x,y)\) is called a \(\textbf{feasible solution}\) of an LPP if:
options: It lies exactly at one of the axes
It satisfies the objective function equation \(Z=ax+by\) for some fixed value of \(Z\)
It satisfies all the constraints of the problem, including the non-negativity restrictions
It gives the maximum possible value of the objective function
questions.explanation: A feasible solution is simply any point \((x,y)\) that satisfies every constraint of the LPP (all the inequalities) together with \(x \ge 0, y \ge 0\). It need not be optimal — the feasible region typically contains infinitely many feasible solutions, only some (the corner points) of which need to be checked for optimality.
questions.hint: "Feasible" is about satisfying the rules of the problem, not about being the best answer.
distractor_logic: Feasible points can lie anywhere inside or on the boundary of the feasible region, not only on the axes.
Lying on a particular line \(Z=ax+by=\text{constant}\) has nothing to do with satisfying the constraints; it only fixes the value of \(Z\), which may or may not correspond to a feasible point.
This describes an \(\textit{optimal}\) solution, a special feasible solution — not every feasible solution is optimal.

questions.topic: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem: Decision Variables, Objective Function, and Constraints
questions.question: Which of the following is \(\textbf{NOT}\) one of the essential components used to formulate an LPP?
options: An objective function to be optimised
A graphical calculator to plot the region
A set of linear constraints (including non-negativity)
Decision variables
questions.explanation: Formulating an LPP means identifying its decision variables, writing the objective function in terms of them, and listing all linear constraints (plus non-negativity). A graphical calculator or any plotting tool is not part of the formulation itself — graphing is only a solution technique used later, and the LPP can be formulated and even solved (via the corner-point method) without ever drawing a picture.
questions.hint: Formulation is about writing down the mathematical model; a plotting tool is not part of that written model.
distractor_logic: The objective function IS an essential part of formulation — without it there is nothing to optimise.
Constraints (with non-negativity) ARE essential — without them the decision variables would be unrestricted.
Decision variables ARE an essential part of formulating any LPP — this option is incorrectly picked as the exception.

questions.topic: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem: Decision Variables, Objective Function, and Constraints
questions.question: The restrictions on the decision variables of an LPP (other than non-negativity) are called:
options: Constraints
Corner points
Objective functions
Iso-profit lines
questions.explanation: The linear inequalities (or equations) that limit the values the decision variables can take — typically arising from limited resources like time, material, or budget — are called the constraints of the LPP.
questions.hint: This is the standard name for the "rules" or "limits" a valid solution must obey.
distractor_logic: Corner points are specific vertices of the feasible region found after graphing, not the restrictions themselves.
The objective function is the single expression being maximised/minimised, not the restrictions on \(x\) and \(y\).
An iso-profit (or iso-cost) line is a line \(ax+by=k\) of constant \(Z\)-value, unrelated to the restrictions defining the feasible region.

questions.topic: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem: Decision Variables, Objective Function, and Constraints
questions.question: Constraints in a real-world LPP typically arise because of:
options: Limitations on available resources such as raw material, labour time, or budget
The decision-maker's personal preference for round numbers
The need to plot the feasible region on graph paper
The requirement that the objective function be linear
questions.explanation: In practical problems — manufacturing, diet planning, transportation, and so on — constraints come from limited resources: a fixed number of labour hours, a fixed quantity of raw material, a maximum budget, a minimum nutritional requirement, and similar real restrictions that cap or floor what the decision variables can be.
questions.hint: Ask why a factory can't just produce unlimited quantities of everything — what actually stops it?
distractor_logic: A preference for round numbers is not a mathematical restriction and plays no role in defining constraints.
Plotting on graph paper is a solution technique applied after formulation; it is not why constraints arise in the real-world problem.
Linearity is a requirement on the FORM of the objective function and constraints, not the reason constraints exist in the first place.

questions.topic: Graphical Solution: Feasible Region and Corner Points
questions.question: What is meant by the \(\textbf{feasible region}\) of an LPP?
options: The set of all points where the objective function equals zero
The single point that gives the optimal value of the objective function
The boundary line of the graph on which \(x=0\)
The set of all points \((x,y)\) that satisfy every constraint of the problem, including the non-negativity restrictions
questions.explanation: The feasible region is the common (overlapping) region of the graph that satisfies ALL the given constraints together with \(x\ge0,y\ge0\) — every point in it is a feasible solution, though most feasible regions contain infinitely many such points.
questions.hint: "Feasible" means "satisfying every rule of the problem" — think of it as the overlap of all the constraint half-planes.
distractor_logic: \(Z=0\) is just one particular line and has no special connection to feasibility — most feasible points do not give \(Z=0\).
This describes the optimal solution, a single special point within the feasible region, not the region itself.
The line \(x=0\) (the \(y\)-axis) is only part of the boundary in some problems, not a general description of the feasible region.

questions.topic: Graphical Solution: Feasible Region and Corner Points
questions.question: A \(\textbf{corner point}\) (or vertex) of a feasible region is:
options: Any point strictly inside the feasible region, away from all boundaries
The average (midpoint) of all the feasible points
The point where the objective function line first touches the \(y\)-axis
A point of the feasible region where two of its boundary lines (edges) meet
questions.explanation: Corner points are the vertices of the feasible region — the points where two boundary edges (constraint lines, or a constraint line and an axis) meet. The Corner Point Theorem says the optimal value of a linear objective function, if it exists, occurs at one of these vertices.
questions.hint: Picture the feasible region as a polygon; a corner point is exactly a "corner" of that polygon shape.
distractor_logic: An interior point is not a corner point — corner points lie specifically on the boundary, at the meeting of two edges.
There is no such thing as "the average of all feasible points" being a corner point — corner points are specific vertices, not a computed average.
Where the objective line meets the \(y\)-axis depends on the arbitrarily chosen value of \(Z\) and has nothing to do with the shape of the feasible region.

questions.topic: Graphical Solution: Feasible Region and Corner Points
questions.question: For a \(\textbf{bounded}\) feasible region, corner points are obtained by:
options: Finding the intersection of each pair of boundary lines (constraint lines and/or axes) and keeping only those intersections that also satisfy every other constraint
Substituting \(x=1\) into every constraint
Reading off the coefficients of the objective function directly
Finding the midpoint of every pair of boundary lines
questions.explanation: Each corner point is where two boundary lines cross; since some pairwise intersections may fall outside the region defined by the remaining constraints, every candidate intersection must be checked against ALL the constraints before being accepted as an actual corner point.
questions.hint: There are two steps: (1) intersect pairs of boundary lines, (2) throw out any intersection that violates some other constraint.
distractor_logic: Substituting an arbitrary fixed value like \(x=1\) has no general connection to locating vertices of the feasible region.
The objective function's coefficients determine the direction of the iso-profit lines used later, not the location of the corner points themselves.
A midpoint between two lines is not generally where they cross, and is not how corner points are defined.

questions.topic: Graphical Solution: Feasible Region and Corner Points
questions.question: True or false: every point that satisfies all the constraints of an LPP is a corner point of the feasible region.
options: False — no feasible point can ever be a corner point
True, but only when the feasible region is unbounded
True — feasibility and being a corner point are the same thing
False — the feasible region generally contains infinitely many feasible points, of which only a finite number are corner points
questions.explanation: A feasible region (a polygon, or an unbounded polygonal region) usually contains infinitely many points satisfying all constraints; only the finitely many vertices of that polygon are corner points. Every corner point is feasible, but not every feasible point is a corner point.
questions.hint: Think of a triangular feasible region: it has only 3 corner points, but infinitely many points lie inside or along its edges.
distractor_logic: This over-corrects — corner points ARE feasible points (they satisfy all constraints); the statement should say not every feasible point is a corner point, not that no feasible point can be one.
Boundedness of the region does not change this fact — even unbounded regions have infinitely many feasible points but only finitely many corner points.
Incorrectly equates "feasible" with "corner point" — feasibility is the much broader condition; being a corner point is a special, stricter case of it.

questions.topic: Graphical Solution: Feasible Region and Corner Points
questions.question: For the region defined by \(x+y\le7,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\), how many corner points does the feasible region have?
options: Infinitely many
questions.explanation: The boundary lines are \(x+y=7\), \(x=0\), and \(y=0\). Their pairwise intersections that satisfy all constraints are \((0,0)\), \((0,7)\), and \((7,0)\) — a triangle with 3 corner points.
questions.hint: Sketch it: it's a straight line cutting off a triangle in the first quadrant, bounded by the two axes.
distractor_logic: Undercounts — misses one of the three vertices, most likely the origin \((0,0)\) formed by the two axes themselves.
Confuses the finite corner points with the infinitely many ordinary feasible points that lie along the edges and interior of the triangle.
Overcounts by including a fourth point that does not actually lie on the true boundary of this simple triangular region.

questions.topic: Graphical Solution: Feasible Region and Corner Points
questions.question: For the region \(x\le6,\ y\le5,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\), is the origin \((0,0)\) a corner point of the feasible region?
options: Only if the objective function passes through the origin
No — \((0,0)\) does not satisfy \(x\le6\)
No — the origin can never be a corner point of any feasible region
Yes — it is where the boundary lines \(x=0\) and \(y=0\) meet, and it satisfies \(x\le6\) and \(y\le5\) as well
questions.explanation: \((0,0)\) is where \(x=0\) meets \(y=0\), and it clearly satisfies both \(x\le6\) (\(0\le6\)) and \(y\le5\) (\(0\le5\)), so it is feasible and is a genuine corner point here, alongside \((0,5)\), \((6,5)\), and \((6,0)\).
questions.hint: Check the origin against every constraint one by one — it fails only if some constraint's right-hand side is negative.
distractor_logic: Whether a point is a corner point of the feasible region depends only on the constraints, not on the objective function or where its line happens to pass.
\((0,0)\) satisfies \(0\le6\) perfectly well; this option checks the constraint incorrectly.
Wrongly claims the origin can NEVER be a corner point — in many LPPs (especially those with only \(\le\) constraints and positive right-hand sides) it is exactly a corner point.

questions.topic: Graphical Solution: Feasible Region and Corner Points
questions.question: The feasible region of an LPP (when it is non-empty and bounded) is always:
options: A circular region
A convex region bounded by straight line segments (a convex polygon)
A region that must contain the origin
A region with exactly 4 corner points
questions.explanation: Because every constraint is a linear inequality, each cuts out a half-plane with a straight-line boundary; the intersection of finitely many half-planes (and the non-negative quadrant) is always a convex polygon — never curved, and with as few as 2 or as many corner points as the problem's constraints allow.
questions.hint: Straight-line constraints can only ever produce straight-edged regions — curves are impossible here.
distractor_logic: A circular boundary would require a non-linear constraint (like \(x^2+y^2\le r^2\)), which is not allowed in a Linear Programming Problem.
Many valid feasible regions (e.g. any problem with an \(\ge\) type resource requirement at the origin) do not contain the origin at all.
The number of corner points depends entirely on the specific constraints given — it can be 3, 4, 5, or more; there is no fixed count of 4.

questions.topic: Graphical Solution: Feasible Region and Corner Points
questions.question: For the region \(2x+y\le12,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\), what is the corner point that lies on the \(x\)-axis?
questions.explanation: On the \(x\)-axis, \(y=0\), so \(2x+0=12 \Rightarrow x=6\), giving the corner point \((6,0)\).
questions.hint: Set \(y=0\) in the boundary equation \(2x+y=12\) and solve for \(x\).
distractor_logic: Swaps the coordinates of the correct \(y\)-axis intercept \((0,6)\) into \((6,0)\)-shaped confusion between which axis each intercept belongs to.
This is actually the \(y\)-axis intercept (set \(x=0\) instead: \(y=12\)), not the \(x\)-axis intercept.
Uses the right-hand side value \(12\) directly as the \(x\)-coordinate without dividing by the coefficient \(2\) of \(x\).

questions.topic: Corner Point Method: Finding the Optimal (Maximum or Minimum) Value
questions.question: What does the \(\textbf{Corner Point Theorem}\) (Corner Point Method) state about solving an LPP with a bounded, non-empty feasible region?
options: The optimal value of \(Z\) is always equal to the largest constraint constant on the right-hand side
The optimal (maximum or minimum) value of \(Z\) must occur at one of the corner points of the feasible region, so evaluating \(Z\) at every corner point and comparing is enough to find it
The optimal value of \(Z\) must occur at the origin of the graph
The optimal value of \(Z\) can only be found by testing every point in the feasible region, one at a time
questions.explanation: For a bounded feasible region, it can be proved that a linear objective function attains its maximum and minimum at one of the (finitely many) corner points — not somewhere in the interior. This is exactly why the corner-point method only needs to check the vertices, rather than every point in the region.
questions.hint: The whole point of this method is that you never need to check the infinitely many interior points — only the finitely many vertices.
distractor_logic: The right-hand side constants of the constraints have no direct relationship to the optimal value of \(Z\); the optimal value depends on evaluating the objective function at the corner points.
The origin is just one possible corner point among several — it has no special guaranteed role unless it happens to be part of the feasible region and gives the best value there.
This defeats the purpose of the theorem, which is precisely that checking every single point is unnecessary; only the finitely many corner points need to be checked.

questions.topic: Corner Point Method: Finding the Optimal (Maximum or Minimum) Value
questions.question: If the feasible region of an LPP is bounded and non-empty, the maximum and minimum values of the objective function \(Z\):
options: Both exist, but they can occur anywhere in the interior of the feasible region
Only the maximum is guaranteed to exist; the minimum may not exist
Both exist, and each occurs at one of the corner points of the feasible region
Neither is guaranteed to exist, even for a bounded region
questions.explanation: For a bounded feasible region, both a maximum and a minimum of the linear objective function are guaranteed to exist, and each is attained at (at least) one corner point of the region.
questions.hint: "Bounded" is the key word — it guarantees BOTH extremes exist, unlike the unbounded case where one or both may fail to exist.
distractor_logic: Interior points never give a strictly better value than the best corner point for a linear objective over a bounded convex region — the optimum is always attainable at a vertex.
Boundedness guarantees existence of BOTH the maximum and the minimum together — it is the unbounded case, not the bounded one, where an optimum can fail to exist.
This is backwards — a bounded, non-empty feasible region always guarantees both the maximum and minimum exist; the concern about non-existence only applies to unbounded regions.

questions.topic: Corner Point Method: Finding the Optimal (Maximum or Minimum) Value
questions.question: For the objective function \(Z=3x+5y\), what is the value of \(Z\) at the corner point \((4,3)\)?
questions.hint: Multiply each coordinate by its matching coefficient, then add.
distractor_logic: Swaps the coefficients between \(x\) and \(y\), computing \(5(4)+3(3)=20+9=29\)... this option instead reflects using \(5(4)+3(3)\) miscalculated as 35, a coefficient-swap arithmetic slip.
Adds instead of multiplying correctly for one term — a slip such as computing \(3(4)+5+3\) instead of \(3(4)+5(3)\).
Only computes the \(y\)-term's contribution scaled incorrectly, dropping the \(x\)-term's contribution from the sum.

questions.topic: Corner Point Method: Finding the Optimal (Maximum or Minimum) Value
questions.question: A LPP asks to \(\textbf{maximise}\) \(Z\). At its three corner points \(A\), \(B\), \(C\), the values are \(Z(A)=0\), \(Z(B)=32\), \(Z(C)=41\). What is the maximum value of \(Z\)?
questions.explanation: Since the problem asks to maximise \(Z\), the answer is the \(\textbf{largest}\) of the computed corner values: \(\max(0,32,41)=41\), attained at corner \(C\).
questions.hint: "Maximise" always means picking the largest of the values you computed — check you're not picking the smallest or a middle value by mistake.
distractor_logic: This value was never actually computed at any of the three corner points — it does not appear among \(Z(A)\), \(Z(B)\), \(Z(C)\) at all.
Picks the second-largest value instead of the true largest — a value that was genuinely computed at a corner, but not the correct one for a maximisation problem.
Picks the smallest of the three values, the opposite of what "maximise" requires — this is exactly the value that would be correct if the problem asked to minimise instead.

questions.topic: Corner Point Method: Finding the Optimal (Maximum or Minimum) Value
questions.question: A LPP asks to \(\textbf{minimise}\) \(Z\). At its three corner points \(A\), \(B\), \(C\), the values are \(Z(A)=12\), \(Z(B)=27\), \(Z(C)=19\). What is the minimum value of \(Z\)?
questions.explanation: Since the problem asks to minimise \(Z\), the answer is the \(\textbf{smallest}\) of the computed corner values: \(\min(12,27,19)=12\), attained at corner \(A\).
questions.hint: "Minimise" always means picking the smallest of the values you computed — the opposite of the rule for a maximisation problem.
distractor_logic: This value was never actually computed at any of the three corner points — it does not appear among \(Z(A)\), \(Z(B)\), \(Z(C)\) at all.
Picks the largest of the three values, the opposite of what "minimise" requires — this is exactly the value that would be correct if the problem asked to maximise instead.
Picks the middle value instead of the true smallest — a value that was genuinely computed at a corner, but not the correct one for a minimisation problem.

questions.topic: Corner Point Method: Finding the Optimal (Maximum or Minimum) Value
questions.question: The feasible region for Maximise \(Z=2x+3y\) subject to \(x+y\le6,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\) has corner points \((0,0)\), \((0,6)\), and \((6,0)\). What is the maximum value of \(Z\)?
questions.hint: Evaluate \(Z\) at all three corners first, then compare — don't stop after checking just one or two.
distractor_logic: The correct location \((0,6)\) is identified, but the \(Z\)-value itself is miscalculated as 20 instead of the correct \(2(0)+3(6)=18\).
This IS the correct location \((6,0)\) among the three, but its \(Z\)-value of \(12\) is the SMALLEST of the three, not the largest — picking it as the maximum reverses the comparison.
This is the correct location for the minimum of \(Z\) (where \(Z=0\)) but is picked here as though it were the maximum, the opposite of what's needed.

questions.topic: Corner Point Method: Finding the Optimal (Maximum or Minimum) Value
questions.question: After the feasible region of an LPP has been graphed, what is the very \(\textbf{first}\) step of the corner point method?
options: Identify (list out) all the corner points (vertices) of the feasible region
Draw the objective function line \(Z=ax+by\) for several different values of \(Z\) and see which one looks best
Immediately state the final maximum or minimum value of \(Z\) by inspection of the graph
Delete any constraint that looks redundant before doing anything else
questions.explanation: The corner point method proceeds in a fixed order: first find (list) every corner point of the feasible region, then evaluate the objective function \(Z\) at each one, and finally compare those values to pick the maximum or minimum, as required.
questions.hint: The method has to know WHERE to evaluate \(Z\) before it can evaluate anything — so listing the vertices comes first.
distractor_logic: This describes a slower graphical approach (the iso-profit/iso-cost line method) rather than the standard corner point method, and is not the first step of the corner point method specifically.
Reading off the optimal value directly from the graph "by inspection" is not the corner point method at all, and is unreliable and imprecise compared to the actual evaluate-and-compare procedure.

Identifying redundant constraints is not part of the standard corner point procedure, and skipping straight to this step (before even finding the corner points) is out of order and unnecessary for solving the LPP.

questions.topic: Corner Point Method: Finding the Optimal (Maximum or Minimum) Value
questions.question: In a \(\textbf{maximisation}\) problem, once \(Z\) has been evaluated at every corner point of a bounded feasible region, the optimal value of \(Z\) is:
options: The smallest of all the computed corner-point values
The value at whichever corner point is closest to the origin
The largest of all the computed corner-point values
The average of all the computed corner-point values
questions.explanation: For a maximisation problem, the Corner Point Theorem says the optimal value is the largest among the values of \(Z\) computed at all the corner points.
questions.hint: "Maximise" and "largest" go together; keep this paired with the opposite pairing for minimisation problems.
distractor_logic: This is the correct rule for a MINIMISATION problem, not a maximisation one — applying it here reverses the required comparison.
Distance from the origin has no bearing on which corner point gives the optimal value of \(Z\) — only the actual computed value of \(Z\) at each corner matters.
There is no rule involving averaging the corner-point values in the corner point method; the method only ever compares values, it does not average them.

questions.topic: Bounded and Unbounded Feasible Regions
questions.question: A feasible region is called \(\textbf{bounded}\) if:
options: It contains the origin
It can be enclosed within some sufficiently large circle (or rectangle) — that is, both \(x\) and \(y\) stay within some finite range over the whole region
Every constraint in the problem is of the \(\le\) type
It has at least 3 corner points
questions.explanation: A feasible region is bounded when it can be entirely enclosed within a sufficiently large circle (equivalently, a large enough rectangle) — meaning neither \(x\) nor \(y\) can grow without limit anywhere in the region. If no such enclosing circle exists, the region is unbounded.
questions.hint: Ask: could you draw a big enough circle around the whole shaded region and have it completely fit inside?
distractor_logic: Whether the origin lies inside the region has nothing to do with boundedness — a region can be bounded without containing the origin, or unbounded while containing it.
This is a common but false shortcut — a region can have only \(\le\) constraints and still be unbounded, for example if a variable has no upper bound placed on it at all.
The number of corner points does not determine boundedness — some unbounded regions still have several corner points, and some bounded regions have as few as 3.

questions.topic: Bounded and Unbounded Feasible Regions
questions.question: A feasible region is called \(\textbf{unbounded}\) if:
options: It \(\textbf{cannot}\) be enclosed within any circle or rectangle, however large — at least one of \(x\) or \(y\) can be made arbitrarily large within the region
The objective function has no coefficients
It has no corner points at all
It lies entirely below the \(x\)-axis
questions.explanation: A feasible region is unbounded when it extends indefinitely in at least one direction — no matter how large a circle you draw, some part of the region always lies outside it, because \(x\) and/or \(y\) can be made arbitrarily large while remaining feasible.
questions.hint: Try to imagine "escaping" further and further from the origin while staying inside the shaded region — if you always can, it's unbounded.
distractor_logic: Every objective function \(Z=ax+by\) has coefficients \(a\) and \(b\) by definition; this has nothing to do with whether the feasible region is bounded.
Unbounded regions still typically have corner points (often just fewer than a bounded region of similar complexity) — having corner points does not by itself indicate boundedness or unboundedness.
In an LPP, \(y\ge0\) means the feasible region lies in the upper half-plane (\(y\ge0\)), never below the \(x\)-axis, regardless of whether the region is bounded or unbounded.

questions.topic: Bounded and Unbounded Feasible Regions
questions.question: If the feasible region of an LPP is \(\textbf{unbounded}\), which statement is correct?
options: Neither the maximum nor the minimum of the objective function can ever exist
The objective function's maximum and/or minimum may or may not exist — this must be checked separately using the half-plane verification step, rather than assumed from the corner points alone
Both the maximum and the minimum of the objective function are guaranteed to exist, just as with a bounded region
The corner point method cannot be applied at all to an unbounded region
questions.explanation: Unboundedness does not automatically rule out an optimal value — a minimum may still exist (and a maximum may not), or vice versa, entirely depending on the objective function's coefficients and the shape of the region. This is exactly why an extra verification step (checking whether an open half-plane beyond the candidate optimal value meets the feasible region) is required whenever the region is unbounded.
questions.hint: "Unbounded" is not automatically "no optimum" — it just means the usual corner-point comparison alone isn't enough; an extra check is required.
distractor_logic: This overstates the case — many unbounded regions genuinely DO have a minimum (or maximum) value; the correct rule is that it must be checked, not that it never exists.
This is the guarantee that applies to BOUNDED regions, not unbounded ones — for an unbounded region, at least one of the maximum/minimum can fail to exist.

The corner point method still applies to locate the CANDIDATE optimal value among the vertices of an unbounded region; it is only the final confirmation step (the half-plane check) that needs to be added on top.

questions.topic: Bounded and Unbounded Feasible Regions
questions.question: The feasible region defined by \(x\le5,\ y\le4,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\) is:
options: Unbounded — \(x\) can be made arbitrarily large
Unbounded — \(y\) can be made arbitrarily large
Neither bounded nor unbounded, since it has no corner points
Bounded — it is a rectangle with corners \((0,0),(0,4),(5,4),(5,0)\)
questions.explanation: Both \(x\) and \(y\) are capped above (\(x\le5\), \(y\le4\)) and below (\(x,y\ge0\)), so the whole region is contained inside the rectangle with corners \((0,0),(0,4),(5,4),(5,0)\) — a bounded region.
questions.hint: Check whether BOTH \(x\) and \(y\) individually have an upper limit stated; here, both do.
distractor_logic: \(x\le5\) explicitly caps \(x\) at 5 — it cannot be made arbitrarily large within this region.
\(y\le4\) explicitly caps \(y\) at 4 — it cannot be made arbitrarily large within this region.
Every non-empty feasible region formed by linear constraints has corner points (at least one); this region in particular has exactly four, so this option is factually wrong on both counts.

questions.topic: Bounded and Unbounded Feasible Regions
questions.question: The feasible region defined by \(x+y\ge5,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\) (with no upper-bound constraint at all) is:
options: Bounded, because \(x+y\ge5\) puts a limit on how large \(x\) and \(y\) can be
Bounded — it forms a triangle with the two axes
Impossible to determine without also knowing the objective function
Unbounded — both \(x\) and \(y\) can be made arbitrarily large while still satisfying \(x+y\ge5\)
questions.explanation: With only a lower-bound constraint \(x+y\ge5\) and no upper limit on either variable, the region extends infinitely away from the origin — for instance \((100,100)\) satisfies \(x+y\ge5\) and remains feasible, so the region is unbounded.
questions.hint: A \(\ge\) constraint (a lower bound) generally does NOT stop \(x\) or \(y\) from growing — it's upper-bound (\(\le\)) constraints that do that.
distractor_logic: This is backwards — \(x+y\ge5\) is a LOWER bound (a minimum requirement), which pushes points AWAY from a small region, not an upper limit that would cap how large \(x\) and \(y\) can grow.
This confuses the shape with a bounded triangle, but there is no upper-bound constraint here at all to close off the region on the far side — it is a half-plane, not a triangle.

Whether a feasible region is bounded or unbounded depends only on its constraints, not on the objective function — the same feasible region is bounded or unbounded regardless of what \(Z\) is being optimised over it.

questions.topic: Bounded and Unbounded Feasible Regions
questions.question: Which feature of a set of constraints most directly tends to make the resulting feasible region \(\textbf{unbounded}\)?
options: The feasible region touches both coordinate axes
The objective function has two decision variables instead of one
At least one decision variable has no upper-bound (\(\le\)) constraint restricting how large it can grow
The right-hand side constants of the constraints are all positive
questions.explanation: If some direction (increasing \(x\), increasing \(y\), or a combination) is never capped by any \(\le\)-type constraint, the region can extend to infinity in that direction, making it unbounded. Conversely, if every variable (and every relevant combination) is capped above, the region is confined to a bounded area.
questions.hint: Ask which direction, if any, is never "closed off" by an upper limit — that missing limit is what lets the region run to infinity.
distractor_logic: Touching the axes is common to almost every feasible region containing the origin's neighbourhood, whether that region turns out to be bounded or unbounded — it is not a distinguishing feature.
Having two decision variables is standard for every 2-variable LPP studied here, bounded or unbounded — it has no bearing on boundedness by itself.

The sign of the right-hand side constants (positive, negative, or zero) does not by itself determine boundedness — what matters is the direction (\(\le\) or \(\ge\)) and whether every direction is eventually capped.

questions.topic: Bounded and Unbounded Feasible Regions
questions.question: For a \(\textbf{bounded}\) feasible region, which of the following is guaranteed by the Corner Point Theorem?
options: The maximum exists but the minimum may or may not, so an extra check is always required
The optimal value must occur strictly inside the region, never on its boundary
Both the maximum and minimum values of the objective function exist, and each occurs at some corner point — no extra verification step is needed
Neither the maximum nor the minimum can be found using the corner point method
questions.explanation: For a bounded, non-empty feasible region, the Corner Point Theorem guarantees that a linear objective function attains both its maximum and its minimum, and that each occurs at one of the (finitely many) corner points — simply comparing the corner-point values is enough, with no additional half-plane check needed (unlike the unbounded case).
questions.hint: "Bounded" is exactly the condition under which the corner-point comparison, by itself, is guaranteed to be the final answer.
distractor_logic: This description — needing an extra check for the minimum — applies to certain UNBOUNDED regions, not to bounded ones, where both extremes are guaranteed without further verification.

Corner points, by definition, lie on the BOUNDARY of the feasible region (where two edges meet), not in its interior — and the optimal value for a bounded region is always found at one of these boundary vertices.
The corner point method is precisely how both the maximum and minimum ARE found for a bounded region; this option denies the method's basic purpose.

questions.topic: Bounded and Unbounded Feasible Regions
questions.question: The feasible region defined by \(x\ge2,\ y\ge3\) (with no upper-bound constraint on either variable) is:
options: Bounded, forming a rectangle
Unbounded
Bounded, forming a triangle
Empty (infeasible)
questions.explanation: There is no constraint capping how large \(x\) or \(y\) can be — only lower bounds \(x\ge2\) and \(y\ge3\) are given — so the region extends to infinity in the direction of increasing \(x\) and \(y\), making it unbounded.
questions.hint: With only lower-bound constraints and nothing capping the variables from above, ask whether the region can extend forever in some direction.
distractor_logic: This wrongly assumes a rectangle needs closing on all sides automatically forms from just two lower-bound constraints; without any upper-bound constraint, there is nothing to close the rectangle off on the far side.
There are only two boundary lines here (\(x=2\) and \(y=3\)), not the three needed to enclose a triangular area; the region is an open, unbounded corner shape, not a triangle.
The point \((2,3)\) clearly satisfies both \(x\ge2\) and \(y\ge3\), so the region is certainly non-empty; the constraints are not contradictory.

questions.topic: Special Cases: Multiple Optimal Solutions, Infeasible Problems, and Unbounded Optimal Values
questions.question: An LPP is said to be \(\textbf{infeasible}\) when:
options: The feasible region is unbounded, so no maximum exists
There is no point \((x,y)\) that satisfies all the constraints (including non-negativity) simultaneously — the feasible region is empty
There are too many decision variables for the problem to be solved
The objective function has a negative coefficient
questions.explanation: An LPP is infeasible when its constraints are mutually contradictory, so that no point satisfies every one of them at once — graphically, the individual half-planes for each constraint simply do not have any region in common; the feasible region is empty.
questions.hint: "Infeasible" is about the CONSTRAINTS having no common ground at all, not about the objective function or the size of the region.
distractor_logic: This describes the "unbounded optimal value" special case, where the region exists (is non-empty) but stretches to infinity in a direction that keeps increasing \(Z\) — a completely different situation from having no feasible region at all.

The number of decision variables (2 in this course) does not determine feasibility; feasibility is about whether the given constraints can be satisfied together, regardless of how many variables are involved.
A negative coefficient in the objective function is perfectly normal (e.g. representing a cost or a loss) and has no bearing on whether the constraints admit a common feasible region.

questions.topic: Special Cases: Multiple Optimal Solutions, Infeasible Problems, and Unbounded Optimal Values
questions.question: An LPP is said to have \(\textbf{multiple optimal solutions}\) when:
options: The feasible region has more than one corner point in total
The objective function can be written in more than one equivalent way
There is more than one constraint in the problem
More than one point of the feasible region (often an entire edge between two adjacent corner points) gives the same, best value of the objective function
questions.explanation: Multiple optimal solutions occur when the optimal value of \(Z\) is achieved not just at a single corner point but at more than one point — typically, this happens when two adjacent corner points give the same optimal \(Z\)-value, which then means EVERY point on the edge joining them also gives that same value.
questions.hint: This is about the OPTIMAL VALUE being reached at more than one place, not simply about the region having several corners.
distractor_logic: Almost every non-trivial feasible region has more than one corner point (a triangle already has three); this alone says nothing about whether the OPTIMAL value happens to repeat at more than one of them.
Rewriting the objective function algebraically does not change the problem or create additional optimal points; the objective function's actual coefficients are what is fixed for a given LPP.
Having multiple constraints is completely standard for any realistic LPP; it does not by itself cause the objective function to repeat its optimal value at more than one point.

questions.topic: Special Cases: Multiple Optimal Solutions, Infeasible Problems, and Unbounded Optimal Values
questions.question: An LPP is said to have an \(\textbf{unbounded optimal value}\) when:
options: The feasible region is unbounded, and the objective function can be made arbitrarily large (for maximisation) or arbitrarily small (for minimisation) within that region, so no finite optimal value exists
The feasible region is bounded, but the corner points happen to give very large values of \(Z\)
The objective function has more than two terms
The feasible region is unbounded, but the optimal value still exists and happens to be a very large number
questions.explanation: This special case arises specifically when the unboundedness of the feasible region translates directly into the objective function growing (or shrinking) without any limit — there is genuinely no finite maximum (or minimum) to report, unlike ordinary unbounded regions where a finite optimum can still exist after verification.
questions.hint: This is stronger than just "the region is unbounded" — it specifically means \(Z\) itself has no finite optimal value, which must be confirmed by the half-plane check.
distractor_logic: A bounded feasible region always guarantees both a finite maximum and a finite minimum exist (by the Corner Point Theorem), however large the individual corner values happen to be — an "unbounded optimal value" cannot occur for a bounded region.
The number of terms in the objective function (which, for this course, always has exactly two, \(ax\) and \(by\)) has no bearing on whether the optimal value is finite or unbounded.

Confuses "unbounded optimal value" (no finite optimum exists at all) with merely having a large but still finite optimal value — many unbounded regions DO have a perfectly finite optimum once the half-plane check is applied; this special case is specifically when that check fails.

questions.topic: Special Cases: Multiple Optimal Solutions, Infeasible Problems, and Unbounded Optimal Values
questions.question: Geometrically, multiple optimal solutions typically arise when:
options: The feasible region is a perfect square
The feasible region contains the origin
Two constraints happen to have the same right-hand side constant
The objective function's iso-profit (or iso-cost) line \(ax+by=k\) is parallel to one of the edges of the feasible region, and that edge lies on the optimal side of the region
questions.explanation: When the direction of the objective function's line (determined by the ratio of its coefficients) exactly matches the direction of one of the feasible region's edges, that entire edge becomes "tied" for the best value of \(Z\) — every point along it, not just its two endpoints, gives the same optimal value.
questions.hint: Think about sliding the objective-function line across the region: if it's parallel to one edge, it touches that WHOLE edge at the extreme position, not just one corner.
distractor_logic: The specific overall shape of the feasible region (square, triangle, pentagon, etc.) is not what causes multiple optimal solutions — what matters is the relationship between the objective function's direction and the direction of a particular edge.
Whether the feasible region happens to contain the origin has no bearing on whether the objective function's line is parallel to one of its edges.

Two constraints sharing the same right-hand side number is a coincidence of the given data and does not, by itself, make the objective function parallel to any particular edge of the resulting region.

questions.topic: Special Cases: Multiple Optimal Solutions, Infeasible Problems, and Unbounded Optimal Values
questions.question: Graphically, how can you recognise that an LPP is \(\textbf{infeasible}\)?
options: The shaded region extends off the edge of the graph paper
The feasible region has an odd number of corner points
The shaded regions representing the individual constraints, when drawn together, do not overlap anywhere at all — there is no common shaded area
The objective function's iso-profit line does not pass through the origin
questions.explanation: When you shade each constraint's half-plane on the same graph, an infeasible LPP shows up as regions that simply never overlap anywhere — there is no common area satisfying every constraint at once, so no feasible solution (and hence no corner points) can be found.
questions.hint: Look for whether there is ANY region where all the individual shadings overlap together — if there is none, the problem is infeasible.
distractor_logic: This describes an unbounded region (one that keeps extending off the visible part of the graph), not an infeasible one — an unbounded region is still a genuine, non-empty feasible region; infeasibility is about having no feasible region at all.

The number of corner points (odd or even) is not connected to feasibility; an infeasible LPP simply has zero corner points because it has no feasible region at all, regardless of any notion of odd/even.

Whether the objective function's line passes through the origin depends on the arbitrary value of \(Z\) chosen for that line; it has nothing to do with whether the constraints themselves admit a common feasible region.

questions.topic: Special Cases: Multiple Optimal Solutions, Infeasible Problems, and Unbounded Optimal Values
questions.question: If an LPP has multiple optimal solutions, is the \(\textbf{optimal value}\) of the objective function \(Z\) unique?
options: No — the optimal value changes depending on which corner point you check first
No — multiple optimal solutions means \(Z\) itself takes on several different "best" values simultaneously
Yes, but only if the feasible region happens to be a triangle
Yes — the optimal VALUE of \(Z\) is still a single, unique number; what is not unique is the set of points (often infinitely many, along an edge) that achieve that value
questions.explanation: "Multiple optimal solutions" refers to multiple POINTS achieving the best value, not multiple different best VALUES. The optimal value of \(Z\) itself remains one fixed number (for example, \(200\)); it is simply attained at more than one \((x,y)\), typically along an entire edge of the feasible region.
questions.hint: Distinguish carefully between "the value of \(Z\)" (a single number) and "the point(s) that achieve it" (which can be more than one, or even infinitely many).
distractor_logic: The optimal value of \(Z\), once correctly identified via the corner point method, does not depend on the order in which corner points happen to be checked — it is a fixed property of the problem.

Misunderstands the term — "multiple" refers to the number of points achieving the optimum, not the number of distinct "best" \(Z\)-values; \(Z\) does not take on several different optimal values at once.

This special case is not restricted to triangular feasible regions — it can occur for a feasible region of any shape (quadrilateral, pentagon, or even an unbounded region), as long as the objective line happens to be parallel to one of its edges.

questions.topic: Special Cases: Multiple Optimal Solutions, Infeasible Problems, and Unbounded Optimal Values
questions.question: If the constraints of an LPP directly contradict each other — for instance, one constraint requires \(x\ge5\) while another requires \(x\le2\) — the LPP is:
options: Guaranteed to have multiple optimal solutions
Unbounded, since the constraints don't restrict \(x\) to a single value
Still solvable in the usual way, just with a smaller feasible region
Infeasible, since no value of \(x\) can simultaneously satisfy both \(x\ge5\) and \(x\le2\)
questions.explanation: No number can be both at least 5 and at most 2 at the same time, so these two constraints alone already make the feasible region empty — the LPP is infeasible, regardless of what any other constraints say.
questions.hint: Check whether the two stated bounds on \(x\) can ever both be true for the same value of \(x\).
distractor_logic: Multiple optimal solutions require an actual, non-empty feasible region in the first place (with an edge parallel to the objective line); an infeasible LPP has no feasible region at all, so this special case cannot apply.

"Unbounded" describes a region that extends to infinity in some direction — but here, the two constraints together allow NO values of \(x\) at all, which is the opposite situation (an empty region, not an infinitely large one).

With no value of \(x\) satisfying both constraints, there is no feasible region whatsoever to "shrink" — the corner point method cannot be applied at all, since there are no corner points to evaluate.

questions.topic: Special Cases: Multiple Optimal Solutions, Infeasible Problems, and Unbounded Optimal Values
questions.question: Besides the "ordinary" case of a single, unique optimal solution at one corner point, which \(\textbf{three}\) special cases can an LPP fall into?
options: Infeasibility (no feasible region at all), multiple optimal solutions (the optimum is attained along a whole edge), and unbounded optimal value (no finite optimum exists despite a non-empty feasible region)
Maximisation-only, minimisation-only, and dual-objective LPPs
Linear, quadratic, and exponential LPPs
Bounded, semi-bounded, and doubly-bounded LPPs
questions.explanation: The three special cases that can occur, beyond the usual situation of a single optimal corner point, are: (1) infeasibility — no feasible region exists at all; (2) multiple optimal solutions — the optimal value is attained at more than one point; and (3) unbounded optimal value — the feasible region is non-empty but the objective function has no finite optimum over it.
questions.hint: These three names correspond exactly to the topic title being studied here — recall them as a set.
distractor_logic: Every LPP is either a maximisation problem or a minimisation problem (never "dual-objective" with two simultaneous objectives) — this is not what distinguishes the three special cases being asked about here.
"Quadratic" and "exponential" LPPs do not exist within Linear Programming at all — by definition, every LPP studied here has strictly linear objective functions and constraints.

"Semi-bounded" and "doubly-bounded" are not standard classifications used in this topic; the relevant classification of feasible regions is simply bounded versus unbounded (a separate, related topic), not a three-way split like this.

questions.topic: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem: Decision Variables, Objective Function, and Constraints
questions.question: A furniture manufacturer makes tables and chairs. Profit is \(\textbf{₹}250\) per table and \(\textbf{₹}150\) per chair. If \(x\) tables and \(y\) chairs are produced, what is the objective function to be maximised?
questions.explanation: Total profit is (profit per table) \(\times\) (number of tables) plus (profit per chair) \(\times\) (number of chairs): \(Z = 250x + 150y\), to be maximised since profit is being sought.
questions.hint: Match each per-unit profit to the correct variable: \(x\) = tables, ₹250 per table; \(y\) = chairs, ₹150 per chair.
distractor_logic: Swaps the two coefficients — assigns the chair's profit rate to \(x\) (tables) and the table's profit rate to \(y\) (chairs).
Incorrectly assumes both products earn the same combined per-unit profit (₹400 total, split evenly) instead of their actual distinct rates of ₹250 and ₹150.
Uses a minus sign between the profit terms, as if chair production reduced profit, instead of adding both contributions.

questions.topic: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem: Decision Variables, Objective Function, and Constraints
questions.question: A carpenter has \(60\) hours of work-time available per week. Making one table takes \(4\) hours and making one chair takes \(2\) hours. If \(x\) tables and \(y\) chairs are made, which is the correct time constraint?
questions.explanation: Total time used is \(4x+2y\) hours (4 hours per table, 2 hours per chair). This cannot exceed the available \(60\) hours, so the constraint uses \(\le\): \(4x + 2y \le 60\).
questions.hint: Available hours is an upper limit on how much time can be USED, so total time used must be \(\textit{at most}\) 60.
distractor_logic: Swaps the per-unit times — assigns the table's 4-hour requirement to \(y\) (chairs) and the chair's 2-hour requirement to \(x\) (tables).
Uses \(\ge\) instead of \(\le\) — treats a maximum available resource as if it were a minimum requirement, reversing the direction of the inequality.
Uses a strict equation \(=60\), forcing exactly 60 hours to be used every time, instead of allowing any amount up to that limit.

questions.topic: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem: Decision Variables, Objective Function, and Constraints
questions.question: A diet must contain \(\textbf{at least}\) \(80\) units of vitamin A. If food I contributes \(2\) units per unit consumed \((x)\) and food II contributes \(4\) units per unit consumed \((y)\), the correct constraint on vitamin A is:
questions.explanation: "At least 80 units" is a minimum requirement, so the total vitamin A supplied, \(2x+4y\), must be greater than or equal to 80: \(2x+4y \ge 80\).
questions.hint: "At least" always signals a lower bound — the total must be no smaller than the stated amount.
distractor_logic: Forces vitamin A to equal exactly 80 units, removing the flexibility to supply more than the minimum that "at least" actually allows.
Swaps the per-unit vitamin contributions between food I and food II before applying the (correct) \(\ge\) direction.
Uses \(\le\) — treats a minimum nutritional requirement ("at least") as though it were an upper limit, reversing the correct direction.

questions.topic: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem: Decision Variables, Objective Function, and Constraints
questions.question: A bakery has \(40\ \text{kg}\) of flour available. Each cake needs \(2\ \text{kg}\) and each batch of cookies needs \(1\ \text{kg}\) of flour. If \(x\) cakes and \(y\) batches of cookies are made, the flour constraint is:
questions.explanation: Flour used is \(2x\) kg for cakes plus \(y\) kg for cookie batches, and this cannot exceed the 40 kg available: \(2x+y \le 40\).
questions.hint: Total flour consumed by both products together must stay within the 40 kg on hand.
distractor_logic: Halves the available flour to 20 kg by mistake, instead of using the full 40 kg actually stated.
Uses \(\ge\) — treats the available flour as a minimum requirement rather than an upper supply limit.
Swaps the flour requirements — gives cookies (\(y\)) the cake's 2 kg rate and cakes (\(x\)) the cookie's 1 kg rate.

questions.topic: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem: Decision Variables, Objective Function, and Constraints
questions.question: An investor has a total of \(₹1{,}00{,}000\) to split between two schemes, investing \(x\) rupees in scheme A and \(y\) rupees in scheme B. The correct budget constraint is:
questions.explanation: The total amount invested across both schemes, \(x+y\), cannot exceed the total available capital: \(x+y \le 1{,}00{,}000\), since the investor need not necessarily invest the entire amount.
questions.hint: "A total of ₹1,00,000 available" is a ceiling on total spending, not a requirement to spend it all or a fixed 50-50 split.
distractor_logic: Uses subtraction \(x-y\) instead of the total invested \(x+y\), which does not represent the combined amount put into both schemes.
Incorrectly assumes the ₹1,00,000 must be split exactly in half between the two schemes, when the problem only fixes the total, not the split.
Uses \(\ge\) — treats the total capital as a minimum investment requirement rather than an available ceiling.

questions.topic: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem: Decision Variables, Objective Function, and Constraints
questions.question: A company wants to spend as little as possible on advertising while meeting reach targets. If \(x\) is the number of TV ads (cost ₹5,000 each) and \(y\) is the number of radio ads (cost ₹2,000 each), the correct objective function is:
options: Maximise \(Z = 5000x + 2000y\)
Minimise \(Z = 5000x + 2000y\)
Minimise \(Z = 2000x + 5000y\)
Minimise \(Z = 7000(x+y)\)
questions.explanation: Total advertising cost is \(5000x+2000y\) (cost per ad times number of ads, summed over both media), and since the goal is to spend as little as possible, the objective is to \(\textbf{minimise}\) this: Minimise \(Z=5000x+2000y\).
questions.hint: "As little as possible" always signals minimise, not maximise — check the direction before checking the coefficients.
distractor_logic: Correctly matches the coefficients to \(x\) and \(y\) but uses \(\textit{Maximise}\) instead of \(\textit{Minimise}\), the opposite of what "spend as little as possible" requires.
Swaps the two cost coefficients between TV ads and radio ads before applying the (correct) minimise direction.
Wrongly assumes both ad types cost the same combined rate (₹7,000 total, applied to \(x+y\)) instead of their distinct actual costs of ₹5,000 and ₹2,000.

questions.topic: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem: Decision Variables, Objective Function, and Constraints
questions.question: A farmer has \(50\) acres of land to allocate between growing wheat and growing rice. If he devotes \(x\) acres to wheat and \(y\) acres to rice, which pair correctly identifies the decision variables and the land constraint?
options: Decision variables: kilograms of wheat and rice harvested; constraint: \(x + y \le 50\)
Decision variables: acres under wheat (\(x\)) and acres under rice (\(y\)); constraint: \(x + y = 50\)
Decision variables: acres under wheat (\(x\)) and acres under rice (\(y\)); constraint: \(x + y \le 50\)
Decision variables: acres under wheat (\(x\)) and acres under rice (\(y\)); constraint: \(x + y \ge 50\)
questions.explanation: The quantities being decided are how many acres go to each crop, so \(x\) and \(y\) (acres under wheat and rice) are the decision variables, and since total land used cannot exceed the 50 acres available, the constraint is \(x+y \le 50\).
questions.hint: The farmer is choosing acreage, not the harvest weight — and 50 acres is a maximum available, not a minimum to be reached.
distractor_logic: Confuses the decision variables with the eventual output (harvested kilograms) rather than what is actually being decided (land allocation).
Correctly identifies the decision variables but forces total land used to equal exactly 50 acres, removing the option of leaving some land unused, which "has 50 acres to allocate" does not require.
Correctly identifies the decision variables but flips the constraint direction to \(\ge\), as though the farmer were required to use at least 50 acres of a smaller available plot.

questions.topic: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem: Decision Variables, Objective Function, and Constraints
questions.question: A word problem states: "the number of chairs produced must not exceed twice the number of tables produced." With \(x\) = tables and \(y\) = chairs, the correct constraint is:
options: \(2y \le x\)
\(y \le 2x\)
\(y \ge 2x\)
\(x \le 2y\)
questions.explanation: "Chairs must not exceed twice the tables" means \(y\) (chairs) is at most \(2x\) (twice the tables): \(y \le 2x\).
questions.hint: Identify which variable is being capped ("must not exceed") and what it's being compared to ("twice the number of tables").
distractor_logic: Places the factor of 2 on the wrong side of the inequality (\(2y \le x\) instead of \(y \le 2x\)), which reverses which quantity is actually being doubled.
Uses \(\ge\) instead of \(\le\) — turns an upper limit ("must not exceed") into a lower requirement.
Swaps the roles of \(x\) and \(y\) — caps tables at twice the chairs instead of capping chairs at twice the tables.

questions.topic: Graphical Solution: Feasible Region and Corner Points
questions.question: The feasible region is defined by \(x+y\le8,\ x\le5,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\). Which of the following is the \(\textbf{complete}\) list of its corner points?
questions.explanation: Boundary lines are \(x+y=8\), \(x=5\), and the two axes. Checking all pairwise intersections against every constraint gives exactly four feasible corner points: \((0,0)\), \((0,8)\), the intersection of \(x=5\) and \(x+y=8\) which is \((5,3)\), and \((5,0)\).
questions.hint: Don't forget the corner point formed by \(x=5\) meeting \(x+y=8\) — it isn't on either axis, so it's easy to miss.
distractor_logic: Adds \((8,0)\) as an extra point, but this point violates \(x\le5\) (since \(8>5\)) and so is not actually feasible — it looks like a corner only because it's the \(x\)-intercept of \(x+y=8\) taken in isolation.
Drops \((0,8)\), the \(y\)-axis intercept of \(x+y=8\), treating the region as if it were bounded only by \(x\le5\).
Drops \((5,3)\), the vertex formed by the two non-axis boundary lines \(x=5\) and \(x+y=8\) intersecting — a genuine corner point that is easy to overlook if only axis intercepts are checked.

questions.topic: Graphical Solution: Feasible Region and Corner Points
questions.question: The feasible region is defined by \(x+y\le10,\ y\le6,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\). What is the corner point that lies on \(\textbf{neither}\) axis?
questions.explanation: This corner point is where \(y=6\) meets \(x+y=10\): substituting \(y=6\) gives \(x+6=10 \Rightarrow x=4\), so the point is \((4,6)\), which indeed lies on neither axis.
questions.hint: Set \(y=6\) into \(x+y=10\) and solve for \(x\) — don't swap which variable is fixed at 6.
distractor_logic: This is the \(y\)-axis intercept of \(x+y=10\) taken alone, ignoring that \(y\le6\) caps \(y\) before the line reaches the axis.
Swaps the coordinates of the correct point \((4,6)\), placing 6 first and 4 second instead of the correct order.
This is the \(x\)-axis intercept of \(x+y=10\), which lies on the axis and is a different corner point altogether, not the one asked for.

questions.topic: Graphical Solution: Feasible Region and Corner Points
questions.question: The feasible region is defined by \(3x+2y\le18,\ x+y\le7,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\). How many corner points does this feasible region have?
questions.explanation: The corner points are \((0,0)\), \((0,7)\) [from \(x+y=7\) meeting the \(y\)-axis], \((6,0)\) [from \(3x+2y=18\) meeting the \(x\)-axis], and \((4,3)\) [where the two slanted lines \(3x+2y=18\) and \(x+y=7\) intersect] — a total of 4.
questions.hint: There are 4 boundary lines in total (two constraints plus two axes); check every pair for a feasible intersection.
distractor_logic: Overcounts, likely including an infeasible pairwise intersection (such as the axis intercept of one line ignoring the other, tighter constraint) as if it were a genuine corner point.
Undercounts by one, most likely missing the vertex \((4,3)\) where the two slanted constraint lines meet each other (not an axis).
Severely undercounts, effectively treating the region as a simple two-vertex segment rather than the actual bounded quadrilateral it forms.

questions.topic: Graphical Solution: Feasible Region and Corner Points
questions.question: The feasible region is defined by \(x+y\ge3,\ x+y\le9,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\). Which point is feasible but is \(\textbf{NOT}\) a corner point of this region?
questions.explanation: \((4,4)\) gives \(x+y=8\), which satisfies \(3\le8\le9\), so it is feasible — but it lies strictly inside the strip between the two boundary lines, not at a meeting point of two edges, so it is not a corner point. The actual corner points are \((3,0)\), \((9,0)\), \((0,9)\), and \((0,3)\).
questions.hint: Check whether each point lies exactly where two boundary lines cross, or just somewhere inside the feasible band between them.
distractor_logic: This IS one of the true corner points, the \(y\)-axis intercept of \(x+y=9\) — incorrectly picked as the exception.
This IS one of the true corner points, the \(y\)-axis intercept of \(x+y=3\) — incorrectly picked as the exception.
This IS one of the true corner points, formed where \(x+y=3\) meets the \(x\)-axis — incorrectly picked as the exception.

questions.topic: Graphical Solution: Feasible Region and Corner Points
questions.question: The feasible region is defined by \(2x+3y\le24,\ x\le9,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\). Find the corner point formed by the intersection of \(x=9\) and \(2x+3y=24\).
questions.explanation: Substituting \(x=9\) into \(2x+3y=24\): \(18+3y=24 \Rightarrow 3y=6 \Rightarrow y=2\), giving the point \((9,2)\).
questions.hint: Substitute \(x=9\) directly into the equation of the slanted line and solve for \(y\).
distractor_logic: This point does satisfy \(2x+3y=24\) but not \(x=9\) — it is a point on the slanted line only, not the actual intersection asked for.
This is the \(y\)-axis intercept of \(2x+3y=24\), found by setting \(x=0\) instead of the required \(x=9\).
This is the \(x\)-axis intercept of \(x=9\) alone (ignoring the slanted constraint entirely), not the intersection of the two given lines.

questions.topic: Graphical Solution: Feasible Region and Corner Points
questions.question: The feasible region is defined by \(x+y\le9,\ 2x+y\le14,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\). What is the corner point formed by the two slanted constraint lines meeting each other?
