questions.explanation: Solving \(x+y=9\) and \(2x+y=14\) simultaneously: subtracting gives \(x=5\), and then \(y=9-5=4\), so the intersection is \((5,4)\).
questions.hint: Subtract one equation from the other to eliminate \(y\) first, then back-substitute.
distractor_logic: This is the \(x\)-axis intercept of \(2x+y=14\) alone, not the intersection of the two slanted lines together.
This is the \(y\)-axis intercept of \(x+y=9\) alone, not the intersection of the two slanted lines together.
Swaps the coordinates of the correct answer \((5,4)\) into \((4,5)\), most likely from solving for the wrong variable first.

questions.topic: Graphical Solution: Feasible Region and Corner Points
questions.question: The feasible region is defined by \(x+y\ge5,\ 3x+2y\le24,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\). Which of these is \(\textbf{NOT}\) a corner point of the feasible region?
questions.explanation: Check where \(x+y=5\) meets \(3x+2y=24\): solving gives \(x=14,y=-9\), which is infeasible (negative \(y\)), so the two slanted lines do not meet inside the first quadrant at all here. The true corner points are only \((0,5)\), \((0,12)\), \((5,0)\), and \((8,0)\); \((4,4)\) satisfies both inequalities but is not where any two boundary lines actually cross.
questions.hint: Two constraint lines only give a genuine corner point if they intersect at a point that ALSO satisfies every other constraint — check that intersection's coordinates directly.
distractor_logic: \((0,5)\) IS a genuine corner point, the \(y\)-axis intercept of \(x+y=5\) — incorrectly picked as the exception.
\((0,12)\) IS a genuine corner point, the \(y\)-axis intercept of \(3x+2y=24\) — incorrectly picked as the exception.
\((8,0)\) IS a genuine corner point, the \(x\)-axis intercept of \(3x+2y=24\) — incorrectly picked as the exception.

questions.topic: Graphical Solution: Feasible Region and Corner Points
questions.question: The feasible region is defined by \(x+2y\ge6,\ x+y\le10,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\). How many corner points does this feasible region have?
questions.explanation: Checking all pairwise intersections of \(x+2y=6\), \(x+y=10\), and the two axes against every constraint gives exactly four feasible corner points: \((0,3)\), \((0,10)\), \((6,0)\), and \((10,0)\).
questions.hint: List every boundary-line pair, find each intersection, then discard any that fails one of the given inequalities.
distractor_logic: Undercounts by one, most likely by merging two distinct axis-intercept points into one or missing a valid vertex.

Overcounts by treating the intersection of the two slanted lines as an additional corner point, even though (as here) that intersection may fall outside the feasible region (or, as in this case, the two lines meet at a point where \(y\) is negative, so it's not counted at all).
Substantially overcounts by including points that do not lie on the actual boundary of this region.

questions.topic: Corner Point Method: Finding the Optimal (Maximum or Minimum) Value
questions.question: A furniture maker's feasible region for Maximise \(Z=3x+5y\) has corner points \((0,0)\), \((0,600)\), \((800,600)\), \((1000,500)\), and \((1500,0)\). What is the maximum value of \(Z\)?
questions.hint: Evaluate \(Z\) at all five corner points before comparing — two of the values are close (5400 and 5500), so don't stop early.
distractor_logic: Correctly computes \(Z=5400\) at \((800,600)\), a genuine corner-point value, but this is the second-largest, not the true maximum — stopping the comparison one corner too early.
Correctly computes \(Z=3000\) at \((0,600)\), a genuine corner-point value, but it is the smallest of the five, not the maximum.
Correctly computes \(Z=4500\) at \((1500,0)\), a genuine corner-point value, but it is far from the largest among the five.

questions.topic: Corner Point Method: Finding the Optimal (Maximum or Minimum) Value
questions.question: A transport company's feasible region for Minimise \(Z=5x+3y\) has corner points \((0,30)\), \((0,40)\), \((30,0)\), \((40,0)\), and \((40,40)\). What is the minimum value of \(Z\)?
questions.hint: Evaluate \(Z\) at every corner and pick the SMALLEST value, since this is a minimisation problem.
distractor_logic: Correctly computes \(Z=120\) at \((0,40)\), a genuine corner-point value, but it is not the smallest — \((0,30)\) gives a lower value still.
Correctly computes \(Z=320\) at \((40,40)\), the LARGEST of the five values — picking it as the minimum reverses the required comparison entirely.
Correctly computes \(Z=150\) at \((30,0)\), a genuine corner-point value, but it is far from the minimum.

questions.topic: Corner Point Method: Finding the Optimal (Maximum or Minimum) Value
questions.question: The feasible region for Maximise \(Z=5x+4y\) subject to \(2x+3y\le30,\ x+y\le12,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\) has corner points \((0,0)\), \((0,10)\), \((6,6)\), and \((12,0)\). What is the maximum value of \(Z\)?
questions.hint: Don't assume the "interior-looking" corner such as \((6,6)\) is automatically the best — compare all four values directly.
distractor_logic: Correctly computes \(Z=40\) at \((0,10)\), a genuine corner-point value, but it is well below the maximum.
This is the value at the origin, the SMALLEST of the four — picking it as the maximum reverses the required comparison.
Correctly computes \(Z=54\) at \((6,6)\), a genuine corner-point value, but it is the second-largest, not the true maximum.

questions.topic: Corner Point Method: Finding the Optimal (Maximum or Minimum) Value
questions.question: The feasible region for Minimise \(Z=2x+3y\) subject to \(x\le5,\ y\le4,\ x+y\ge3,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\) has corner points \((0,3)\), \((0,4)\), \((3,0)\), \((5,0)\), and \((5,4)\). What is the minimum value of \(Z\)?
questions.hint: Compute \(Z\) at all five corners before deciding — the smallest value isn't necessarily at the corner closest to the \(y\)-axis.
distractor_logic: Correctly computes \(Z=9\) at \((0,3)\), a genuine corner-point value, but it is not the smallest — \((3,0)\) gives a lower value still.
Correctly computes \(Z=10\) at \((5,0)\), a genuine corner-point value, but it is not the minimum.
This is the LARGEST of the five values, at \((5,4)\) — picking it as the minimum reverses the required comparison entirely.

questions.topic: Corner Point Method: Finding the Optimal (Maximum or Minimum) Value
questions.question: The feasible region for Maximise \(Z=6x+5y\) subject to \(x+y\le9,\ 2x+y\le14,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\) has corner points \((0,0)\), \((0,9)\), \((5,4)\), and \((7,0)\). What is the maximum value of \(Z\)?
questions.hint: The optimal corner isn't always an axis intercept — here it's the point where the two slanted constraint lines meet.
distractor_logic: Correctly computes \(Z=45\) at \((0,9)\), a genuine corner-point value, but it is the second-largest, not the true maximum.
Correctly computes \(Z=42\) at \((7,0)\), a genuine corner-point value, but it falls short of the maximum at \((5,4)\).
This is the value at the origin, the smallest of the four — picking it as the maximum reverses the required comparison.

questions.topic: Corner Point Method: Finding the Optimal (Maximum or Minimum) Value
questions.question: The feasible region for Maximise \(Z=8x+6y\) subject to \(3x+2y\le18,\ x+y\le7,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\) has corner points \((0,0)\), \((0,7)\), \((4,3)\), and \((6,0)\). What is the maximum value of \(Z\)?
questions.hint: The two largest values here are close (50 and 48) — compute both fully and carefully rather than estimating.
distractor_logic: Correctly computes \(Z=42\) at \((0,7)\), a genuine corner-point value, but well below the maximum.
This is the value at the origin, the smallest of the four — picking it as the maximum reverses the required comparison.
Correctly computes \(Z=48\) at \((6,0)\), a genuine corner-point value very close to the true maximum, but still second-largest, not the maximum itself.

questions.topic: Corner Point Method: Finding the Optimal (Maximum or Minimum) Value
questions.question: The feasible region for Maximise \(Z=4x+3y\) subject to \(x+y\le11,\ x+2y\le16,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\) has corner points \((0,0)\), \((0,8)\), \((6,5)\), and \((11,0)\). What is the maximum value of \(Z\)?
questions.hint: Here the axis intercept beats the "interior-looking" corner — check all four values rather than assuming the corner where two slanted lines meet is always best.
distractor_logic: Correctly computes \(Z=24\) at \((0,8)\), a genuine corner-point value, but far below the maximum.

Correctly computes \(Z=39\) at \((6,5)\), a genuine corner-point value, but it is the second-largest, not the true maximum — the corner point where two constraint lines meet is not automatically optimal.
This is the value at the origin, the smallest of the four — picking it as the maximum reverses the required comparison.

questions.topic: Corner Point Method: Finding the Optimal (Maximum or Minimum) Value
questions.question: The feasible region for Maximise \(Z=5x+2y\) subject to \(3x+y\le21,\ x+y\le9,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\) has corner points \((0,0)\), \((0,9)\), \((6,3)\), and \((7,0)\). What is the maximum value of \(Z\)?
questions.hint: These two candidate values are only 1 apart (36 vs 35) — recompute each carefully rather than rounding or estimating.
distractor_logic: This is the value at the origin, the smallest of the four — picking it as the maximum reverses the required comparison.
Correctly computes \(Z=18\) at \((0,9)\), a genuine corner-point value, but well below the maximum.

questions.topic: Bounded and Unbounded Feasible Regions
questions.question: Is the feasible region defined by \(x+2y\ge10,\ 3x+4y\le24,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\) bounded or unbounded?
options: Cannot be determined without first finding the corner points
Unbounded — because \(x+2y\ge10\) is a \(\ge\)-type constraint
Unbounded — because there are two different constraints acting together
Bounded — the constraint \(3x+4y\le24\) together with \(x,y\ge0\) already confines the region to a triangle, and \(x+2y\ge10\) can only trim part of that triangle away, not extend it
questions.explanation: Even though \(x+2y\ge10\) is a lower-bound constraint, the other constraint \(3x+4y\le24\) (with \(x,y\ge0\)) already forms a bounded triangle with vertices \((0,0)\), \((8,0)\), \((0,6)\). Adding \(x+2y\ge10\) can only remove part of that triangle (the part near the origin) — it cannot make the resulting region extend beyond the already-bounded triangle. So the overall region remains bounded.
questions.hint: Don't judge boundedness from a single constraint in isolation — check whether the FULL set of constraints together still traps the region inside a finite area.
distractor_logic: Boundedness can (and should) be reasoned about directly from the constraints themselves before ever computing corner points; here, one constraint alone already guarantees a bounded triangle.
Jumps to "unbounded" purely because one constraint happens to be of the \(\ge\) type, without checking whether the OTHER constraints already confine the region regardless.
The presence of two constraints together does not by itself indicate unboundedness; what matters is whether, together, they leave some direction uncapped — here they do not.

questions.topic: Bounded and Unbounded Feasible Regions
questions.question: Is the feasible region defined by \(x+y\ge4,\ x+2y\ge6,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\) bounded or unbounded?
options: Bounded, because two constraints together are always enough to close off a region
Bounded — it forms a quadrilateral with the two axes
Cannot be determined without knowing the objective function
Unbounded — both constraints are lower bounds with no \(\le\)-type constraint capping \(x\) or \(y\) from above
questions.explanation: Both constraints, \(x+y\ge4\) and \(x+2y\ge6\), only impose lower bounds, and there is no upper-bound constraint anywhere to cap \(x\) or \(y\); as a result, points like \((100,100)\) remain feasible, and the region stretches to infinity, making it unbounded.
questions.hint: Two lower-bound (\(\ge\)) constraints alone, with no \(\le\) constraint present, can never close off a region on the far side.
distractor_logic: Having two constraints is not by itself sufficient to guarantee a bounded region — what matters is whether at least one of them (or their combination) actually caps the variables from above, which neither does here.

Wrongly assumes the two constraint lines plus the axes automatically form a closed quadrilateral shape; without any upper-bound constraint, the true region actually extends away to infinity instead of closing up.
As with all boundedness questions, the answer depends only on the constraints defining the feasible region, not on the objective function chosen to optimise over it.

questions.topic: Bounded and Unbounded Feasible Regions
questions.question: Is the feasible region defined by \(6x+10y\ge60,\ y\le8,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\) bounded or unbounded?
options: Unbounded, because \(y\le8\) is an unusual constraint to include
Unbounded — \(x\) has no upper-bound constraint at all, so it can be made arbitrarily large while \(y\) stays within \([0,8]\)
Bounded — because \(6x+10y\ge60\) eventually limits \(x\)
Bounded — because \(y\le8\) caps one of the two variables
questions.explanation: \(y\le8\) only caps \(y\); there is no constraint capping \(x\) from above, so for any \(y\in[0,8]\), choosing \(x\) large enough that \(6x+10y\ge60\) is easily satisfied and \(x\) can grow without bound — the region is unbounded (extending to the right).
questions.hint: Capping only ONE of the two variables is not enough to guarantee a bounded region — check whether the OTHER variable is left completely free to grow.
distractor_logic: There is nothing unusual about a \(y\le8\)-type constraint appearing in an LPP; the region's unboundedness here comes from the complete absence of any upper limit on \(x\), not from this constraint being present.
\(6x+10y\ge60\) is a LOWER bound — it requires the sum to be at least 60, which large \(x\) values satisfy easily; it does not cap \(x\) from above at all.
Capping just \(y\) alone is not sufficient for boundedness — \(x\) remains completely free to increase without limit, which alone makes the region unbounded.

questions.topic: Bounded and Unbounded Feasible Regions
questions.question: Is the feasible region defined by \(2x+y\ge8,\ x+2y\ge10,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\) bounded or unbounded?
options: Cannot be determined without solving for the corner points first
Unbounded — both constraints only impose lower bounds, leaving the region free to extend to infinity away from the origin
Bounded — because both right-hand sides (8 and 10) are positive numbers
Bounded — the two lines intersect at a single point, so the region is a triangle
questions.explanation: With only two \(\ge\)-type constraints and no upper bound on either variable, points such as \((100,100)\) remain feasible (both \(2(100)+100=300\ge8\) and \(100+2(100)=300\ge10\)), so the region extends indefinitely and is unbounded.
questions.hint: The two lines DO intersect at one point, but that intersection is just ONE corner — check whether the region is closed off on all sides, or open toward infinity beyond that point.
distractor_logic: Boundedness can be determined directly by reasoning about the constraints (whether every direction is capped) without needing to compute the corner points first.

The sign of the right-hand side constants has no bearing on boundedness — what determines it is the direction of each inequality and whether every direction is eventually capped, which is not the case here.

The two lines intersecting at a single point only gives one corner of the region; without an upper-bound constraint, the boundary continues away from that point to infinity in two directions rather than closing into a triangle.

questions.topic: Bounded and Unbounded Feasible Regions
questions.question: Is the feasible region defined by \(2x+y\le10,\ x+3y\le15,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\) bounded or unbounded?
options: Bounded — both constraints are upper bounds, together with \(x,y\ge0\) they enclose a quadrilateral region
Unbounded — because the coefficients of \(x\) and \(y\) differ between the two constraints
Cannot be determined without first checking the objective function
Unbounded — because there are two separate constraints
questions.explanation: Both constraints are of the \(\le\) type, capping \(2x+y\) and \(x+3y\) respectively; combined with \(x,y\ge0\), this fully encloses the feasible region into a finite quadrilateral with corners \((0,0)\), \((0,5)\), \((3,4)\), and \((5,0)\).
questions.hint: Both constraints here cap the variables from above — check whether that's enough to close the region off entirely.
distractor_logic: Different coefficients between constraints (like 2 vs 1, or 1 vs 3) do not affect whether the region is bounded — only the direction (\(\le\) vs \(\ge\)) and whether every direction is capped matters.
Boundedness is a property of the feasible region determined purely by its constraints; it does not depend on which objective function is later optimised over that same region.
Having two constraints is not a sign of unboundedness by itself — what matters is the direction of each inequality, and here both are \(\le\)-type upper bounds that close the region off.

questions.topic: Bounded and Unbounded Feasible Regions
questions.question: Is the feasible region defined by \(x+y\le12{,}000,\ x\le8{,}000,\ y\le8{,}000,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\) bounded or unbounded?
options: Unbounded — because the right-hand side values (12,000 and 8,000) are large numbers
Bounded, but only if \(x\) and \(y\) are restricted to whole numbers
Unbounded — because three separate constraints are given instead of just one or two
Bounded — every constraint is an upper bound, so \(x\) and \(y\) are both confined to finite ranges
questions.explanation: All three constraints, \(x+y\le12{,}000\), \(x\le8{,}000\), and \(y\le8{,}000\), are upper bounds; together with \(x,y\ge0\), they confine the entire feasible region within a finite pentagon — there is no direction in which \(x\) or \(y\) can grow without eventually violating one of them.
questions.hint: Count how many of the given constraints are upper bounds (\(\le\)) versus lower bounds (\(\ge\)) — here, every single one caps the variables from above.
distractor_logic: The actual size of the right-hand side numbers (large or small) has no bearing on boundedness — a region bounded by \(x\le8{,}000\) is just as bounded as one bounded by \(x\le8\); only the direction of the inequality matters.

Boundedness of the feasible region has nothing to do with whether the decision variables are restricted to integers; it is a purely geometric property of the region itself, which is finite here regardless.
Having more constraints does not make a region unbounded — if anything, additional \(\le\)-type constraints tend to shrink the region further, not extend it.

questions.topic: Bounded and Unbounded Feasible Regions
questions.question: Is the feasible region defined by \(x+y\ge5,\ 3x+2y\le24,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\) bounded or unbounded?
options: Bounded — \(3x+2y\le24\) together with \(x,y\ge0\) already forms a bounded triangle, and \(x+y\ge5\) only removes the corner near the origin from it
Bounded, but only because \(x+y\ge5\) happens to be a smaller number than 24
Unbounded — because \(x+y\ge5\) is a lower-bound constraint
Unbounded — because the two constraint lines have different slopes
questions.explanation: \(3x+2y\le24\) with \(x,y\ge0\) already forms a bounded triangle with vertices \((0,0)\), \((8,0)\), \((0,12)\). Adding the lower bound \(x+y\ge5\) can only cut off the small corner of that triangle near the origin — it cannot extend the region beyond the triangle's already-finite boundary, so the resulting region stays bounded.
questions.hint: As before, check whether the \(\le\)-type constraint already confines the region on its own, before worrying about the \(\ge\)-type constraint layered on top.
distractor_logic: The specific numeric comparison between the two right-hand sides (5 versus 24) is irrelevant to boundedness; what matters is that \(3x+2y\le24\) alone already guarantees a finite triangle, regardless of what number appears on the other constraint.
Wrongly concludes unboundedness purely from the presence of a \(\ge\)-type constraint, without checking that the accompanying \(\le\)-type constraint already confines the whole region regardless.

The relative slopes (steepness) of the two boundary lines have no bearing on whether the resulting region is bounded — what matters is whether some direction is left uncapped, which is not the case here.

questions.topic: Bounded and Unbounded Feasible Regions
questions.question: Is the feasible region defined by \(y\le10,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\) (with no constraint restricting \(x\) from above) bounded or unbounded?
options: Unbounded — \(x\) is completely free to grow without limit, even though \(y\) is capped at 10
Bounded — because the region still touches both axes
Bounded — because \(y\le10\) is an upper-bound constraint
Cannot be determined since only one constraint besides non-negativity is given
questions.explanation: \(y\le10\) caps only \(y\); since there is no constraint at all restricting how large \(x\) can be, points like \((10^6,\,5)\) remain feasible, and the region extends infinitely to the right — it is unbounded.
questions.hint: One capped variable is not enough — check specifically whether the OTHER variable, \(x\) here, has any upper limit at all.
distractor_logic: Touching the axes near the origin is common to bounded and unbounded regions alike; it says nothing about what happens far from the origin, where this particular region keeps extending.
Having one upper-bound constraint present is not sufficient for the WHOLE region to be bounded — \(x\) remains completely uncapped here, which alone makes the region unbounded.

Boundedness CAN be determined here directly: with only one constraint besides non-negativity, and that constraint capping only \(y\), \(x\) is left completely free, which is already enough to conclude the region is unbounded.

questions.topic: Special Cases: Multiple Optimal Solutions, Infeasible Problems, and Unbounded Optimal Values
questions.question: For Maximise \(Z=4x+4y\) subject to \(x+y\le50,\ 3x+y\le90,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\), the corner points are \((0,0)\), \((0,50)\), \((20,30)\), and \((30,0)\), with \(Z\)-values \(0\), \(200\), \(200\), and \(120\) respectively. What can be concluded?
options: The maximum value of \(Z\) cannot be determined because two corner points tie
This LPP has an unbounded optimal value, since \(Z=200\) is repeated
This LPP has multiple optimal solutions — both \((0,50)\) and \((20,30)\) give the maximum value \(Z=200\), so every point on the edge joining them is also optimal
This LPP is infeasible, since two different corner points give the same value of \(Z\)
questions.explanation: Since \((0,50)\) and \((20,30)\) — two adjacent corner points — both give the largest \(Z\)-value, \(200\), the entire edge of the feasible region connecting them (which lies along \(x+y=50\)) also gives \(Z=200\): the maximum value is uniquely \(200\), but it is attained at infinitely many points, so this LPP has multiple optimal solutions.
questions.hint: A tie between two ADJACENT corner points for the top value is the tell-tale sign of multiple optimal solutions, not a problem to be worried about.
distractor_logic: The maximum value of \(Z\) actually CAN be determined perfectly well here: it is \(200\) — a tie between corner points for the top value does not prevent identifying what that top value is, it only means more than one point achieves it.

"Unbounded optimal value" means \(Z\) can be made arbitrarily large; here, \(Z\) is capped at a genuine finite maximum of \(200\) — the tie between corners does not mean \(Z\) is unbounded, only that the maximum is reached at more than one point.

Infeasibility means having NO feasible points at all; here, the feasible region clearly exists and has several corner points, so this label is simply the wrong special case for what's being described.

questions.topic: Special Cases: Multiple Optimal Solutions, Infeasible Problems, and Unbounded Optimal Values
questions.question: An LPP includes the constraints \(x\ge5\) and \(x\le2\) (along with other conditions). What can immediately be concluded about this LPP?
options: It has multiple optimal solutions, since two separate constraints both involve \(x\)
It has an unbounded optimal value, since \(x\) is restricted from two opposite directions
It is infeasible — no value of \(x\) can satisfy both \(x\ge5\) and \(x\le2\) at once, so the feasible region is empty regardless of the other constraints
It is a perfectly ordinary LPP and can be solved normally by the corner point method
questions.explanation: \(x\ge5\) and \(x\le2\) directly contradict each other; there is no real number that is both at least 5 and at most 2. This alone guarantees the feasible region is empty, making the LPP infeasible, no matter what the remaining constraints say.
questions.hint: Check the two constraints on \(x\) against each other directly — can any single value of \(x\) satisfy both simultaneously?
distractor_logic: Multiple optimal solutions require an actual feasible region with an edge parallel to the objective function's line; a contradictory pair of constraints on the same variable prevents any feasible region from existing at all, ruling this case out.

Being restricted "from two directions" is completely normal for many variables in an LPP (e.g. \(2\le x\le10\) is a perfectly fine, non-empty range) — the issue here is specifically that the two bounds given are contradictory (5 is not less than or equal to 2), not merely that there are two of them.
With the feasible region empty, there are no corner points to evaluate at all, so the corner point method cannot be applied — this cannot be treated as an ordinary, solvable LPP.

questions.topic: Special Cases: Multiple Optimal Solutions, Infeasible Problems, and Unbounded Optimal Values
questions.question: An LPP includes the constraints \(x-y\le-1\) and \(-x+y\le0\) (along with \(x,y\ge0\)). Rewriting these as \(y\ge x+1\) and \(y\le x\), what can be concluded?
options: The feasible region is simply the single line \(y=x\), which is a valid (if unusual) bounded region
The LPP has multiple optimal solutions along the line \(y=x\)
The LPP is infeasible — \(y\) would have to be simultaneously at least \(x+1\) and at most \(x\), which is impossible for any \(x\), so no feasible region exists
The LPP has an unbounded optimal value, since \(y\) is restricted relative to \(x\) rather than by a fixed number
questions.explanation: Since \(x+1>x\) for every real \(x\), the requirement \(y\ge x+1\) always demands a strictly LARGER value of \(y\) than the requirement \(y\le x\) allows; no \(y\) can satisfy both simultaneously, for any \(x\) at all — so the feasible region is empty and the LPP is infeasible.
questions.hint: Compare the two bounds on \(y\) directly: one requires \(y\) to be at least \(x+1\), the other requires \(y\) to be at most \(x\) — can both ever hold together?
distractor_logic: The line \(y=x\) is not actually part of the feasible region at all here: points exactly on it fail \(y\ge x+1\) (since \(x\) is never \(\ge x+1\)); the true feasible region is empty, not a single line.

Multiple optimal solutions require an actual non-empty feasible region with an edge parallel to the objective line; since no feasible region exists here at all, there is nothing for the objective function to be optimised over, let alone tied along a shared edge.

Constraints relating two variables to each other (rather than to a fixed number) are completely ordinary in LPPs and do not by themselves cause unboundedness; the actual issue here is that the two relative bounds on \(y\) directly contradict one another for every value of \(x\).

questions.topic: Special Cases: Multiple Optimal Solutions, Infeasible Problems, and Unbounded Optimal Values
questions.question: For Maximise \(Z=x+y\) subject to \(x\ge1,\ y\ge1\) (with no upper bound on either variable), the only corner point is \((1,1)\), giving \(Z=2\). Checking further, points such as \((10,10)\) give \(Z=20\), and \((1000,1000)\) gives \(Z=2000\). What special case applies here?
options: Unbounded optimal value — the feasible region is non-empty, but \(Z\) can be made arbitrarily large within it, so no finite maximum exists
An ordinary unique optimal solution — the maximum is \(Z=2\), attained at the single corner point \((1,1)\)
Infeasibility — since \((1,1)\) is the only corner point, there aren't enough feasible points for a proper solution
Multiple optimal solutions — since many different points give different values of \(Z\)
questions.explanation: The feasible region here is clearly non-empty (it contains \((1,1)\) and infinitely many other points), so infeasibility does not apply. But as shown by checking points further and further from the origin, \(Z=x+y\) keeps growing without any limit — there is no finite value it approaches, so this LPP has an unbounded optimal value; no maximum exists at all.
questions.hint: "Multiple optimal solutions" means many points share the SAME best value; here, the values keep getting bigger and bigger without any repeat or limit — that's a different situation entirely.
distractor_logic: \(Z=2\) at \((1,1)\) is not actually the maximum at all, since larger feasible points keep giving larger \(Z\)-values without limit; treating \(2\) as "the" optimal value here ignores that no finite maximum genuinely exists.

\((1,1)\) being feasible (and infinitely many other points like \((10,10)\) too) already rules out infeasibility, which requires the feasible region to be completely empty — that is not the case here.

"Multiple optimal solutions" specifically requires several points to share the SAME optimal value; here the values keep increasing without bound (\(2, 20, 2000,\ldots\)) rather than repeating at a fixed best value, so this is a different special case entirely.

questions.topic: Special Cases: Multiple Optimal Solutions, Infeasible Problems, and Unbounded Optimal Values
questions.question: For Minimise \(Z=x+2y\) subject to \(2x+y\ge3,\ x+2y\ge6,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\), the feasible region is unbounded, with corner points \((0,3)\) and \((6,0)\), both giving \(Z=6\). Which special case(s) genuinely apply here?
options: None of the special cases apply; this is an entirely ordinary LPP with a single unique optimum
Infeasibility — since the region is unbounded, it cannot contain a proper feasible solution
Unbounded optimal value — since the region is unbounded, no finite minimum can exist
Multiple optimal solutions — the entire edge between \((0,3)\) and \((6,0)\) gives \(Z=6\); the minimum \(Z=6\) itself DOES still exist despite the region being unbounded
questions.explanation: Both \((0,3)\) and \((6,0)\) give \(Z=6\), and since this edge lies exactly along the constraint line \(x+2y=6\) (which matches the objective function's direction), the entire edge shares this value — multiple optimal solutions. Crucially, even though the FEASIBLE REGION is unbounded, the minimum value \(Z=6\) genuinely exists (verified since every feasible point satisfies \(x+2y\ge6\) directly); an unbounded region does not automatically mean an unbounded optimal value.
questions.hint: Unboundedness of the REGION and unboundedness of the OPTIMAL VALUE are two different things — a region can be unbounded while the optimum still exists and is even tied along an edge.
distractor_logic: This ignores the tie between \((0,3)\) and \((6,0)\), both giving the same optimal value \(Z=6\) — that repetition is exactly the hallmark of multiple optimal solutions, not an "entirely ordinary" single-optimum case.

An empty feasible region is what makes an LPP infeasible; here the region is clearly non-empty (and unbounded, which is a different property entirely) — unboundedness of the region is not the same thing as having no feasible solutions.

Wrongly assumes unboundedness of the feasible region automatically means the optimal value itself is unbounded; here, the minimum genuinely exists (it is confirmed as \(6\)) even though the region stretches to infinity in other directions.

questions.topic: Special Cases: Multiple Optimal Solutions, Infeasible Problems, and Unbounded Optimal Values
questions.question: For Maximise \(Z=2x+3y\) subject to \(2x+3y\le36,\ x+y\le14,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\), the corner points are \((0,0)\), \((0,12)\), \((6,8)\), and \((14,0)\), with \(Z\)-values \(0\), \(36\), \(36\), and \(28\) respectively. What can be concluded, and why does the tie occur?
options: This LPP is infeasible, since two corner points cannot legitimately give the same value

Multiple optimal solutions occur — the tie happens because the objective function \(Z=2x+3y\) has exactly the same coefficients as the binding constraint \(2x+3y\le36\), making the objective line parallel to (in fact, coincide in direction with) that entire edge
Multiple optimal solutions occur, purely by coincidence, with no particular reason connecting the objective function to the constraints
This LPP has an unbounded optimal value, since \(36\) appears twice among the corner values
questions.explanation: \((0,12)\) and \((6,8)\) both give \(Z=36\) because the objective function \(2x+3y\) uses exactly the same coefficients as the constraint \(2x+3y\le36\) that forms the edge between them — the iso-profit line for \(Z=36\) coincides in direction with that whole edge, so every point along it (not just the two corners) also gives \(Z=36\).
questions.hint: Compare the objective function's coefficients directly against each constraint's coefficients — a match (or a constant multiple) is the geometric reason behind a tie like this.
distractor_logic: Two corner points sharing the same value of \(Z\) is not a contradiction or an error — it simply means the optimum is achieved at more than one point, which is exactly what defines the "multiple optimal solutions" case; it has nothing to do with the feasible region being empty.

Correctly identifies multiple optimal solutions but misses the actual geometric reason — the tie is not a coincidence; it happens specifically because the objective function's coefficients match those of the binding constraint, making the two lines parallel.

\(36\) is a genuine, finite maximum value here (confirmed since the region is bounded by \(\le\)-type constraints); an unbounded optimal value would mean \(Z\) keeps growing without any limit, which is not happening — \(Z\) is capped at \(36\), just at more than one point.

questions.topic: Special Cases: Multiple Optimal Solutions, Infeasible Problems, and Unbounded Optimal Values
questions.question: An LPP includes the constraints \(x+y\le2\) and \(x+y\ge10\) (along with \(x,y\ge0\)). What can immediately be concluded?
options: The LPP is ordinary and solvable, since both constraints involve the same expression \(x+y\)
The LPP is infeasible — \(x+y\) cannot be simultaneously at most \(2\) and at least \(10\)
The feasible region is the entire strip between the two lines \(x+y=2\) and \(x+y=10\)
The LPP has an unbounded optimal value, since \(x+y\) is restricted between two extreme values
questions.explanation: No value of \(x+y\) can be both \(\le2\) and \(\ge10\) at the same time (2 is nowhere close to being at least 10), so the two constraints directly contradict each other — the feasible region is empty and the LPP is infeasible.
questions.hint: Compare the two bounds placed on the same combined expression, \(x+y\) — can both hold together for any values of \(x\) and \(y\)?
distractor_logic: Having both constraints reference the same combined expression does not automatically make them compatible; here, comparing the two bounds directly shows they cannot both be satisfied, so the problem is not solvable in the ordinary way.

This describes the region BETWEEN two parallel lines when the lower bound is smaller than the upper bound (like \(2\le x+y\le10\)); here the order is reversed — an upper bound of \(2\) sits below a lower bound of \(10\), leaving no valid strip between them at all.

Being restricted "between two extreme values" is not the issue by itself; the real problem is that \(2\) and \(10\), as an upper and lower bound on the SAME expression, are contradictory (2 is less than 10, so \(x+y\) can't be both at most 2 and at least 10) rather than forming a valid range.

questions.topic: Special Cases: Multiple Optimal Solutions, Infeasible Problems, and Unbounded Optimal Values
questions.question: True or false: "If the feasible region of an LPP is unbounded, then its optimal value is automatically unbounded too."
options: False — an unbounded feasible region can still have a genuine, finite optimal value once verified with the half-plane check; "unbounded region" and "unbounded optimal value" are related but distinct notions
False, because no feasible region can ever be unbounded in the first place
True — unboundedness of the region always transfers directly to the objective function
True, but only for minimisation problems
questions.explanation: The two ideas are related but not the same: the feasible region being unbounded only means the SHAPE extends to infinity; whether \(Z\) itself becomes unbounded over that shape depends on the specific objective function's coefficients relative to the direction the region extends in — a minimum (or maximum) can still very much exist, as confirmed by the half-plane verification.
questions.hint: Region shape and objective-function behaviour are two separate things linked only through the specific coefficients of \(Z\) — unboundedness of one doesn't automatically force unboundedness of the other.
distractor_logic: Unbounded feasible regions certainly can and do occur in LPPs (this is a whole topic in its own right); this option's premise is simply false.

This wrongly assumes an automatic link between the region's shape and the objective function's behaviour; many genuinely unbounded regions still have a perfectly finite optimal value, which is exactly why the half-plane verification step exists.

This restricts the (false) claim to minimisation problems only, but the same reasoning failure applies regardless of whether the problem is a maximisation or a minimisation — unboundedness of the region does not automatically transfer to the objective value in either case.

questions.topic: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem: Decision Variables, Objective Function, and Constraints
questions.question: A firm makes two products, A and B. Each unit of A needs 3 hours of machine time and 1 hour of labour; each unit of B needs 2 hours of machine time and 2 hours of labour. Only 18 hours of machine time and 10 hours of labour are available per day. Profit is ₹60 per unit of A and ₹40 per unit of B. Taking \(x\) = units of A, \(y\) = units of B, which is the \(\textbf{correct complete}\) formulation?
options: Maximise \(Z=60x+40y\) subject to \(3x+2y\ge18,\ x+2y\ge10,\ x,y\ge0\)
Maximise \(Z=60x+40y\) subject to \(3x+2y\le18,\ x+2y\le10,\ x,y\ge0\)
Maximise \(Z=40x+60y\) subject to \(3x+2y\le18,\ x+2y\le10,\ x,y\ge0\)
Minimise \(Z=60x+40y\) subject to \(3x+2y\le18,\ x+2y\le10,\ x,y\ge0\)
questions.explanation: Machine time used is \(3x+2y\), capped at 18 hours: \(3x+2y\le18\). Labour used is \(x+2y\), capped at 10 hours: \(x+2y\le10\). Profit ₹60 per A and ₹40 per B gives \(Z=60x+40y\), and since profit is being sought, it is maximised. The correct complete formulation is therefore Maximise \(Z=60x+40y\) subject to \(3x+2y\le18,\ x+2y\le10,\ x,y\ge0\).
questions.hint: Check all three pieces separately — the objective coefficients, and the direction of BOTH constraints — before picking; a distractor may get most pieces right and only one wrong.
distractor_logic: Keeps the correct objective and coefficients but flips both constraints to \(\ge\), as if the available hours were minimum requirements rather than upper limits on a scarce resource.
Keeps the correct constraints and Maximise direction but swaps the two profit coefficients, assigning B's rate to \(x\) and A's rate to \(y\).
Keeps the correct objective coefficients and constraints but says Minimise instead of Maximise, the opposite of what a profit-seeking firm should do.

questions.topic: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem: Decision Variables, Objective Function, and Constraints
questions.question: A dietician wants the cheapest possible mix of two foods, I and II, that supplies at least 8 units of vitamin A and at least 10 units of vitamin C. Food I has 2 units of A and 1 unit of C per unit consumed and costs ₹5 per unit; food II has 1 unit of A and 2 units of C per unit consumed and costs ₹7 per unit. With \(x\) = units of food I, \(y\) = units of food II, the correct formulation is:
options: Maximise \(Z=5x+7y\) subject to \(2x+y\ge8,\ x+2y\ge10,\ x,y\ge0\)
Minimise \(Z=7x+5y\) subject to \(2x+y\ge8,\ x+2y\ge10,\ x,y\ge0\)
Minimise \(Z=5x+7y\) subject to \(2x+y\ge8,\ x+2y\ge10,\ x,y\ge0\)
Minimise \(Z=5x+7y\) subject to \(2x+y\le8,\ x+2y\le10,\ x,y\ge0\)
questions.explanation: Cost is \(5x+7y\), to be minimised (cheapest mix). Vitamin A supplied is \(2x+y\), needing \(\ge8\); vitamin C supplied is \(x+2y\), needing \(\ge10\). The correct complete formulation is therefore Minimise \(Z=5x+7y\) subject to \(2x+y\ge8,\ x+2y\ge10,\ x,y\ge0\).
questions.hint: "At least" nutrient requirements always give \(\ge\) constraints, regardless of whether the objective itself is a minimisation.
distractor_logic: Keeps the correct \(\ge\) constraints but says Maximise instead of Minimise, the opposite of what "cheapest possible mix" requires.
Keeps the correct Minimise direction and constraints but swaps the two cost coefficients between food I and food II.
Keeps the correct Minimise objective but flips both nutrient constraints to \(\le\), treating "at least" minimum requirements as upper limits.

questions.topic: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem: Decision Variables, Objective Function, and Constraints
questions.question: A company sells two products, P and Q. It can produce at most 200 units of P and at most 150 units of Q per week, and total production of both combined cannot exceed 300 units due to warehouse space. Profit is ₹30 on P and ₹45 on Q. With \(x\)= units of P, \(y\)= units of Q, which formulation is \(\textbf{fully correct}\)?
options: Maximise \(Z=30x+45y\) subject to \(x\le200,\ y\le150,\ x+y\le300,\ x,y\ge0\)
Maximise \(Z=45x+30y\) subject to \(x\le200,\ y\le150,\ x+y\le300,\ x,y\ge0\)
Maximise \(Z=30x+45y\) subject to \(x\le200,\ y\le150,\ x+y\ge300,\ x,y\ge0\)
Maximise \(Z=30x+45y\) subject to \(x\le200,\ y\le150,\ x,y\ge0\)
questions.explanation: There are three separate constraints here: the individual production caps \(x\le200\) and \(y\le150\), AND the combined warehouse cap \(x+y\le300\) — all three must appear together with the correct objective \(Z=30x+45y\).
questions.hint: Count how many separate restrictions the paragraph actually states before matching options — there are three, not two.
distractor_logic: Swaps the two profit coefficients between products P and Q while keeping all three constraints correct.
Flips the warehouse constraint to \(\ge300\), as if the warehouse required at least 300 combined units rather than capping total production at 300.

Drops the warehouse-space constraint \(x+y\le300\) entirely, evaluating the region using only the two individual product caps — an incomplete corner-point list would follow from this missing constraint.

questions.topic: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem: Decision Variables, Objective Function, and Constraints
questions.question: A factory produces two grades of fertiliser, x kg and y kg per day. Grade 1 needs 2 hours of blending and 1 hour of packing per kg; Grade 2 needs 1 hour of blending and 3 hours of packing per kg. Blending capacity is 40 hours/day and packing capacity is 45 hours/day. Cost per kg is ₹20 for Grade 1 and ₹25 for Grade 2, and the factory wants to \(\textbf{minimise}\) cost while producing \(\textbf{at least}\) 15 kg of Grade 1 daily due to a standing order. The correct formulation is:
options: Minimise \(Z=20x+25y\) subject to \(2x+y\le40,\ x+3y\le45,\ x,y\ge0\)
Maximise \(Z=20x+25y\) subject to \(2x+y\le40,\ x+3y\le45,\ x\ge15,\ y\ge0\)
Minimise \(Z=20x+25y\) subject to \(2x+y\le40,\ x+3y\le45,\ x\ge15,\ y\ge0\)
Minimise \(Z=20x+25y\) subject to \(2x+y\ge40,\ x+3y\ge45,\ x\ge15,\ y\ge0\)
questions.explanation: Blending used \(2x+y\le40\) and packing used \(x+3y\le45\) are capacity (upper) limits. The standing order adds \(x\ge15\) (replacing the usual \(x\ge0\)), while \(y\ge0\) still applies. Cost \(Z=20x+25y\) is minimised.
questions.hint: This problem layers an ordinary lower bound (\(x \ge 15\)) on top of the usual capacity constraints — missing that extra condition is the most likely slip.
distractor_logic: Drops the standing-order requirement \(x\ge15\) entirely, using the plain non-negativity \(x\ge0\) instead — an incomplete constraint set that ignores stated information.
Keeps every constraint correct but says Maximise instead of Minimise, the opposite of the stated cost-minimisation goal.
Flips the two capacity constraints to \(\ge\), treating blending and packing hours as minimum requirements instead of the maximum available capacities they actually are.

questions.topic: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem: Decision Variables, Objective Function, and Constraints
questions.question: A transport company runs mini-trucks (x) and large-trucks (y). Each mini-truck carries 2 tonnes and costs ₹800/trip; each large-truck carries 5 tonnes and costs ₹1500/trip. The company must transport \(\textbf{at least}\) 40 tonnes and has at most 12 trucks available in total. It wants to \(\textbf{minimise}\) transport cost. Which formulation is correct?
options: Maximise \(Z=800x+1500y\) subject to \(2x+5y\ge40,\ x+y\le12,\ x,y\ge0\)
Minimise \(Z=800x+1500y\) subject to \(2x+5y\ge40,\ x+y\le12,\ x,y\ge0\)
Minimise \(Z=800x+1500y\) subject to \(2x+5y\le40,\ x+y\le12,\ x,y\ge0\)
Minimise \(Z=800x+1500y\) subject to \(2x+5y\ge40,\ x+y\ge12,\ x,y\ge0\)
questions.explanation: Total capacity carried, \(2x+5y\), must meet the \(\textbf{at least}\) 40-tonne requirement: \(2x+5y\ge40\). The truck count, \(x+y\), cannot exceed the 12 available: \(x+y\le12\). Cost \(Z=800x+1500y\) is minimised.
questions.hint: Two different requirement types appear here — a minimum ("at least" tonnage) and a maximum ("at most" trucks available) — keep their directions separate.
distractor_logic: Keeps both constraints correct but says Maximise instead of Minimise, the opposite of the stated cost-minimisation goal.
Flips the tonnage requirement to \(\le40\), treating a minimum haulage target as an upper cap instead.
Keeps the tonnage requirement correct but flips the truck-availability constraint to \(\ge12\), as though at least 12 trucks were required rather than at most 12 being available.

questions.topic: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem: Decision Variables, Objective Function, and Constraints
questions.question: A cooperative farm grows two crops on x and y hectares. Crop A needs 3 labour-days/hectare and yields profit ₹4,000/hectare; crop B needs 5 labour-days/hectare and yields profit ₹6,000/hectare. Only 900 labour-days and 250 hectares of land are available in total. The farm wants to maximise profit. Which formulation correctly captures \(\textbf{every}\) stated restriction?
options: Maximise \(Z=4000x+6000y\) subject to \(x+y\le250,\ x,y\ge0\)
Maximise \(Z=6000x+4000y\) subject to \(3x+5y\le900,\ x+y\le250,\ x,y\ge0\)
Maximise \(Z=4000x+6000y\) subject to \(3x+5y\le900,\ x+y\le250,\ x,y\ge0\)
Maximise \(Z=4000x+6000y\) subject to \(3x+5y\le900,\ x,y\ge0\)
questions.explanation: Both the labour restriction \(3x+5y\le900\) and the land restriction \(x+y\le250\) are stated and must both appear; dropping either one loses part of the true feasible region, and profit \(Z=4000x+6000y\) is maximised.
questions.hint: Two separate resources are limited here (labour-days AND land) — a formulation using only one of the two constraints is incomplete.
distractor_logic: Keeps only the land constraint and silently drops the labour constraint \(3x+5y\le900\) — this would treat labour-days as unlimited, again expanding the feasible region incorrectly.
Keeps both constraints correct but swaps the profit coefficients between crop A and crop B.
Keeps only the labour constraint and silently drops the land constraint \(x+y\le250\) — this would treat land as unlimited, expanding the feasible region beyond what is actually available.

questions.topic: Graphical Solution: Feasible Region and Corner Points
questions.question: The feasible region is defined by \(x+y\ge2,\ 2x+y\le10,\ x+2y\le10,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\). Which is the \(\textbf{complete}\) list of corner points?
questions.explanation: Besides the four points found from the constraint lines meeting the axes and each other along the non-negativity boundary — \((0,2)\), \((0,5)\), \((2,0)\), \((5,0)\) — the two slanted lines \(2x+y=10\) and \(x+2y=10\) also intersect each other, at \(\left(\dfrac{10}{3},\dfrac{10}{3}\right)\), which satisfies \(x+y\ge2\) as well and so is a genuine fifth corner point.
questions.hint: Two slanted constraint lines can meet each other directly, not just the axes — check that intersection too, even if it's not a whole number.
distractor_logic: Drops \((0,2)\), the corner point where \(x+y=2\) meets the \(y\)-axis, while incorrectly including the fractional point along with the remaining axis points.

Replaces the correct fractional intersection \(\left(\dfrac{10}{3},\dfrac{10}{3}\right)\) with \((5,5)\), a plausible-looking round-number guess that does not actually satisfy \(2x+y\le10\) (since \(2(5)+5=15>10\)).

Drops the fractional corner point \(\left(\dfrac{10}{3},\dfrac{10}{3}\right)\) formed by the two slanted lines meeting each other — an easy point to miss since it isn't a whole number and doesn't touch either axis.

questions.topic: Graphical Solution: Feasible Region and Corner Points
questions.question: The feasible region is defined by \(x\le6,\ y\le5,\ x+y\ge4,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\). Which is the \(\textbf{complete}\) list of corner points?
questions.explanation: Checking all pairwise intersections of \(x=6\), \(y=5\), \(x+y=4\), and the axes gives five feasible corner points, including \((6,5)\) — the point where the two upper-bound lines \(x=6\) and \(y=5\) meet, which also satisfies \(x+y=11\ge4\) and so is genuinely feasible.
questions.hint: Even though \((6,5)\) doesn't come from the "main" constraint \(x+y\ge4\), check it anyway — it's where the OTHER two boundary lines cross, and it may still be feasible.
distractor_logic: Drops \((6,5)\), the corner point formed by the two upper-bound lines \(x=6\) and \(y=5\) meeting — easy to miss if attention stays only on the \(x+y\ge4\) boundary.
Drops \((0,5)\), the \(y\)-axis intercept of \(y=5\), while still (correctly) including \((6,5)\).
Drops \((0,5)\) and \((6,0)\) both, keeping only some of the true vertices.

questions.topic: Graphical Solution: Feasible Region and Corner Points
questions.question: The feasible region is defined by \(x+y\le12,\ x\le7,\ y\le8,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\). Which is the \(\textbf{complete}\) list of corner points?
questions.explanation: The full boundary is traced by \((0,0)\to(0,8)\) [along the \(y\)-axis up to \(y\le8\)] \(\to(4,8)\) [along \(y=8\) until it meets \(x+y=12\)] \(\to(7,5)\) [along \(x+y=12\) until it meets \(x\le7\)] \(\to(7,0)\) [down along \(x=7\)] \(\to(0,0)\). Both \((4,8)\) and \((7,5)\) come from \(x+y=12\) crossing the two OTHER upper bounds and are easy to miss individually.
questions.hint: Trace the boundary continuously from corner to corner — the line \(x+y=12\) actually contributes two different vertices here, not one.
distractor_logic: Drops \((4,8)\), the vertex where \(y=8\) meets \(x+y=12\), keeping only the vertex where \(x=7\) meets \(x+y=12\).
Drops \((7,5)\), the vertex where \(x=7\) meets \(x+y=12\), keeping only the vertex where \(y=8\) meets \(x+y=12\).
Adds an extra point \((7,8)\) which fails \(x+y\le12\) (since \(7+8=15>12\)) and so is not actually feasible, alongside otherwise listing every genuine vertex.

questions.topic: Graphical Solution: Feasible Region and Corner Points
questions.question: A company's feasible region is \(x+y\le12{,}000,\ x\le8{,}000,\ y\le8{,}000,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\). What is the corner point formed by \(x+y=12{,}000\) meeting \(y=8{,}000\) (\(\textbf{not}\) the one meeting \(x=8{,}000\))?
questions.explanation: Substituting \(y=8000\) into \(x+y=12000\): \(x=12000-8000=4000\), giving \((4000,8000)\). This is different from the intersection of \(x+y=12000\) with \(x=8000\), which instead gives \((8000,4000)\) — the two are easy to swap.
questions.hint: Fix \(y=8000\) (not \(x=8000\)) and solve \(x+y=12000\) for \(x\); double-check which coordinate you actually held fixed.
distractor_logic: This is the OTHER nearby corner point — the intersection of \(x+y=12{,}000\) with \(x=8{,}000\) instead of \(y=8{,}000\) as asked; the coordinates get swapped between the two similar-looking vertices.
This is only the \(x\)-axis intercept of \(x=8{,}000\) alone, ignoring the \(x+y=12{,}000\) constraint entirely.
This is only the \(y\)-axis intercept of \(y=8{,}000\) alone, ignoring the \(x+y=12{,}000\) constraint entirely.

questions.topic: Graphical Solution: Feasible Region and Corner Points
questions.question: The feasible region is defined by \(x\le6,\ y\le6,\ x+y\le9,\ 2x+y\le14,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\). How many corner points does this feasible region have?
questions.explanation: Tracing the boundary: \((0,0)\to(0,6)\) [along \(y\)-axis to \(y\le6\)] \(\to(3,6)\) [along \(y=6\) to \(x+y=9\)] \(\to(5,4)\) [along \(x+y=9\) to \(2x+y=14\)] \(\to(6,2)\) [along \(2x+y=14\) to \(x\le6\)] \(\to(6,0)\) [down along \(x=6\)] \(\to(0,0)\) — six vertices in total, formed by four different constraint lines contributing edges.
questions.hint: With four active constraint lines besides the axes, this region can have more vertices than a simple two- or three-constraint problem — trace the full boundary carefully rather than stopping early.
distractor_logic: Overcounts by treating some non-adjacent pairwise intersection (that fails one of the other constraints) as an extra, genuine corner point.
Undercounts by one, most likely missing the vertex \((6,2)\) where \(2x+y=14\) meets \(x=6\), since it's easy to stop tracing the boundary at \((5,4)\) and jump straight to \((6,0)\).
Undercounts further, likely also merging or dropping the vertex \((3,6)\) where \(y=6\) meets \(x+y=9\).

questions.topic: Graphical Solution: Feasible Region and Corner Points
questions.question: Which statement correctly describes how the corner points of a feasible region (bounded by several linear constraints plus non-negativity) should be obtained?
options: Only the points where a constraint line meets an axis need to be checked; intersections of two constraint lines with each other are never corner points
Find the intersection of every pair of boundary lines (each constraint line and each axis), then keep only those intersections that also satisfy every remaining constraint
Only the origin and the two axis points nearest to it need to be checked, regardless of how many constraints are given
Find the intersection of every pair of boundary lines and treat ALL such intersections as corner points, since every constraint line must contribute a vertex
questions.explanation: The correct method checks every pairwise intersection of boundary lines (which line meets which) and then filters out any intersection that fails to satisfy one of the OTHER constraints — only the intersections that pass every check are genuine corner points.
questions.hint: There are always two steps: generate candidate intersections, then filter by feasibility against everything else; skipping either step causes errors.
distractor_logic: Wrongly rules out intersections of two constraint (non-axis) lines with each other, even though such intersections are often genuine corner points, as seen whenever two slanted constraint lines meet inside the feasible region.

Wrongly assumes only points near the origin matter; feasible regions with several constraints commonly have corner points far from the origin, formed by constraint lines that don't involve the axes at all.

Skips the essential feasibility check — not every pairwise intersection of boundary lines actually lies within the feasible region; some fail other constraints and must be discarded, not automatically kept.

questions.topic: Corner Point Method: Finding the Optimal (Maximum or Minimum) Value
questions.question: An investor's feasible region for Maximise \(Z=8x+10y\) has corner points \((0,0)\), \((0,8000)\), \((4000,8000)\), \((8000,0)\), and \((8000,4000)\). What is the maximum value of \(Z\)?
questions.hint: With five corner points, it's easy to stop comparing after checking only three or four — make sure every single one is evaluated before deciding.
distractor_logic: Correctly computes \(Z=1{,}04{,}000\) at \((8000,4000)\), a genuine corner-point value and the second-largest, but not the true maximum — these two large, similarly-shaped points are easy to swap.
Correctly computes \(Z=80{,}000\) at \((0,8000)\), a genuine corner-point value, but well below the maximum.
Correctly computes \(Z=64{,}000\) at \((8000,0)\), a genuine corner-point value, but the smallest of the four non-zero ones, not the maximum.

questions.topic: Corner Point Method: Finding the Optimal (Maximum or Minimum) Value
questions.question: The feasible region for Maximise \(Z=3x+2y\) subject to \(x\le6,\ y\le6,\ x+y\le9,\ 2x+y\le14,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\) has corner points \((0,0)\), \((0,6)\), \((3,6)\), \((5,4)\), \((6,2)\), and \((6,0)\). What is the maximum value of \(Z\)?
questions.hint: With six corner points from four different constraint lines, evaluate every single one methodically — the maximum is not at either extreme corner here.
distractor_logic: Correctly computes \(Z=22\) at \((6,2)\), a genuine corner-point value and very close to the true maximum, but still one less than the actual maximum at \((5,4)\).
Correctly computes \(Z=21\) at \((3,6)\), a genuine corner-point value, but not the largest — stopping the comparison at this corner would miss the true maximum found two vertices further along.
Correctly computes \(Z=18\) at \((6,0)\), a genuine corner-point value, but the smallest of the non-zero ones, far from the maximum.

questions.topic: Corner Point Method: Finding the Optimal (Maximum or Minimum) Value
questions.question: The feasible region for Minimise \(Z=3x+5y\) subject to \(x+3y\ge3,\ x+y\ge2,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\) has corner points \((0,2)\), \(\left(\dfrac{3}{2},\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\), and \((3,0)\). What is the minimum value of \(Z\), and why is this value \(\textbf{genuinely}\) the minimum even though the feasible region is unbounded?
options: \(Z=9\) at \((3,0)\); it is genuinely the minimum because it is the largest of the three corner values
\(Z=7\) at \(\left(\dfrac{3}{2},\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\); it is genuinely the minimum because the open half-plane \(3x+5y<7\) shares no point with the feasible region
\(Z=10\) at \((0,2)\); it is genuinely the minimum because \((0,2)\) lies on the \(y\)-axis
\(Z=7\) at \(\left(\dfrac{3}{2},\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\); it is genuinely the minimum simply because it is the smallest of the three corner values, with no further check needed
questions.explanation: \(Z(0,2)=10\), \(Z\left(\tfrac32,\tfrac12\right)=\tfrac92+\tfrac52=7\), \(Z(3,0)=9\); the smallest corner value is \(7\). But because the region is unbounded, this is only confirmed as the true minimum after checking that \(3x+5y<7\) has no point in common with the feasible region — which it does not, since every feasible point satisfies \(x+3y\ge3\) and \(x+y\ge2\) together forcing \(3x+5y\ge7\).
questions.hint: Being the smallest of the corner-point values is necessary but, for an UNBOUNDED region, not by itself sufficient — the half-plane test is what makes it certain.
distractor_logic: Picks \(Z=9\) at \((3,0)\), which is a genuine corner value but not the smallest, and justifies it by picking the LARGEST value instead of the smallest — the reasoning for a minimisation problem is reversed entirely.
Picks \(Z=10\) at \((0,2)\), the LARGEST of the three corner values, and offers an irrelevant geometric reason (lying on an axis) that has no bearing on optimality.

Identifies the correct minimum value and point, but gives an incomplete justification — for an unbounded region, being the smallest corner value alone does not guarantee it is the true minimum without the half-plane verification step.

questions.topic: Corner Point Method: Finding the Optimal (Maximum or Minimum) Value
questions.question: The feasible region for Maximise \(Z=x+y\) is bounded only by \(x\ge1,\ y\ge1\) (no upper bound on either variable). Its only corner point is \((1,1)\), where \(Z=2\). What is the correct conclusion about the maximum value of \(Z\)?
options: No maximum value of \(Z\) exists, because the feasible region is unbounded in the direction of increasing \(x\) and \(y\), and \(Z=x+y\) increases without limit in that same direction
The maximum value of \(Z\) is \(2\), because a region with only one corner point can never be unbounded
The maximum value of \(Z\) is undefined because a feasible region with only one corner point is not a valid LPP
The maximum value of \(Z\) is \(2\), attained at \((1,1)\), since that is the only corner point of the region
questions.explanation: Although \((1,1)\) is the only corner point and gives \(Z=2\), the feasible region \(\{x\ge1,y\ge1\}\) stretches to infinity in the direction of increasing \(x\) and \(y\). Since \(Z=x+y\) also increases without bound in that same direction (e.g. at \((100,100)\), \(Z=200\)), no finite maximum exists — the corner-point value \(2\) is only a local candidate, not a genuine maximum here.
questions.hint: Having just one corner point is a strong hint the region is unbounded — always ask whether the region stretches to infinity in a direction where \(Z\) keeps growing.
distractor_logic: Wrongly claims a single corner point rules out unboundedness — in fact, a region with only one vertex (like a quarter-plane shifted from the origin) is a classic example of an unbounded region.
An LPP with a single corner point is still perfectly valid; the issue here is not validity but whether a finite optimal value actually exists, which it does not for this maximisation.

Confidently declares \(2\) as the maximum purely because it's the only corner value available, without checking whether the region is unbounded in a direction that lets \(Z\) grow further — exactly the unverified-corner-point trap for an unbounded region.

questions.topic: Corner Point Method: Finding the Optimal (Maximum or Minimum) Value
questions.question: The feasible region for Minimise \(Z=3x+2y\) subject to \(x+y\ge2,\ 2x+y\le10,\ x+2y\le10,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\) has corner points \((0,2)\), \((0,5)\), \((2,0)\), \((5,0)\), and \(\left(\dfrac{10}{3},\dfrac{10}{3}\right)\). What is the minimum value of \(Z\)?
options: \(\dfrac{50}{3}\), at \(\left(\dfrac{10}{3},\dfrac{10}{3}\right)\)
questions.explanation: \(Z(0,2)=4\), \(Z(0,5)=10\), \(Z(2,0)=6\), \(Z(5,0)=15\), \(Z\left(\tfrac{10}{3},\tfrac{10}{3}\right)=10+\tfrac{20}{3}=\tfrac{50}{3}\approx16.7\). Every corner, including the fractional one, must be checked even though it does not turn out to be optimal; the smallest overall is \(4\), at \((0,2)\).
questions.hint: The fractional corner point still needs to be evaluated for completeness, even though (as it turns out) it is not where the minimum occurs.
distractor_logic: Correctly computes \(Z=6\) at \((2,0)\), a genuine corner-point value, but it is not the smallest — \((0,2)\) gives a lower value still.
Correctly computes \(Z=\dfrac{50}{3}\) at the fractional corner point, the LARGEST of the five values — picking it as the minimum reverses the required comparison entirely.
Correctly computes \(Z=10\) at \((0,5)\), a genuine corner-point value, but well above the minimum.

questions.topic: Corner Point Method: Finding the Optimal (Maximum or Minimum) Value
questions.question: The feasible region for Maximise \(Z=3x+y\) is bounded only by \(y\le10,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\) (no upper bound on \(x\)). Its corner points are \((0,0)\) and \((0,10)\), where \(Z=0\) and \(Z=10\) respectively. What is the correct conclusion?
options: The maximum value of \(Z\) is \(10\), attained at \((0,10)\), since it is the larger of the two corner values found
The maximum value of \(Z\) cannot be determined because there are only two corner points
No maximum value of \(Z\) exists, because \(x\) can increase without limit while \(y\) stays within \([0,10]\), and \(Z=3x+y\) grows without bound as \(x\to\infty\)
The maximum value of \(Z\) is \(0\), attained at \((0,0)\), since that is the first corner point checked
questions.explanation: The two corner points found are \((0,0)\) and \((0,10)\), but the region is unbounded — \(x\) can be made arbitrarily large while \(y\) stays in \([0,10]\) and every such point remains feasible. Since \(Z=3x+y\) then grows without bound (e.g. at \((1000,10)\), \(Z=3010\)), there is no finite maximum, despite \(10\) being the larger of the two corner values.
questions.hint: Notice that only \(y\) is capped here — \(x\) has no upper-bound constraint at all, so check whether that missing bound lets \(Z\) grow forever.
distractor_logic: Takes the larger of the two corner-point values as the final answer without checking whether the region is unbounded in a direction that lets \(Z\) increase further — exactly the unverified-corner-point trap for an unbounded region.

Having only two corner points is not by itself a barrier to determining the optimal value; the real issue is that this particular region is unbounded in a direction where \(Z\) increases without limit, so no maximum exists.

Picks the smaller corner value, \(Z=0\), simply for being "checked first", which is not a valid reason to select any value in the corner point method, whether or not the region happens to be unbounded.

questions.topic: Bounded and Unbounded Feasible Regions
questions.question: The feasible region for Minimise \(Z=x+2y\) subject to \(2x+y\ge3,\ x+2y\ge6,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\) is unbounded, with corner points \((0,3)\) and \((6,0)\), both giving \(Z=6\). Which statement correctly describes the situation?
options: The feasible region is unbounded, yet the minimum value of \(Z\) still exists and equals \(6\) — the open half-plane \(x+2y<6\) shares no point with the feasible region, so no smaller value of \(Z\) is attainable; a maximum, however, does not exist since \(Z\) increases without bound as the region is traversed away from these corners
The feasible region is actually bounded, since it has exactly two corner points
Since the feasible region is unbounded, neither the maximum nor the minimum value of \(Z\) can exist
The minimum value of \(Z\) is \(6\) simply because both corner points happen to give the same value, with no further reasoning needed
questions.explanation: Being unbounded does not automatically rule out a minimum: here, every feasible point satisfies \(x+2y\ge6\) directly (it is one of the given constraints), so \(x+2y<6\) is impossible for any feasible point, confirming \(Z_{\min}=6\). But since the region also stretches to infinity in directions where \(Z=x+2y\) keeps increasing (e.g. along the unbounded edges), no finite maximum exists.
questions.hint: An unbounded region can still have a genuine minimum (or maximum) — the two are not the same question; check each one separately using the half-plane test.
distractor_logic: Having exactly two corner points does not make a region bounded — an unbounded region can have as few as one or two corner points, with the boundary continuing to infinity beyond them.
Wrongly generalises that unboundedness rules out BOTH extremes; in fact a minimum can exist for an unbounded region even when a maximum does not (or vice versa) — each must be checked on its own.

Two corner points sharing the same \(Z\)-value is a genuine clue (it signals the edge between them may be optimal throughout), but for an UNBOUNDED region it is not, by itself, a substitute for the half-plane verification that confirms no smaller value exists elsewhere in the region.

questions.topic: Bounded and Unbounded Feasible Regions
questions.question: The feasible region for the constraints \(x\le5,\ y\le4,\ x+y\ge3,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\) has corner points \((0,3)\), \((0,4)\), \((3,0)\), \((5,0)\), and \((5,4)\). Is this region bounded or unbounded, and why?
options: Bounded — both \(x\le5\) and \(y\le4\) cap the two variables from above, and \(x+y\ge3\) only trims a corner near the origin without opening the region up to infinity
Cannot be determined from the corner points alone; the objective function is also required
Unbounded — because \(x+y\ge3\) is a lower-bound constraint present alongside the two upper bounds
Unbounded — because the region has as many as five corner points
questions.explanation: \(x\le5\) and \(y\le4\) together with \(x,y\ge0\) confine the region to the rectangle with corners \((0,0),(0,4),(5,4),(5,0)\); the extra constraint \(x+y\ge3\) simply removes the small triangular corner of that rectangle nearest the origin, leaving a bounded pentagon — it cannot make the region extend beyond the rectangle's already-fixed limits.
questions.hint: Whenever a \(\ge\)-type constraint is layered on top of constraints that already cap both variables, it can only shrink the region further — it cannot re-open it toward infinity.
distractor_logic: Whether the feasible REGION is bounded or unbounded is determined entirely by its constraints and is fixed before any objective function is chosen — the objective function only matters later, for finding where on that region the optimum occurs.

Focuses on the presence of one \(\ge\)-type constraint without checking that the OTHER two constraints (\(x\le5\) and \(y\le4\)) already cap the entire region regardless of what \(x+y\ge3\) does to it.

The number of corner points has no direct bearing on boundedness — a bounded pentagon (5 corners) is just as legitimately bounded as a bounded triangle (3 corners); what matters is whether the region is enclosed, not how many vertices it has.

questions.topic: Bounded and Unbounded Feasible Regions
questions.question: For the region defined by \(x+3y\ge3,\ x+y\ge2,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\), which of the following correctly carries out the half-plane verification to confirm that \(Z_{\min}=7\) at \(\left(\dfrac{3}{2},\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\) for Minimise \(Z=3x+5y\), given that the region is unbounded?
options: Check whether the open half-plane \(3x+5y>7\) has any point in common with the feasible region; since it does, \(Z=7\) is confirmed as the true minimum

Check whether the open half-plane \(3x+5y<7\) has any point in common with the feasible region defined by \(x+3y\ge3,\ x+y\ge2,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\); since it does not, \(Z=7\) is confirmed as the true minimum
Recompute \(Z\) at the origin instead, since the origin is always the deciding point for verifying an unbounded region
Simply note that \(\left(\dfrac32,\dfrac12\right)\) is a corner point and stop there, since every corner-point value is automatically the true minimum for any region
questions.explanation: For a claimed minimum \(m\) on an unbounded region, the correct verification is to check whether the OPEN half-plane \(ax+by<m\) (strictly less than the candidate minimum) shares any point with the feasible region. If it does not, no feasible point can beat \(m\), confirming it as the genuine minimum.
questions.hint: For a MINIMUM claim, the verifying half-plane uses the \(<\) direction (points that would be BETTER than the candidate) — not \(>\).
distractor_logic: Uses the wrong direction of inequality (\(>7\) instead of \(<7\)); checking whether points with LARGER \(Z\) exist says nothing about whether a SMALLER value is attainable, which is what actually needs to be ruled out for a minimum.

The origin is not always relevant to this check, and in this case \((0,0)\) is not even a feasible point (it fails \(x+3y\ge3\)); the correct method checks the half-plane condition directly, not a specific fixed point.

Skips the verification step entirely and assumes the corner-point value is automatically correct — this is only safe for BOUNDED regions; for an unbounded region like this one, the half-plane check is required.

questions.topic: Bounded and Unbounded Feasible Regions
questions.question: For Maximise \(Z=3x+y\) over the unbounded region \(y\le10,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\), which of the following correctly carries out the half-plane verification to check whether \(Z=10\) (the larger of the two corner values found at \((0,0)\) and \((0,10)\)) is genuinely the maximum?
options: Simply accept \(Z=10\) as the maximum, since it is the larger of the two corner-point values found
Check the value of \(Z\) at the point \((0,0)\) only, since it is the first corner point listed
Check whether the open half-plane \(3x+y<10\) has any point in common with the feasible region; since it does, \(Z=10\) is confirmed as the maximum

Check whether the open half-plane \(3x+y>10\) has any point in common with the feasible region; since it does (for example \((10,0)\), where \(3(10)+0=30>10\)), \(Z=10\) is \(\textbf{not}\) the true maximum, and in fact no maximum exists
questions.explanation: For a claimed maximum \(M\), the verification checks whether the open half-plane \(ax+by>M\) (points strictly BETTER than the candidate) meets the feasible region. Here, \((10,0)\) satisfies \(y\le10\) (since \(0\le10\)) and gives \(Z=30>10\), so points beating \(Z=10\) do exist in the feasible region — meaning \(10\) is not the maximum, and since \(x\) is completely unbounded above in this region, no finite maximum exists at all.
questions.hint: For a MAXIMUM claim, the verifying half-plane uses the \(>\) direction (points that would be BETTER/larger than the candidate) — the opposite direction from the minimum case.
distractor_logic: Accepts the larger corner-point value without any verification — exactly the unverified shortcut that fails for unbounded regions, since a still-larger feasible value exists here.

Checking only one arbitrarily chosen corner point (and not even comparing it against the other, or performing the half-plane test) is not a valid way to determine the maximum over an unbounded region.

Uses the half-plane condition \(<10\), which tests for WORSE points, not better ones — that can never disprove a claimed maximum; the correct check looks for points that would beat the candidate, using \(>10\).

questions.topic: Bounded and Unbounded Feasible Regions
questions.question: Consider the feasible region defined by \(x\le24,\ y\le16,\ x+y\le24,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\). It turns out that the constraint \(x\le24\) is \(\textbf{redundant}\) — it is already implied by \(x+y\le24\) together with \(y\ge0\). Does this redundancy affect whether the overall feasible region is bounded?
options: No — the region is still bounded, because the remaining constraints \(y\le16\) and \(x+y\le24\) (with \(x,y\ge0\)) already confine it to a finite quadrilateral, regardless of whether \(x\le24\) happens to add anything extra
Yes — a redundant constraint always makes the region unbounded, since it contributes nothing to closing off the shape
Yes — without the redundant constraint being "useful", the region has too few effective constraints to be bounded
It cannot be determined whether the region is bounded without first removing the redundant constraint and starting over
questions.explanation: A constraint being redundant only means it doesn't change the shape of the feasible region (since the other constraints already imply it) — it has no bearing on whether that resulting region is bounded or unbounded. Here, \(y\le16\) and \(x+y\le24\) together with \(x,y\ge0\) already form the bounded quadrilateral \((0,0),(0,16),(8,16),(24,0)\), with or without \(x\le24\) explicitly listed.
questions.hint: Redundancy is about whether a constraint changes the SHAPE of the region; boundedness is a separate question about whether that shape (however it's described) is finite.
distractor_logic: Wrongly assumes redundancy implies unboundedness; a redundant constraint changes nothing about the actual shape of the region, so it cannot be responsible for making an otherwise-bounded region unbounded.

Wrongly treats "usefulness" of a constraint as necessary for boundedness; what determines boundedness is the ACTUAL shape formed by all the constraints together, not how many of them are individually doing distinct work.

Boundedness can be determined directly from the actual shape of the feasible region as already described by the remaining (non-redundant) constraints; there is no need to remove anything and "start over" to answer this.

questions.topic: Bounded and Unbounded Feasible Regions
questions.question: True or false: "A feasible region defined only by \(\le\)-type constraints (together with \(x\ge0,\ y\ge0\)) is always bounded."
options: False — for example, the region \(x\le5,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\) uses only a \(\le\)-type constraint, yet \(y\) is left completely uncapped and can grow without limit, making the region unbounded
False, because \(\le\)-type constraints always make a region unbounded, never bounded
True — every \(\le\)-type constraint, by definition, caps the region and therefore guarantees boundedness
True, as long as at least one \(\le\)-type constraint is present, regardless of how many variables it restricts
questions.explanation: Having only \(\le\)-type constraints does not guarantee boundedness — what matters is whether EVERY variable (and every relevant direction) actually ends up capped. \(x\le5\) alone caps only \(x\); with no constraint on \(y\) at all, \(y\) can be made arbitrarily large, and the region \(\{x\le5,x\ge0,y\ge0\}\) is an unbounded vertical strip, not a bounded shape.
questions.hint: A single \(\le\) constraint only caps whichever direction it actually restricts — check whether EVERY direction (not just one) ends up capped by the full set of constraints.
distractor_logic: This claims the opposite extreme, that \(\le\)-type constraints always produce unboundedness, which is equally false — plenty of bounded regions (such as any simple rectangle or triangle) are formed using only \(\le\)-type constraints, provided every direction is actually capped.
Wrongly assumes any single \(\le\)-type constraint automatically bounds the WHOLE region, regardless of how many variables or directions are actually left uncapped by the rest of the constraint set.

Similarly overgeneralises — the mere presence of at least one \(\le\)-type constraint says nothing about whether every direction is capped; a single such constraint restricting only one variable clearly is not enough, as the counterexample shows.

questions.topic: Special Cases: Multiple Optimal Solutions, Infeasible Problems, and Unbounded Optimal Values
questions.question: A tailoring workshop has: fabric constraint \(2x+3y\le30\), a client requirement of at least 20 finished pieces combined (\(x+y\ge20\)), and a machine-time constraint \(x+2y\le16\), with \(x,y\ge0\). What can be concluded about this LPP?
options: It is infeasible — combining \(x+2y\le16\) (which forces \(x\le16\)) with \(x+y\ge20\) requires \(x\ge24\), which is impossible together with \(x\le16\), so no point satisfies all three constraints at once
