It has multiple optimal solutions, since three separate constraints are given
It is an ordinary, solvable LPP, since none of the three constraints directly contradicts another by itself
It has an unbounded optimal value, since the client requirement \(x+y\ge20\) has no upper limit stated
questions.explanation: From \(x+2y\le16\) and \(y\ge0\): \(x\le16\). From \(x+y\ge20\): \(y\ge20-x\). Substituting into \(x+2y\le16\): \(x+2(20-x)\le16 \Rightarrow 40-x\le16 \Rightarrow x\ge24\). But \(x\le16\) and \(x\ge24\) cannot both hold — so no feasible point exists at all; the LPP is infeasible, even though no SINGLE pair of constraints looks contradictory by itself.
questions.hint: No two constraints look directly contradictory on their own here — the contradiction only shows up once you combine all three together algebraically.
distractor_logic: Having three constraints does not by itself cause multiple optimal solutions; that special case requires an actual feasible region with an edge parallel to the objective line, and here there is no feasible region at all to speak of.

Even though no two constraints directly contradict each other when compared in isolation, combining all three together algebraically reveals an impossible requirement (\(x\ge24\) and \(x\le16\) simultaneously); infeasibility can arise from the joint effect of several constraints, not only from an obviously contradictory pair.

The absence of an explicit upper limit on \(x+y\) does not create an unbounded optimal value here; in fact, once the machine-time constraint is combined with the client requirement, there turns out to be no feasible region at all — a completely different special case.

questions.topic: Special Cases: Multiple Optimal Solutions, Infeasible Problems, and Unbounded Optimal Values
questions.question: For Maximise \(Z=2x+3y\) subject to \(x-y\le4,\ x\ge2,\ y\ge0\), checking the point \((2,1000)\): it satisfies \(x-y=2-1000=-998\le4\), \(x=2\ge2\), and \(y=1000\ge0\), giving \(Z=2(2)+3(1000)=3004\). What special case applies to this LPP?
options: Infeasibility, since \(x-y\) becomes a large negative number at this point

Unbounded optimal value — \(y\) is left completely free to increase (the constraint \(x-y\le4\) only requires \(y\ge x-4\), a lower bound on \(y\), not an upper one), so \(Z=2x+3y\) grows without limit and no finite maximum exists
Multiple optimal solutions, since \((2,1000)\) and other points give different values of \(Z\) that could be compared
An ordinary unique optimal solution, since \(x\ge2\) provides a clear starting corner point
questions.explanation: The constraint \(x-y\le4\) rearranges to \(y\ge x-4\), which is only a LOWER bound on \(y\); nothing caps \(y\) from above. Since \(Z=2x+3y\) has a positive coefficient on \(y\), letting \(y\to\infty\) (with \(x=2\) fixed, satisfying \(x\ge2\)) makes \(Z\) grow without any limit — so this LPP has an unbounded optimal value; no finite maximum exists.
questions.hint: Rewrite \(x-y\le4\) to see which variable it actually bounds, and in which direction — it may not cap the variable you expect.
distractor_logic: A large negative value of \(x-y\) does not violate \(x-y\le4\) at all (being very negative is well within "at most 4"); this point is perfectly feasible, not evidence of an empty feasible region.

"Multiple optimal solutions" requires different points to share the SAME best value; here, \(Z\) keeps climbing higher and higher without ever settling on a repeated maximum, so this is not the right special case.

Having a clear starting corner point (such as one where \(x=2\)) does not guarantee a finite optimum exists; the region here is unbounded in the direction of increasing \(y\), and \(Z\) keeps growing in that same direction without any limit.

questions.topic: Special Cases: Multiple Optimal Solutions, Infeasible Problems, and Unbounded Optimal Values
questions.question: Which of the following four LPPs (each with \(x,y\ge0\)) has \(\textbf{no feasible solution}\) (is infeasible)?
options: \(x+y\le4\) and \(x+y\ge9\)
\(x+y\le4\) and \(x+y\ge2\)
\(x\ge3\) and \(y\ge3\)
questions.explanation: For \(x+y\le4\) and \(x+y\ge9\) to both hold, \(x+y\) would need to be simultaneously at most 4 and at least 9 — impossible, since \(4<9\). This pair of constraints alone makes the feasible region empty; the other three options each describe a perfectly ordinary, non-empty feasible region.
questions.hint: For each option, check whether the stated bounds could ever both be satisfied by the same values of \(x,y\) — three of the four are perfectly compatible ranges.
distractor_logic: \(x\le10\) and \(y\le10\) are two completely independent upper bounds on different variables, easily satisfied together (e.g. by the origin \((0,0)\)); there is no contradiction here at all.
\(x+y\le4\) and \(x+y\ge2\) are perfectly compatible — any point with \(2\le x+y\le4\) (such as \((1,2)\)) satisfies both; this describes a genuine, non-empty strip, not an infeasible problem.
\(x\ge3\) and \(y\ge3\) are two completely independent lower bounds on different variables, easily satisfied together (e.g. by \((3,3)\)); there is no contradiction here at all.

questions.topic: Special Cases: Multiple Optimal Solutions, Infeasible Problems, and Unbounded Optimal Values
questions.question: For Maximise \(Z=3x+2y\) subject to \(x\le6,\ x+y\le9,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\), the corner points are \((0,0)\), \((0,9)\), \((6,3)\), and \((6,0)\), with \(Z\)-values \(0\), \(18\), \(24\), and \(18\) respectively. Does this LPP have multiple optimal solutions?
options: No — although two different corner points, \((0,9)\) and \((6,0)\), happen to tie at \(Z=18\), neither of them is the actual maximum; the true maximum is the single, strictly largest value \(Z=24\) at \((6,3)\) alone
Yes — since the feasible region has four corner points in total
Yes — since two corner points, \((0,9)\) and \((6,0)\), give the same value of \(Z\)
It cannot be determined without also checking whether the region is bounded or unbounded
questions.explanation: A tie between corner points only signals multiple optimal solutions when the TIED value is itself the optimum. Here, \(Z=18\) is tied between \((0,9)\) and \((6,0)\), but neither is the maximum — the true maximum is \(Z=24\) at \((6,3)\) alone, with no other corner point matching it. So this LPP has an ordinary, unique optimal solution, despite the coincidental tie elsewhere.
questions.hint: A tie only matters for "multiple optimal solutions" if the tied value IS the optimum — a tie among non-optimal corner values is just a coincidence and doesn't create the special case.
distractor_logic: The number of corner points in total (four here) has no bearing on whether multiple optimal solutions occur; what matters is only whether the single BEST value among them is repeated, which it is not in this case.

Mistakes a coincidental tie between two NON-optimal corner values (\(18=18\), neither the maximum) for the genuine special case, which specifically requires the OPTIMAL value itself to be repeated — here the actual maximum, \(24\), occurs at only one corner point.

Multiple optimal solutions can be determined directly from the computed \(Z\)-values at the corner points, by checking whether the single best (optimal) value repeats; boundedness of the region is a separate question that doesn't need to be resolved first for this particular check.

questions.topic: Special Cases: Multiple Optimal Solutions, Infeasible Problems, and Unbounded Optimal Values
questions.question: For Minimise \(Z=3x+5y\) subject to \(x+3y\ge3,\ x+y\ge2,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\), the region is unbounded with corner points \((0,2)\), \(\left(\dfrac32,\dfrac12\right)\), and \((3,0)\), giving \(Z\)-values \(10\), \(7\), and \(9\). After verifying with the half-plane test that \(3x+5y<7\) shares no point with the feasible region, what is the \(\textbf{correct}\) overall conclusion about this LPP?
options: It has an unbounded optimal value, since the feasible region is unbounded
It is infeasible, since the half-plane \(3x+5y<7\) shares no point with the feasible region

It is an ordinary LPP with a single, unique optimal solution \(Z=7\) at \(\left(\dfrac32,\dfrac12\right)\); none of the three special cases (infeasibility, multiple optimal solutions, or unbounded optimal value) applies, even though the feasible region itself is unbounded
It has multiple optimal solutions, since three different corner points were checked
questions.explanation: The half-plane check confirms \(Z=7\) genuinely is the minimum (nothing smaller is achievable), and since it occurs at only one corner point with no tie, there is a single unique optimal solution. The feasible region being unbounded does NOT by itself create either of the other two special cases here — it simply means the ordinary corner-point comparison needed this extra verification step before being trusted.
questions.hint: An unbounded region doesn't automatically trigger a "special case" label — once verified, a perfectly ordinary unique optimum can still exist on it, exactly as it does here.
distractor_logic: Wrongly assumes unboundedness of the feasible region automatically means the optimal VALUE is unbounded; here the minimum was explicitly verified to exist and equal \(7\), which is the opposite conclusion.

The half-plane sharing no point with the feasible region is exactly what CONFIRMS \(Z=7\) as the genuine minimum — it is a successful verification, not a sign of infeasibility; infeasibility would mean the feasible region itself is empty, which it clearly is not here.

Checking three corner points (which is simply the standard corner point method) does not by itself indicate a tie; here, all three \(Z\)-values (\(10\), \(7\), \(9\)) are different, so there is no repetition of the optimal value at all.

questions.topic: Special Cases: Multiple Optimal Solutions, Infeasible Problems, and Unbounded Optimal Values
questions.question: An LPP's feasible region is unbounded, and for a \(\textbf{maximisation}\) problem, a candidate optimal value \(M\) is found at a corner point. Checking further, the open half-plane \(ax+by>M\) is found to \(\textbf{share points}\) with the feasible region (for example, points arbitrarily far from the origin keep giving larger and larger values of \(Z\)). What is the correct conclusion?
options: This LPP has an unbounded optimal value — since feasible points exist that beat \(M\), and this keeps happening without limit, no finite maximum exists at all
The LPP has multiple optimal solutions, since more than one point now gives a value of \(Z\) at least as large as \(M\)
\(M\) is confirmed as the correct maximum, since it was the largest value found among the corner points checked
The LPP is infeasible, since the half-plane \(ax+by>M\) overlapping the feasible region means the constraints are contradictory
questions.explanation: When the half-plane \(ax+by>M\) (points strictly BETTER than the candidate \(M\)) does share points with the feasible region, this proves \(M\) is not actually the maximum, since better points exist; if this keeps happening without any limit (arbitrarily larger values keep being found), there is no finite maximum at all — the LPP has an unbounded optimal value.
questions.hint: Sharing points with \(ax+by>M\) means \(M\) FAILS the verification test for a maximum — the conclusion should follow that failure, not restate \(M\) as if it had passed.
distractor_logic: "Multiple optimal solutions" requires several points to share the SAME single best value; here, the values keep growing past \(M\) without settling on any repeated maximum, which is a fundamentally different situation from a tie.

Treats \(M\) as confirmed simply because it was the best value found among the corner points, ignoring that the half-plane check specifically found feasible points that beat it — this is exactly the unverified-corner-point trap the check exists to catch.

The half-plane test overlapping the feasible region says something about how large \(Z\) can get over that region — it has nothing to do with whether the constraints themselves are mutually contradictory, which is what infeasibility actually means.

questions.topic: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem: Decision Variables, Objective Function, and Constraints
questions.question: A bakery makes cakes (\(x\)) and pastries (\(y\)), earning a profit of \(\textrm{\textrupee}50\) per cake and \(\textrm{\textrupee}30\) per pastry. Oven time limits production to \(2x+y\le120\) (minutes), and packaging capacity limits it to \(x+y\le70\). Formulate the LPP and find the maximum profit.
options: Maximise \(Z=50x+30y\) subject to \(2x+y\le120,\ x+y\le70,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\); maximum profit \(\textrm{\textrupee}3000\) at \((60,0)\)
Minimise \(Z=50x+30y\) subject to \(2x+y\le120,\ x+y\le70,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\); minimum cost \(\textrm{\textrupee}0\) at \((0,0)\)
Maximise \(Z=50x+30y\) subject to \(2x+y\le120,\ x+y\le70,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\); maximum profit \(\textrm{\textrupee}3100\) at \((50,20)\)
Maximise \(Z=50x+30y\) subject to \(2x+y\ge120,\ x+y\ge70,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\); maximum profit \(\textrm{\textrupee}3100\) at \((50,20)\)
questions.explanation: The decision variables are the number of cakes \(x\) and pastries \(y\); the objective is to maximise profit \(Z=50x+30y\), subject to the oven-time constraint \(2x+y\le120\), the packaging constraint \(x+y\le70\), and non-negativity. The corner points are \((0,0)\), \((0,70)\), \((50,20)\) (intersection of the two lines), and \((60,0)\), giving \(Z=0,\ 2100,\ 3100,\ 3000\) respectively. The largest is \(3100\) at \((50,20)\).
questions.hint: First translate the word problem into the correct objective and constraints (correct direction of every inequality), then apply the ordinary corner-point method.
distractor_logic: This picks a genuine corner-point value (\(3000\) at \((60,0)\)) but not the largest one — the intersection corner \((50,20)\) gives more profit and must not be skipped.
This wrongly switches the goal to minimising cost, and treats \(Z\) as a cost rather than the stated profit — the problem explicitly asks for maximum profit, not a minimum of any kind.

This reverses the sense of the \(\le\) limits into \(\ge\), which would describe minimum production requirements rather than the given capacity limits — the formulation itself is wrong even though the final numeric answer happens to match the correct one.

questions.topic: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem: Decision Variables, Objective Function, and Constraints
questions.question: A furniture maker produces tables (\(x\)) and chairs (\(y\)). Carpentry time gives \(2x+3y\le36\) and wood availability gives \(x+2y\le20\) (both in suitable units). After formulating these two constraints (with non-negativity), how many corner points does the resulting feasible region have, and what are they?
options: 2 corner points: \((0,10)\) and \((18,0)\), the two axis intercepts closest to the constraints
3 corner points: \((0,10)\), \((12,4)\), \((18,0)\) — the origin is not a corner since it lies inside both lines
questions.explanation: With \(2x+3y\le36\), \(x+2y\le20\), \(x\ge0\), \(y\ge0\), the boundary lines meet the axes at \((0,12)\) and \((18,0)\) for the first line, and \((0,10)\) and \((20,0)\) for the second; solving the two lines together gives \((12,4)\). Checking feasibility of all candidate intersection points, the true corner points of the bounded region are \((0,0)\) (from non-negativity), \((0,10)\) (the binding wood-axis intercept, since \((0,12)\) violates the wood constraint), \((12,4)\) (intersection of the two lines), and \((18,0)\) (the binding carpentry-axis intercept, since \((20,0)\) violates the carpentry constraint).
questions.hint: Always check EVERY axis intercept against the OTHER constraint too — only the tighter one on each axis survives as a genuine corner.
distractor_logic: This keeps only the two axis intercepts and drops both the origin and the genuine intersection corner \((12,4)\), missing more than half of the true corner-point list.

This wrongly drops the origin, which is always a genuine corner whenever both non-negativity constraints are active there and the origin satisfies both remaining inequalities (it trivially does, since both right-hand sides are positive).

This uses the un-tightened axis intercepts \((0,12)\) and \((20,0)\) directly from each line without checking them against the OTHER constraint — \((0,12)\) fails \(x+2y\le20\) (since \(24>20\)) and \((20,0)\) fails \(2x+3y\le36\) (since \(40>36\)), so neither is actually feasible.

questions.topic: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem: Decision Variables, Objective Function, and Constraints
questions.question: A dietician needs a mix of two foods (\(x\) units of food A, \(y\) units of food B) to meet two minimum nutrient requirements: \(2x+y\ge3\) and \(x+2y\ge6\), at a cost of \(\textrm{\textrupee}4\) per unit of A and \(\textrm{\textrupee}3\) per unit of B. After formulating this LPP, is the resulting feasible region bounded or unbounded?
options: Bounded — the two constraint lines intersect at a single point, and any region with an intersection point must be bounded
Unbounded, but only because the cost coefficients \(4\) and \(3\) are unequal; equal coefficients would make it bounded
Unbounded — both constraints are \(\ge\) type lower bounds, so the feasible region extends to infinity for large \(x\) and \(y\), with no upper limit imposed on either variable
Bounded — every LPP arising from a real-world minimum-requirement problem is automatically bounded
questions.explanation: The constraints \(2x+y\ge3\) and \(x+2y\ge6\) (with \(x,y\ge0\)) place only LOWER bounds on \(x\) and \(y\) — nothing stops either variable from growing arbitrarily large while still satisfying both \(\ge\) inequalities (e.g. \((100,100)\) easily satisfies both). Since no constraint caps \(x\) or \(y\) from above, the feasible region stretches to infinity and is unbounded, even though it has a well-defined, finite set of corner points near the origin.
questions.hint: Look at whether every direction of increasing \(x\) and \(y\) is eventually blocked by some \(\le\)-type constraint — here, none exists.
distractor_logic: Having two lines that intersect at a point says nothing about whether the overall region is bounded — boundedness depends on whether the region also closes off in every direction, which it does not here since both constraints only push outward from below.
The relative size of the cost coefficients in the OBJECTIVE function has no bearing on whether the feasible region (determined purely by the constraints) is bounded or unbounded.
Minimum-requirement (\(\ge\)) problems are actually a classic source of UNBOUNDED feasible regions in this course, precisely because they only restrict variables from below, not above.

questions.topic: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem: Decision Variables, Objective Function, and Constraints
questions.question: A factory line must produce at least \(24\) units per shift to meet a standing order (\(x\ge24\)), but the machine on that line can process at most \(16\) units per shift (\(x\le16\)), where \(x\) is the number of units produced. After formulating these two constraints together (with \(y\ge0\) as a second, unrelated variable, and any objective function), what can be concluded about this LPP?
options: The LPP has multiple optimal solutions, one at \(x=24\) and one at \(x=16\)
The LPP is a perfectly ordinary problem with feasible region \(16\le x\le24\)
The LPP has an unbounded optimal value, since \(x\) is constrained on only one side by each inequality
The LPP is infeasible — \(x\ge24\) and \(x\le16\) directly contradict each other, so no value of \(x\) (and hence no point) can satisfy both simultaneously
questions.explanation: The two constraints on \(x\) alone — \(x\ge24\) and \(x\le16\) — are directly contradictory: no real number can be simultaneously at least \(24\) and at most \(16\). Since this makes it impossible to satisfy even these two constraints together, regardless of \(y\) or the objective function, the feasible region is empty and the LPP is infeasible.
questions.hint: Before going any further, check whether the constraints on a single variable are even simultaneously satisfiable — here they plainly are not.
distractor_logic: "Multiple optimal solutions" requires a genuine feasible region where more than one point achieves the same optimal value; here there is no feasible region whatsoever, so this special case cannot apply.

This incorrectly reverses the direction, treating \(x\ge24\) as an upper bound and \(x\le16\) as a lower bound; read correctly, they require \(x\) to be both at least \(24\) and at most \(16\) at once, which is impossible, not a valid range.

Each inequality is indeed one-sided, but TOGETHER they don't leave any room for \(x\) at all — unbounded optimal value requires a genuinely non-empty region that stretches to infinity, which is not the case here.

questions.topic: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem: Decision Variables, Objective Function, and Constraints
questions.question: A workshop assembles lamps (\(x\)) and fans (\(y\)). Assembly time gives \(x+2y\le40\) and packaging gives \(2x+y\le50\), with profit \(\textrm{\textrupee}30\) per lamp and \(\textrm{\textrupee}40\) per fan. Formulate the LPP, list its corner points, and find the maximum profit.
options: \(Z=30x+40y\) subject to \(x+2y\le40,\ 2x+y\le50\); corners \((0,0)\) and \((25,0)\) only; maximum profit \(\textrm{\textrupee}750\) at \((25,0)\)
questions.explanation: Decision variables \(x\) (lamps) and \(y\) (fans); objective \(Z=30x+40y\) (profit per lamp times lamps, plus profit per fan times fans), subject to \(x+2y\le40\), \(2x+y\le50\), \(x,y\ge0\). The four corner points are \((0,0)\), \((0,20)\), \((20,10)\) (intersection of the two lines), and \((25,0)\), with \(Z=0,\ 800,\ 1000,\ 750\). The maximum, \(1000\), occurs at \((20,10)\).
questions.hint: Set up the objective with the correct coefficient attached to each variable, find all four corners including the intersection point, then compare all four \(Z\)-values.
distractor_logic: This drops two genuine corner points, \((0,20)\) and \((20,10)\), leaving only the two extreme axis points and missing the true maximum entirely.

This swaps the profit coefficients, attaching \(\textrm{\textrupee}40\) to lamps and \(\textrm{\textrupee}30\) to fans instead of the other way around; although it happens to reach the same final numeric maximum here, the objective function itself misrepresents the stated per-unit profits.
This has the correct constraints and corner list but stops the comparison too early, picking \(800\) at \((0,20)\) rather than continuing to check \((20,10)\), which gives more.

questions.topic: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem: Decision Variables, Objective Function, and Constraints
questions.question: An investor requires at least \(\textrm{\textrupee}1000\) in scheme A (\(x\ge1000\)) and at least \(\textrm{\textrupee}1000\) in scheme B (\(y\ge1000\)), with no upper limit on either, and wants to maximise the total invested, \(Z=x+y\). After formulating this LPP and classifying its feasible region, what is the correct conclusion about the maximum value of \(Z\)?
options: The feasible region is unbounded, but the only corner point, \((1000,1000)\), still gives the maximum value \(Z=2000\)
The feasible region is unbounded, and since \(Z=x+y\) keeps increasing as \(x\) and \(y\) grow without any upper limit, this LPP has an unbounded optimal value — no finite maximum exists
The LPP is infeasible, since \(x\ge1000\) and \(y\ge1000\) cannot both be satisfied along with non-negativity
The feasible region is bounded, since it has exactly one corner point, and the maximum is \(Z=2000\) at \((1000,1000)\)
questions.explanation: The constraints \(x\ge1000\), \(y\ge1000\) (with the usual non-negativity, which is automatically satisfied) place only lower bounds, with the only corner point being \((1000,1000)\); but the region stretches to infinity as both \(x\) and \(y\) increase, so it is unbounded. Since \(Z=x+y\) grows without any limit in exactly that same direction (e.g. \(Z=200000\) at \((100000,100000)\), which is still feasible), there is no finite maximum — this LPP has an unbounded optimal value, despite \((1000,1000)\) being the only corner point found.
questions.hint: A single corner point is a strong hint the region is unbounded — then ask specifically whether \(Z\) keeps growing in the direction the region extends.
distractor_logic: This correctly identifies the region as unbounded but wrongly treats the lone corner-point value as automatically the maximum, without checking whether \(Z\) can be pushed higher by moving further into the unbounded region — exactly the unverified-corner-point trap.
Both constraints are easily satisfied together (e.g. by \((1000,1000)\) itself), so the feasible region is clearly non-empty; this is not an infeasibility situation at all.

This wrongly concludes the region is bounded purely because it happens to have only one corner point; a region with a single vertex (like this one) is actually a classic shape for an UNBOUNDED region, not a sign of boundedness.

questions.topic: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem: Decision Variables, Objective Function, and Constraints
questions.question: A garment unit stitches shirts (\(x\)) and trousers (\(y\)), constrained by total stitching time \(x+y\le9\) and total fabric \(2x+y\le14\), with profit \(\textrm{\textrupee}4\) per shirt and \(\textrm{\textrupee}3\) per trouser. A colleague formulates this correctly but then evaluates \(Z\) only at \((0,0)\), \((0,9)\), and \((7,0)\), reporting a maximum profit of \(\textrm{\textrupee}27\) at \((0,9)\). What has gone wrong, and what is the actual maximum?
options: The colleague missed the intersection corner \((5,4)\) (where the two constraint lines meet); including it gives \(Z(5,4)=32\), which is the true maximum, higher than \(27\)
The colleague should have evaluated \(Z\) only at \((7,0)\), since that is the only corner satisfying both constraints with equality
The colleague's working is entirely correct; \(\textrm{\textrupee}27\) at \((0,9)\) is indeed the maximum profit
The colleague's error is using \(Z=4x+3y\) instead of \(Z=3x+4y\); the profit coefficients have been swapped
questions.explanation: Solving \(x+y=9\) and \(2x+y=14\) together gives the genuine intersection corner \((5,4)\), which the colleague never checked. The complete corner list is \((0,0)\), \((0,9)\), \((5,4)\), and \((7,0)\), with \(Z=0,\ 27,\ 32,\ 28\); the true maximum is \(\textrm{\textrupee}32\) at \((5,4)\), not \(\textrm{\textrupee}27\) at \((0,9)\).
questions.hint: Whenever two non-axis constraint lines are both active in a problem, always solve them together for their intersection — it is very often a genuine corner that must be checked.
distractor_logic: This drops the two axis corners \((0,0)\) and \((0,9)\) needed for a complete comparison, and even the single corner it keeps, \((7,0)\), does not give the maximum profit on its own.
This wrongly claims the incomplete three-point check was already correct, even though a whole corner point — and, as it turns out, the actual optimal one — was left out entirely.

The stated profit figures (\(\textrm{\textrupee}4\) per shirt, \(\textrm{\textrupee}3\) per trouser) translate directly and correctly into \(Z=4x+3y\); the actual issue is an incomplete corner-point list, not a coefficient swap.

questions.topic: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem: Decision Variables, Objective Function, and Constraints
questions.question: A supplier wants to minimise cost \(Z=4x+2y\) while meeting two minimum stock levels, \(x\ge2\) and \(y\ge2\), and a total-capacity limit \(x+y\le10\). After formulating this LPP, a trainee correctly finds the corner points \((2,2)\), \((2,8)\), \((8,2)\) with \(Z=12,\ 24,\ 36\), but reports the minimum cost as \(\textrm{\textrupee}36\). What is the correct minimum cost, and what mistake did the trainee make?
options: The minimum cost cannot be determined without also checking whether the region is bounded or unbounded
The trainee is correct; \(\textrm{\textrupee}36\) at \((8,2)\) is indeed the minimum cost
The minimum cost is \(\textrm{\textrupee}24\) at \((2,8)\), the middle of the three values, since minimum problems always pick the median value
The minimum cost is \(\textrm{\textrupee}12\) at \((2,2)\); the trainee picked the LARGEST \(Z\)-value instead of the smallest, even though a minimum was asked for
questions.explanation: All three \(Z\)-values are correctly computed: \(Z(2,2)=12\), \(Z(2,8)=24\), \(Z(8,2)=36\). Since this is a MINIMISATION problem, the correct choice is the SMALLEST of these, \(12\) at \((2,2)\), not the largest. The trainee applied the maximisation rule (pick the biggest value) to a minimisation problem, giving exactly the wrong corner.
questions.hint: Once all the \(Z\)-values are correctly computed, re-read the problem statement to confirm whether it asks for a maximum or a minimum before picking one.
distractor_logic: The region here is bounded (a triangle with vertices \((2,2)\), \((2,8)\), \((8,2)\)), so the ordinary Corner Point Theorem already guarantees the minimum exists among these three values with no further check needed — the actual error is simply picking the wrong one of the three.
This restates the trainee's incorrect answer as if it were correct, repeating the max/min mix-up rather than catching it.

\(24\) is neither the smallest nor the largest of the three values, and "pick the median" is not a rule of the corner point method at all — the method always requires the strict maximum or strict minimum, never a middle value.

questions.topic: Graphical Solution: Feasible Region and Corner Points
questions.question: A feasible region is defined only by the single constraint \(x+y\ge5\) (together with \(x,y\ge0\)), giving exactly two corner points, \((0,5)\) and \((5,0)\). Is this feasible region bounded or unbounded?
options: Bounded — a region with only two corner points must be a line segment, which is always bounded
Unbounded, but only if a third constraint is added later
Unbounded — having only two corner points from a single \(\ge\) constraint means the region extends to infinity away from the origin, with nothing capping \(x\) or \(y\) from above
Cannot be determined from the corner points alone; the number of corner points has no bearing on boundedness
questions.explanation: The single constraint \(x+y\ge5\) only pushes the region AWAY from the origin, with no upper bound on \(x\) or \(y\) anywhere. Even though the region happens to have just two corner points, \((0,5)\) and \((5,0)\), points like \((1000,1000)\) remain perfectly feasible, so the region stretches to infinity and is unbounded.
questions.hint: Don't judge boundedness purely by counting corner points — check whether every direction of increase is actually blocked by some \(\le\)-type constraint.
distractor_logic: A region with two corner points here is actually the two ends of the boundary LINE where the unbounded region begins; it is not a bounded line segment, since the shaded feasible area continues past that line to infinity.

The region is unbounded already, with the constraints exactly as given — no additional constraint is needed for that conclusion (though an added \(\le\) constraint could, of course, later make it bounded).

The number and pattern of corner points is in fact a useful first clue: very few corner points from only \(\ge\)-type (or only one-sided) constraints is a strong sign of an unbounded region, even though it is not, by itself, a complete boundedness test.

questions.topic: Graphical Solution: Feasible Region and Corner Points
questions.question: For the constraints \(x+y\le2\) and \(x+y\ge6\) (with \(x,y\ge0\)), attempting to list the corner points of the feasible region yields none at all. What does this indicate about the LPP?
options: The LPP has an unbounded optimal value, since no finite corner points were found
The feasible region is simply the single point where the two parallel lines would meet, if extended
The LPP is infeasible — the two lines \(x+y=2\) and \(x+y=6\) are parallel, and the regions \(x+y\le2\) and \(x+y\ge6\) share no point in common, so the feasible region is empty
The corner-point-finding process has failed and must be redone with different constraint pairs
questions.explanation: Since \(x+y\le2\) and \(x+y\ge6\) are two parallel constraint lines (same left-hand side, different constants) pointing in opposite directions, no point can satisfy \(x+y\) being at most \(2\) AND at least \(6\) simultaneously. This means the individual half-planes never overlap anywhere, the feasible region is genuinely empty, and finding zero corner points is the correct (not a failed) outcome — it directly signals that the LPP is infeasible.
questions.hint: Finding NO corner points at all is itself a meaningful result — for parallel, oppositely-directed \(\le\)/\(\ge\) constraints, it specifically signals infeasibility.
distractor_logic: "Unbounded optimal value" requires a real, non-empty feasible region that stretches to infinity with \(Z\) growing without limit on it; with no feasible region at all, this special case cannot apply.

Parallel lines with no shared feasible region do not meet at any point (finite or otherwise); there is no single intersection point to speak of, and the feasible region is empty, not a solitary point.
Finding zero corner points is not a sign of a computational error to be redone; here, it is the correct and expected outcome given genuinely contradictory constraints.

This wrongly includes the origin, which is infeasible here since it violates \(x\ge2\), while still missing the two genuine intersection corners that are actually part of the region.
This finds \((2,4)\) correctly but still misses the intersection of the two \(\le\)-lines, \(\left(\tfrac{10}{3},\tfrac{10}{3}\right)\), which gives an even larger \(Z\)-value than \((2,4)\) does.

questions.question: A school is choosing between buses (\(x\)) and vans (\(y\)) for a trip, with total-vehicle limit \(x+y\le12\) and a fuel-budget-driven limit \(2x+y\le18\). Formulate these constraints and determine which of the following is \(\textbf{NOT}\) a corner point of the feasible region: \((0,0)\), \((0,12)\), \((6,6)\), \((9,0)\).
options: \((6,6)\) is not a corner point, since it does not lie on either axis
All four points are corner points of this feasible region
\((0,12)\) is not a corner point, since it violates \(2x+y\le18\) (as \(2(0)+12=12\le18\) is actually satisfied, so this point IS feasible and IS a corner)

\((9,0)\) is not a corner point — it fails \(x+y\le12\) is fine, but it is not where two boundary lines actually meet; the true corner on the \(x\)-axis is \((9,0)\) only if it satisfies BOTH constraints with the tighter one active, which requires checking \(2x+y=18\) gives \((9,0)\) exactly, so in fact all four ARE genuine corners
questions.explanation: Checking each point: \((0,0)\) satisfies non-negativity trivially. \((0,12)\): from \(x+y\le12\) directly (\(x=0\)), and \(2(0)+12=12\le18\) holds, so it is feasible and is where the \(y\)-axis meets the tighter constraint. \((9,0)\): from \(2x+y=18\) with \(y=0\), giving \(x=9\), and \(9+0=9\le12\) holds. \((6,6)\): solving \(x+y=12\) and \(2x+y=18\) together gives \(x=6,y=6\), which satisfies both with equality. All four points are therefore genuine corner points of this bounded quadrilateral region.
questions.hint: A corner point does not need to lie on an axis — the intersection of two non-axis boundary lines is just as valid a corner as an axis intercept.
distractor_logic: This wrongly assumes only axis points can be corners; the intersection of two constraint lines away from either axis, like \((6,6)\) here, is a completely standard and valid type of corner point.
This wrongly claims \((0,12)\) is infeasible; checking it directly against \(2x+y\le18\) gives \(12\le18\), which is true, so the point is feasible and is indeed a genuine corner.

This option's own reasoning is muddled and ultimately concludes all four points ARE corners, matching the correct final answer, but arrives there through an unnecessarily confused justification about \((9,0)\) rather than simply verifying it directly.

Finding the correct corner list and boundedness, this stops the \(Z\)-comparison one corner too early and reports \((4,6)\)'s value (\(26\)) instead of continuing to \((3,7)\), which gives more.

No corner is actually missing; the given list of four points is already complete
Missing corner: \((6,0)\); correct maximum becomes \(Z=18\) at \((6,0)\)
Missing corner: \((3,6)\) (where \(y=6\) meets \(x+y=9\)); correct maximum is still \(Z=23\) at \((5,4)\), since \(Z(3,6)=21\) does not exceed it

\(Z=8\) at \((0,4)\); this is genuinely the minimum, since checking confirms the region does not extend in any direction where \(3x+2y\) decreases below \(8\) (the region only stretches where \(x,y\) both grow, which increases \(Z\))
\(Z=8\) at \((0,4)\); this is automatically the minimum with no further check needed, since it is unbounded regions specifically where corner-point values can always be trusted directly
\(Z=10\) at \((2,2)\), since this is the middle value and minimisation problems favour the middle of the range

The minimum is genuinely \(8\).

distractor_logic: This applies the MAXIMISATION rule (pick the largest) to a problem that explicitly asks for a MINIMUM, giving exactly the wrong corner.

This gets the right numeric value and point but for the wrong reason — it is unbounded regions specifically that require the EXTRA verification step, not ones where it can be skipped; the correct justification is the escape-direction check, not an automatic rule.

questions.question: For Maximise \(Z=3x+4y\) subject to \(x\le8,\ y\le6,\ x+y\le11,\ x,y\ge0\), the corner points and \(Z\)-values are \((0,0)\to0\), \((0,6)\to24\), \((5,6)\to39\), \((8,0)\to24\), \((8,3)\to36\). Does this LPP have multiple optimal solutions?
options: Cannot be determined without checking whether the region is bounded
No — although \((0,6)\) and \((8,0)\) happen to tie at \(Z=24\), neither is the actual maximum; the true, strictly largest maximum is \(Z=39\) at \((5,6)\) alone, so the optimal solution is unique
Yes — since the feasible region has five corner points, an odd number
Yes — since two different corner points, \((0,6)\) and \((8,0)\), give the same \(Z\)-value
questions.explanation: A tie between corner-point values only signals multiple optimal solutions when the TIED value is itself the optimum. Here \(24\) is tied between \((0,6)\) and \((8,0)\), but neither reaches the maximum — the true maximum is the strictly larger, unique value \(Z=39\) at \((5,6)\) alone. This is an ordinary LPP with a single optimal solution, despite the coincidental tie elsewhere among non-optimal corners.
questions.hint: A tie only matters for "multiple optimal solutions" if the TIED value is the optimum itself — a tie among non-optimal values is simply a coincidence.
distractor_logic: This region is in fact bounded (every constraint is a finite \(\le\) bound), and in any case boundedness must be resolved first only to decide whether extra unbounded-region verification is needed — it has no direct bearing on whether a tie counts as multiple optimal solutions.
The total number of corner points (five here) has no bearing on whether multiple optimal solutions occur; what matters is only whether the single best value among them is repeated, which it is not.

Mistakes a coincidental tie between two NON-optimal corner values (\(24=24\), neither the maximum) for the genuine special case, which specifically requires the OPTIMAL value to repeat — here the actual maximum, \(39\), occurs at only one corner.

The maximum is \(Z=24\) at \((0,8)\), since it is the only value that is not tied with another

The maximum value is \(Z=30\), and since it is achieved at BOTH \((6,4)\) and \((10,0)\), this LPP has multiple optimal solutions — in fact, every point on the entire edge joining them also gives \(Z=30\), since the objective's direction exactly matches that edge
The maximum value is \(Z=30\), achieved uniquely at \((6,4)\), since it is checked before \((10,0)\)

This is a genuine case of multiple optimal solutions, not a coincidental tie among non-optimal corners.

distractor_logic: Having two corner points tie at the SAME optimal value does not indicate infeasibility at all; infeasibility is about having no feasible region whatsoever, which is clearly not the case here.
\(24\) is not tied with anything, but more importantly it is not even the largest value; \(30\) (achieved at two corners) is larger and is the actual maximum.

This picks one of the two tied maximum values arbitrarily as if it were uniquely optimal, missing that \((10,0)\) achieves exactly the same value and that the whole connecting edge is therefore also optimal.

questions.question: While applying the corner point method to Maximise \(Z=x+y\) subject to \(x\ge6,\ x+y\le5,\ x,y\ge0\), a student finds no corner points at all. What should the student conclude?
options: The LPP is infeasible — \(x\ge6\) requires \(x\) to be at least \(6\), but \(x+y\le5\) together with \(y\ge0\) forces \(x\le5\), a direct contradiction, so the feasible region is empty
The maximum value of \(Z\) is \(0\), attained at the origin, since the origin always satisfies non-negativity
The feasible region is unbounded, since \(x\ge6\) has no upper bound
The student made an error and must keep searching for corner points, since every LPP has at least one
questions.explanation: From \(x+y\le5\) and \(y\ge0\), it follows that \(x\le5\); but the other constraint requires \(x\ge6\). No value of \(x\) can be both at most \(5\) and at least \(6\), so the two constraints are directly contradictory and the feasible region is empty. Finding zero corner points is therefore the correct outcome of the corner point method here, not a mistake to be corrected — it signals that the LPP is infeasible.
questions.hint: Not every LPP has a feasible region at all — when the corner point method genuinely turns up nothing, check whether the constraints are simply contradictory.
distractor_logic: The origin \((0,0)\) is not actually feasible here, since it violates \(x\ge6\); with an empty feasible region, no point at all (including the origin) is available to evaluate \(Z\) at.

\(x\ge6\) alone has no upper bound, but this is irrelevant once combined with \(x+y\le5\) and \(y\ge0\), which together force \(x\le5\) — the two constraints leave no feasible \(x\) at all, so the region isn't unbounded, it's empty.
Assuming every LPP must have corner points is false; when constraints are mutually contradictory, as they are here, the correct and complete result of the search is indeed zero corner points.

questions.topic: Corner Point Method: Finding the Optimal (Maximum or Minimum) Value
questions.question: For Minimise \(Z=2x+5y\) subject to \(x\le8,\ y\le8,\ x+y\le12,\ x,y\ge0\), the corner points are \((0,0)\), \((0,8)\), \((4,8)\), \((8,0)\), \((8,4)\). Confirm this region is bounded, and find the minimum value of \(Z\).
options: Unbounded, since the region has five corner points, more than the usual four
Bounded; minimum \(Z=36\) at \((8,4)\), the point with the largest sum of coordinates
Bounded; minimum \(Z=16\) at \((8,0)\), since minimisation always favours the corner with the largest \(x\)-coordinate
Bounded (all three main constraints are finite \(\le\) bounds); minimum \(Z=0\) at \((0,0)\)
questions.explanation: With \(x\le8\), \(y\le8\), and \(x+y\le12\) all being finite \(\le\) constraints (together with non-negativity), the region is closed off in every direction and is bounded, guaranteeing both a maximum and a minimum exist among the corner points. Evaluating \(Z=2x+5y\): \(0,\ 40,\ 48,\ 16,\ 36\); the smallest is \(0\), at the origin \((0,0)\).
questions.hint: Since the region is bounded, the Corner Point Theorem guarantees the minimum is simply the smallest of the computed corner values — here that happens to be the origin.
distractor_logic: "Largest \(x\)-coordinate" is not a rule of the corner point method for minimisation (or maximisation); every corner's actual \(Z\)-value must be computed and compared, and here the origin, not \((8,0)\), gives the smallest.
"Largest sum of coordinates" is likewise not a valid shortcut; \((8,4)\) in fact gives one of the LARGEST \(Z\)-values here, not the smallest, because of the heavier coefficient \(5\) on \(y\).

The number of corner points (five, from three active constraint lines beyond the axes) has no bearing on boundedness; what determines it is whether every constraint eventually caps the region, which they all do here.

questions.topic: Corner Point Method: Finding the Optimal (Maximum or Minimum) Value
questions.question: For Maximise \(Z=x+2y\) subject to \(x+2y\le16,\ x+y\le10,\ x,y\ge0\), the corner points are \((0,0)\), \((0,8)\), \((4,6)\), \((10,0)\), with \(Z=0,\ 16,\ 16,\ 10\). Explain \(\textbf{why}\) this LPP has multiple optimal solutions.
options: Because \(10\), the value at \((10,0)\), is smaller than \(16\); smaller values always indicate multiple solutions
Because two DIFFERENT constraints were used to build the region; using only one constraint would avoid this

Because the tie at \(Z=16\) occurs between \((0,8)\) and \((4,6)\), which is the true maximum, AND the objective's coefficients \((1,2)\) are exactly proportional to the coefficients of the binding constraint \(x+2y\le16\) — so the objective line is parallel to that entire edge, making every point on it optimal, not just the two endpoints
Because the feasible region has exactly four corner points, and any four-cornered region automatically has multiple optimal solutions
questions.explanation: The maximum \(Z=16\) is tied between \((0,8)\) and \((4,6)\) — and crucially, both of these lie on the boundary line \(x+2y=16\), which is exactly the constraint whose left-hand side matches the objective function \(Z=x+2y\) coefficient-for-coefficient. This means the objective's direction is parallel to that entire edge, so every point along it (the full segment from \((0,8)\) to \((4,6)\), not merely its endpoints) achieves the same maximum value \(16\) — the defining geometric reason for multiple optimal solutions.
questions.hint: Look for whether the tied optimal corners both lie on the SAME boundary line, and whether that line's coefficients match the objective's coefficients — that match is the real geometric cause.
distractor_logic: The relative size of a non-optimal value like \(10\) compared to the optimal \(16\) is irrelevant to why multiple solutions occur; the cause lies entirely in the tie at the optimal value and its geometric alignment with an edge.

Using two constraints to build a region is completely standard for any non-trivial LPP and does not, by itself, cause or prevent multiple optimal solutions; the real cause is the specific coefficient match described above.

Having four corner points is completely ordinary for a two-constraint bounded region and has no automatic connection to multiple optimal solutions; what matters is the specific relationship between the objective and one particular edge, not the corner count.

questions.topic: Corner Point Method: Finding the Optimal (Maximum or Minimum) Value
questions.question: A workshop manufactures two products (\(x\) and \(y\)) under \(x+y\le20\) and \(2x+y\le30\), with profit \(Z=2x+y\). Formulate the LPP, apply the corner point method, and determine whether the maximum profit is unique.
options: Corners \((0,0)\), \((0,20)\), \((10,10)\), \((15,0)\); \(Z=0,\ 20,\ 30,\ 30\); the LPP is infeasible since two corners tie

Corners \((0,0)\), \((0,20)\), \((10,10)\), \((15,0)\); \(Z=0,\ 20,\ 30,\ 30\); the maximum \(\textrm{\textrupee}30\) is tied between \((10,10)\) and \((15,0)\), so it has multiple optimal solutions (the entire edge between them is optimal, since the objective \((2,1)\) matches the binding constraint \(2x+y\le30\))
The LPP cannot be solved because the objective coefficients \((2,1)\) do not appear directly among the constraint coefficients
questions.explanation: With \(Z=2x+y\) as profit, subject to \(x+y\le20\), \(2x+y\le30\), \(x,y\ge0\), the corners are \((0,0)\), \((0,20)\), \((10,10)\), \((15,0)\), giving \(Z=0,\ 20,\ 30,\ 30\). The maximum, \(\textrm{\textrupee}30\), is tied between \((10,10)\) and \((15,0)\); since both lie on \(2x+y=30\) and the objective's coefficients \((2,1)\) exactly match that constraint's, the entire edge between them shares the maximum — a genuine case of multiple optimal solutions, not just a coincidental tie.
questions.hint: After correctly formulating and solving, check whether a tie at the MAXIMUM value corresponds to two points on the same binding edge with matching objective coefficients.
distractor_logic: A tie at the optimal value between two feasible corner points is the definition of multiple optimal solutions, not infeasibility; infeasibility requires an empty feasible region, which this clearly is not.

There is no requirement for the objective's coefficients to already appear among the constraints' coefficients in order to solve an LPP; the objective is simply evaluated at whatever corner points the constraints produce, exactly as done here.
This gets the correct corner list and values but wrongly declares the maximum unique, missing that \((15,0)\) ties with \((10,10)\) at the very same value \(30\).

questions.topic: Bounded and Unbounded Feasible Regions
questions.question: For Maximise \(Z=2x+y\) subject to \(x-y\le4,\ x\ge2,\ x,y\ge0\), the only corner points are \((2,0)\) and \((4,0)\), giving \(Z=4\) and \(Z=8\). The region is unbounded. Is \(Z=8\) genuinely the maximum?
options: Yes, because a region with only two corner points can never be unbounded
No maximum can be determined because there are only two corner points, which is too few for this method

No — the region extends without limit along the line \(x-y=4\) (e.g. through points like \((104,100)\), which remain feasible), and along that direction \(Z=2x+y\) keeps growing past \(8\) without any limit, so no maximum actually exists
Yes — \(8\) is the larger of the two corner values found, so it is automatically the maximum
questions.explanation: The two corner points give \(Z(2,0)=4\) and \(Z(4,0)=8\), with \(8\) the larger. But the feasible region is unbounded along the boundary line \(x-y=4\): points like \((104,100)\) satisfy \(x-y=4\le4\) and \(x=104\ge2\), so they remain feasible, and there \(Z=2(104)+100=308\), far beyond \(8\). Since \(Z\) keeps growing without any limit along this direction, no finite maximum exists at all, despite \(8\) looking like a plausible answer from the corner points alone.
questions.hint: Two corner points from constraints that are not all \(\le\)-bounded on both variables is a strong hint of an unbounded region — always check whether \(Z\) can be pushed further along the direction the region extends.
distractor_logic: Having only two corner points does not, by itself, rule out an unbounded region; in fact a region with very few corners arising from one-sided constraints (like \(x\ge2\) here) is a classic pattern for unboundedness.

Two corner points is a perfectly sufficient starting point for the corner point method (which always evaluates whatever corners exist); the real issue here is not an insufficient corner count but a missing verification step for the unbounded region.

Taking the larger of the corner-point values as automatically correct, without checking whether the unbounded region allows \(Z\) to grow even further, is exactly the unverified-corner-point trap that the half-plane check exists to catch.

questions.topic: Bounded and Unbounded Feasible Regions
questions.question: For Maximise \(Z=2x+y\) subject only to \(y\le8\) (with \(x,y\ge0\), and no upper bound on \(x\)), the corner points are \((0,0)\) and \((0,8)\), giving \(Z=0\) and \(Z=8\). What is the correct conclusion about the maximum value of \(Z\)?
options: The maximum value of \(Z\) is \(0\), attained at \((0,0)\), since the origin is always the safest choice
The maximum value of \(Z\) is \(8\), attained at \((0,8)\), since it is the larger of the two corner values found
The maximum cannot be found because only one constraint, \(y\le8\), was given
No maximum value of \(Z\) exists, because \(x\) can grow without limit while \(y\) stays within \([0,8]\), and \(Z=2x+y\) then grows without bound as \(x\to\infty\)
questions.explanation: The corner points \((0,0)\) and \((0,8)\) give \(Z=0\) and \(Z=8\), but notice that only \(y\) is capped here (by \(y\le8\)) — \(x\) has no upper-bound constraint at all. So \(x\) can be made arbitrarily large while \(y\) stays anywhere in \([0,8]\), and every such point remains feasible. Since \(Z=2x+y\) then grows without bound (e.g. at \((1000,8)\), \(Z=2008\)), no finite maximum exists, despite \(8\) being the larger of the two corner values.
questions.hint: Notice which variable has NO upper bound at all here (\(x\), not \(y\)) — that missing bound is exactly what lets \(Z\) grow without limit.
distractor_logic: Picking the smaller corner value for being "the safest choice" is not a valid reasoning step in the corner point method under any circumstance, and the origin certainly is not the maximum of this maximisation problem regardless.

Taking the larger of the two corner-point values as the final answer, without checking whether the region is unbounded in a direction that lets \(Z\) increase further, is exactly the unverified-corner-point trap for an unbounded region.

A single constraint (plus non-negativity) is a perfectly valid, if simple, basis for a feasible region; the real issue here is not an insufficient number of constraints but that this particular region is unbounded in the \(x\)-direction, where \(Z\) grows without limit.

questions.topic: Bounded and Unbounded Feasible Regions
questions.question: For Maximise \(Z=x+3y\) subject only to \(x\le10\) (with \(x,y\ge0\), and no upper bound on \(y\)), the corner points are \((0,0)\) and \((10,0)\), giving \(Z=0\) and \(Z=10\). What is the correct conclusion?
options: The region is bounded, since only one constraint restricts it, and a single restriction always produces a bounded region
No maximum exists, because \(y\) can grow without limit while \(x\) stays within \([0,10]\), and \(Z=x+3y\) grows without bound as \(y\to\infty\)
The maximum is \(Z=0\) at \((0,0)\), since it is checked first
The maximum is \(Z=10\) at \((10,0)\), the larger of the two corner values
questions.explanation: This time it is \(y\), not \(x\), that has no upper bound. The two corner points \((0,0)\) and \((10,0)\) give \(Z=0\) and \(Z=10\), but \(y\) can be made arbitrarily large while \(x\) stays anywhere in \([0,10]\) and the point remains feasible. Since \(Z=x+3y\) then grows without bound as \(y\to\infty\) (e.g. at \((0,1000)\), \(Z=3000\)), no finite maximum exists, despite \(10\) being the larger of the two corner values found.
questions.hint: Identify exactly which variable is left unbounded (here it's \(y\), the one with the heavier coefficient in \(Z\), making the growth even more dramatic) before trusting any corner-point value as final.
distractor_logic: A single active constraint restricting only one variable, with the other left completely free, is in fact a classic recipe for an UNBOUNDED region, not a guarantee of boundedness.
"Checked first" is never a valid reason to select a value in the corner point method, and \(0\) is in any case the smaller of the two values found, not a plausible maximum candidate either way.
Taking the larger corner value as the answer without checking whether \(Z\) can grow further in the unbounded direction is exactly the unverified-corner-point trap.

questions.topic: Bounded and Unbounded Feasible Regions
questions.question: A nutritionist requires a diet to provide at least \(3\) units of nutrient X (\(x\ge3\)) and at least \(2\) units of nutrient Y (\(y\ge2\)), from two food sources costed at \(Z=x+y\) per combined unit. After formulating this LPP, classify the feasible region as bounded or unbounded.
options: Bounded, since minimum-requirement constraints in nutrition problems always produce a natural upper limit as well
Bounded — since there are only two constraints, the region formed is always a simple rectangle, which is bounded
Unbounded — both constraints are lower bounds only (\(\ge\)), so \(x\) and \(y\) can be increased indefinitely beyond the minimums with no constraint capping them from above
Unbounded, but only in the \(x\)-direction, since the coefficients in \(Z\) are unequal
questions.explanation: The constraints \(x\ge3\) and \(y\ge2\) (with the usual non-negativity, already implied) only require \(x\) and \(y\) to be AT LEAST these minimums — nothing prevents either from being made much larger while remaining feasible (e.g. \((3000,2000)\) easily satisfies both). With no \(\le\)-type constraint capping either variable from above, the feasible region stretches to infinity and is unbounded.
questions.hint: Two lower-bound-only constraints, with nothing capping the variables from above, is a textbook unbounded pattern — regardless of how few constraints there are.
distractor_logic: Nutrition problems with minimum-requirement (\(\ge\)) constraints do not automatically gain an upper limit; an upper bound must be EXPLICITLY stated as a separate \(\le\) constraint, and none is given here.

Two constraints do not automatically produce a rectangle; here, with both being one-sided (\(\ge\)) lower bounds and nothing bounding the variables above, the resulting region is an unbounded corner-shaped area, not a closed rectangle.

The objective function's coefficients have no bearing on the shape of the FEASIBLE REGION, which is determined entirely by the constraints; here, with no upper bound on either variable, the region is unbounded in both directions, not selectively in just one.

questions.topic: Bounded and Unbounded Feasible Regions
questions.question: A region satisfies \(x+y\ge4\), \(x\le10\), \(y\le10\), \(x+y\le16\) (with \(x,y\ge0\)). Even though the first constraint is a \(\ge\) type, is this region bounded or unbounded?
options: Cannot be determined without evaluating a specific objective function first

Bounded — the \(\le\)-type constraints \(x\le10\), \(y\le10\), and \(x+y\le16\) together already close off the region in every direction; the \(\ge\) constraint just cuts a corner OUT of that already-bounded shape, without making it unbounded
Unbounded, since \(x+y\ge4\) alone (ignoring the other constraints) is unbounded, and one unbounded constraint is enough to make the whole region unbounded
Unbounded — the presence of any \(\ge\) constraint always guarantees an unbounded region, regardless of the other constraints
questions.explanation: Boundedness is a property of the intersection of ALL constraints together, not of any single constraint viewed in isolation. Here, \(x\le10\), \(y\le10\), and \(x+y\le16\) together already confine \(x\) and \(y\) to a closed, finite area; the additional constraint \(x+y\ge4\) only removes a small triangular corner (near the origin) from that already-bounded region — it does not open up any new direction of escape. The overall region remains bounded.
questions.hint: Judge boundedness from the INTERSECTION of every constraint together, not from any single constraint read on its own — a \(\ge\) constraint can coexist with an overall bounded region if enough \(\le\) constraints are also present.
distractor_logic: Boundedness is a purely geometric property of the feasible region itself, determined entirely by the constraints; it can be determined without reference to any particular objective function at all.

Judging a single constraint in isolation, ignoring the other three that are present, is the core error here; \(x+y\ge4\) by itself would indeed be unbounded, but combined with the three \(\le\) constraints, the overall feasible region is not.

This wrongly treats the mere presence of a \(\ge\) constraint as automatically decisive; a \(\ge\) constraint only removes part of a region, and if enough \(\le\) constraints already close off the rest, the overall intersection can still be perfectly bounded.

questions.topic: Bounded and Unbounded Feasible Regions
questions.question: For Minimise \(Z=4x+6y\) subject to \(x+3y\ge6,\ x+y\ge4,\ x,y\ge0\), the corner points are \((0,4)\), \((3,1)\), \((6,0)\), with \(Z=24,\ 18,\ 24\). The region is unbounded. What is the correct, fully verified conclusion?
options: No minimum exists, since the region is unbounded, and unbounded regions can never have a finite optimal value
\(Z=18\) at \((3,1)\) is the minimum simply because it is the smallest of the three corner values, with no further check needed since minimisation problems never require verification

\(Z=18\) at \((3,1)\) is genuinely the minimum — checking the direction in which the unbounded region extends shows \(Z\) only increases there, never falls below \(18\), confirming it as the true minimum
\(Z=24\) is the minimum, since it is the value that appears twice among the three corners, and repeated values are always optimal
questions.explanation: \(Z(0,4)=24\), \(Z(3,1)=18\), \(Z(6,0)=24\); the smallest corner value is \(18\). Since the region is unbounded, this must be checked: the region only extends in directions where both \(x+3y\) and \(x+y\) keep growing, and along every such direction \(4x+6y\) also keeps growing rather than falling — so no feasible point can beat \(18\). The minimum is genuinely \(18\) at \((3,1)\); this is an ordinary, verified unique optimum, not a special case.
questions.hint: Being the smallest corner value is necessary but, for an unbounded region, not by itself sufficient without the extra escape-direction check — here that check happens to confirm it.
distractor_logic: This is precisely the false generalisation this topic warns against: many unbounded regions DO have a perfectly finite optimum, exactly as verified here; "unbounded region" and "no optimal value exists" are not the same thing.

This reaches the right numeric answer but for an invalid reason — unbounded regions specifically DO require the extra half-plane/escape-direction verification step before a corner value can be trusted; it is not automatically safe to skip.

A value repeating among the corners (here \(24\), at two DIFFERENT, non-optimal corners) has no special significance for optimality; what matters is only which single value is the genuine smallest (or largest), not which one happens to repeat.

questions.question: A region is defined only by \(x\ge4\) and \(y\ge3\) (with the usual non-negativity, already implied), giving a single corner point \((4,3)\). Classify this region as bounded or unbounded, and explain why.
options: Bounded — a region with only a single corner point is always bounded, since there is nothing further to check
Unbounded — both constraints are lower bounds only, with nothing capping \(x\) or \(y\) from above, so the region stretches to infinity as both variables grow past their minimums
Cannot be classified without first evaluating some objective function \(Z\) at the single corner point
Unbounded, but only because the two lower bounds (\(4\) and \(3\)) are unequal; equal lower bounds would make the region bounded
questions.explanation: The constraints \(x\ge4\) and \(y\ge3\) only require the variables to be at least these amounts, with no \(\le\)-type constraint anywhere to cap them from above. Even though this produces just a single corner point, \((4,3)\), the region itself — every point with \(x\ge4,y\ge3\) — extends to infinity in the direction of increasing \(x\) and \(y\) (e.g. \((10000,10000)\) is feasible), so it is unbounded.
questions.hint: A single corner point is actually a strong hint of an UNBOUNDED region (a shifted quarter-plane), not a sign of boundedness — always check whether the region stretches to infinity in some direction.
distractor_logic: This wrongly assumes having only one corner point implies boundedness; a region like this one, with just a single vertex and no upper caps at all, is a classic example of an unbounded quarter-plane-like shape.
Boundedness is a purely geometric property of the FEASIBLE REGION determined by its constraints; it can be classified directly, with no need to bring in any objective function at all.

The specific numeric values of the lower bounds (\(4\) and \(3\), equal or not) have no bearing on whether the region is bounded; what matters is only whether an upper cap exists on each variable, and here none does.

questions.question: A region satisfies \(x\le6\), \(y\le6\), and \(x+y\le20\) (with \(x,y\ge0\)). Confirm the region is bounded, identify whether the third constraint is redundant, and find the corner points.
options: Unbounded; the presence of a third constraint that never becomes active means the region is not actually closed off
Bounded; \(x+y\le20\) is the only constraint that matters, and \(x\le6,\ y\le6\) can be ignored as redundant instead
Bounded; \(x+y\le20\) is redundant, since \(x\le6\) and \(y\le6\) already force \(x+y\le12<20\) everywhere in the region; corner points are \((0,0)\), \((0,6)\), \((6,0)\), \((6,6)\)
Cannot be determined whether the region is bounded without first removing the redundant constraint from the problem entirely
questions.explanation: Since \(x\le6\) and \(y\le6\) hold throughout the feasible region, their sum satisfies \(x+y\le12\) everywhere — which already satisfies \(x+y\le20\) with room to spare, so that third constraint never actually restricts anything further and is redundant. The region is simply the square \(0\le x\le6,\ 0\le y\le6\), which is bounded, with corner points \((0,0)\), \((0,6)\), \((6,0)\), \((6,6)\).
questions.hint: A constraint being redundant (never the tightest one anywhere) does not affect whether the OVERALL region, from all constraints together, is bounded or unbounded.
distractor_logic: A redundant constraint, by definition, never actually cuts off any additional feasible points beyond what the other constraints already exclude; its presence or absence has no effect on whether the region is open or closed off.

This reverses which constraint is redundant: it is \(x+y\le20\) that adds nothing (since \(x\le6,y\le6\) already force \(x+y\le12\)), not the other way around; \(x\le6\) and \(y\le6\) are exactly what make the region bounded.

Boundedness can be determined directly from the full set of constraints as given; a redundant constraint does not need to be removed first, since including it changes nothing about the resulting feasible region or its corner points.

After verifying that \(2x+3y<7\) shares no point with the feasible region, what is the correct overall conclusion?
options: This LPP is infeasible, since the half-plane \(2x+3y<7\) shares no point with the feasible region
This LPP has multiple optimal solutions, since three different corner points were checked

This is an ordinary LPP with a single, unique optimal solution \(Z=7\) at \((2,1)\); none of the three special cases (infeasibility, multiple optimal solutions, or unbounded optimal value) applies here, even though the feasible region itself is unbounded
This LPP has an unbounded optimal value, since the feasible region is unbounded
questions.explanation: The half-plane check confirms \(Z=7\) genuinely is the minimum (nothing smaller is achievable in the feasible region), and since it occurs at only one corner point with no tie, there is a single unique optimal solution. The feasible region being unbounded does not by itself trigger either of the other special cases — it simply meant the ordinary corner-point comparison needed this extra verification step before being trusted, and that step succeeded.
questions.hint: An unbounded region does not automatically earn a "special case" label — once verified, a perfectly ordinary unique optimum can still exist on it, exactly as it does here.
distractor_logic: The half-plane sharing no point with the feasible region is exactly what CONFIRMS \(Z=7\) as the genuine minimum — a successful verification, not a sign of infeasibility, which would instead mean the feasible region itself is empty (it clearly is not).

Checking three corner points is simply the standard corner point method and does not by itself indicate a tie; all three \(Z\)-values here (\(9\), \(7\), \(8\)) are different, so there is no repetition of the optimal value.
Wrongly assumes unboundedness of the region automatically means the optimal VALUE is unbounded; here the minimum was explicitly verified to exist and equal \(7\), the opposite conclusion.

questions.topic: Special Cases: Multiple Optimal Solutions, Infeasible Problems, and Unbounded Optimal Values
questions.question: One production line must ship at least \(30\) units per week to satisfy a distributor contract (\(x\ge30\)), but the line's total weekly capacity is only \(20\) units (\(x\le20\)), where \(x\) is units shipped. Formulate these two constraints together. What special case does this LPP fall into?
options: Unbounded optimal value — since one constraint is \(\ge\) and has no upper limit by itself
This is a perfectly ordinary LPP with feasible region \(20\le x\le30\)
Multiple optimal solutions — since there are two different bounds given on the same variable
Infeasible — \(x\ge30\) and \(x\le20\) directly contradict each other, so the feasible region is empty regardless of any other variables or the objective function
questions.explanation: No value of \(x\) can simultaneously satisfy \(x\ge30\) (at least \(30\)) and \(x\le20\) (at most \(20\)), since \(30>20\). This makes the two constraints on \(x\) mutually contradictory, so the feasible region is empty and the LPP is infeasible, regardless of what any other variables or the objective function might be.
questions.hint: Before anything else, check whether the constraints given on a single variable are even simultaneously satisfiable — here they plainly are not, since the lower requirement exceeds the upper capacity.
distractor_logic: A one-sided \(\ge\) constraint alone could indeed allow unbounded growth, but here it is directly overridden by a contradictory \(\le\) constraint that makes the region empty before unboundedness is even relevant.

This wrongly treats \(x\ge30\) and \(x\le20\) as if they described a valid range \(20\le x\le30\); read correctly, they require \(x\) to be both at least \(30\) and at most \(20\) simultaneously, which is impossible, not a valid interval.

Having two different numeric bounds stated on the same variable is not, by itself, a sign of multiple optimal solutions; that special case requires an actual feasible region where the optimal VALUE repeats at more than one point, and here there is no feasible region at all.

questions.topic: Special Cases: Multiple Optimal Solutions, Infeasible Problems, and Unbounded Optimal Values
questions.question: For Maximise \(Z=x+y\) subject only to \(x-y\le5\) (with \(x,y\ge0\)), the corner points are \((0,0)\) and \((5,0)\), with \(Z=0\) and \(Z=5\). Checking further, points along the boundary line \(x-y=5\) (such as \((105,100)\)) remain feasible and give ever-larger values of \(Z\). What special case does this LPP illustrate?
options: This is simply an ordinary LPP, and the maximum is confirmed as \(Z=5\), the larger of the two corner values
Infeasible — since points far from the origin, like \((105,100)\), technically extend outside the two corner points originally found
Multiple optimal solutions — since more than one point (all of \((105,100)\), \((5,0)\), etc.) gives a value of \(Z\) at least as large as \(5\)

Unbounded optimal value — the feasible region is unbounded along the direction of the line \(x-y=5\), and \(Z=x+y\) keeps growing without any limit along that same direction, so no finite maximum exists at all
questions.explanation: The corner-point value \(Z=5\) at \((5,0)\) looks like a candidate maximum, but points further along the boundary line \(x-y=5\) (which remains within the feasible region indefinitely) keep giving larger and larger \(Z\)-values with no limit, e.g. \(Z=205\) at \((105,100)\). Since \(Z\) can be pushed arbitrarily high without ever reaching a largest value, this LPP has an unbounded optimal value — a genuinely different situation from an unbounded region that still has a finite optimum after verification.
questions.hint: "Unbounded optimal value" specifically means \(Z\) itself has no finite ceiling (or floor) — distinguish this from an unbounded REGION that might still have a perfectly finite optimum.
distractor_logic: Treating \(5\) as confirmed simply because it was the larger of the two corner-point values, without checking whether \(Z\) could be pushed further along the unbounded direction, is exactly the unverified-corner-point trap this special case exists to catch.

Points being far from the origin does not make them infeasible; \((105,100)\) is checked directly against the constraint \(x-y\le5\) (giving \(5\le5\), true) and is perfectly feasible — "far away" is not a valid infeasibility test.

"Multiple optimal solutions" requires several points to share the exact SAME single best value; here the values keep growing past \(5\) without ever settling on a repeated maximum, which is a fundamentally different situation from a tie.

questions.question: Two constraints are given: \(y\ge x+3\) and \(y\le x\) (with \(x,y\ge0\)). Graphically, how would you recognise that this LPP is infeasible without doing any algebra?
options: The region cannot be judged graphically at all; algebra is always required to determine infeasibility
Since both constraints involve \(y\), the LPP is automatically infeasible whenever two constraints share the same variable
The two boundary lines \(y=x+3\) and \(y=x\) are not parallel, so they must intersect somewhere, meaning the LPP is automatically feasible

The shaded region for \(y\ge x+3\) lies entirely ABOVE the line \(y=x+3\), while the shaded region for \(y\le x\) lies entirely BELOW the line \(y=x\); since the first line is always strictly above the second (by a constant gap of \(3\)), the two shaded half-planes never overlap anywhere
questions.explanation: The lines \(y=x+3\) and \(y=x\) are parallel (both have slope \(1\)), with the first sitting a constant \(3\) units above the second everywhere. Since \(y\ge x+3\) shades the region above the upper line and \(y\le x\) shades the region below the lower line, and the upper line never dips down to meet the lower one, these two shaded regions never overlap anywhere on the graph — visibly confirming, without any algebra, that the LPP is infeasible.
questions.hint: Look at whether the two boundary lines are parallel, and if so, which side each constraint shades — parallel lines shading in opposing directions is a classic visual sign of infeasibility.
distractor_logic: Graphical/visual reasoning is a perfectly valid and standard way to recognise infeasibility (seeing that shaded regions don't overlap); it does not always require algebra, though algebra can confirm the same conclusion.

Sharing a variable between two constraints is completely normal for any LPP with more than one constraint and has no automatic connection to infeasibility; what actually matters is whether the specific half-planes described by the constraints overlap anywhere.

This wrongly assumes non-parallel lines are required for infeasibility, and even claims (incorrectly here) that these two particular lines are non-parallel; in fact they ARE parallel (both slope \(1\)), which is precisely why they never meet and the region is empty.

questions.topic: Special Cases: Multiple Optimal Solutions, Infeasible Problems, and Unbounded Optimal Values
questions.question: An investor formulates: invest at least \(\textrm{\textrupee}2\) lakh in bonds (\(x\ge2\)) and at least \(\textrm{\textrupee}1\) lakh in stocks (\(y\ge1\)), aiming to maximise total investment \(Z=x+y\) with no upper limit stated on either. Formulate this LPP, classify the feasible region, and determine the maximum total investment.
options: The LPP is infeasible, since \(x\ge2\) and \(y\ge1\) cannot both be satisfied at once along with non-negativity
Region is bounded, since it has only one corner point, and the maximum is \(\textrm{\textrupee}3\) lakh at \((2,1)\)
Region is unbounded, but the maximum total investment is still \(\textrm{\textrupee}3\) lakh, at the single corner point \((2,1)\)

Region is unbounded (both constraints are lower bounds only); since \(Z=x+y\) grows without limit as \(x,y\) increase past their minimums with nothing to stop them, this LPP has an unbounded optimal value — no finite maximum total investment exists
questions.explanation: With \(Z=x+y\) to maximise subject to \(x\ge2,\ y\ge1,\ x,y\ge0\), the only corner point is \((2,1)\), giving \(Z=3\). But the region is unbounded (nothing caps \(x\) or \(y\) above their minimums), and since \(Z=x+y\) also grows without any limit in that same unbounded direction (e.g. \(Z=20000\) at \((10000,10000)\), still feasible), there is no finite maximum — this is a genuine case of unbounded optimal value, not merely an unbounded region with a hidden finite optimum.
questions.hint: Formulate first, then check the single corner value against whether \(Z\) can be pushed higher by moving further into the unbounded region — here it clearly can, without limit.
distractor_logic: Both constraints are easily satisfied together (e.g. by \((2,1)\) itself, or many other points), so the feasible region is clearly non-empty; this is not an infeasibility situation at all.
This wrongly concludes the region is bounded purely from having only one corner point; a region with a single vertex and no upper caps, like this one, is a classic unbounded shape, not a bounded one.

This correctly identifies the region as unbounded but wrongly treats the lone corner-point value as automatically the maximum, without checking whether \(Z\) can be pushed higher — exactly the unverified-corner-point trap.
