questions.question: For the constraints \(x\le9\) and \(x+y\le15\) (with \(x,y\ge0\)), the corner points are \((0,0)\), \((0,15)\), \((9,6)\), \((9,0)\). Using the objective \(Z=x+y\), determine whether this LPP has multiple optimal solutions.
options: Cannot be determined without first checking whether the region is bounded or unbounded

Yes — \(Z(0,15)=15\) and \(Z(9,6)=15\) both give the maximum value \(15\), and since both lie on the binding edge \(x+y=15\) (whose direction exactly matches the objective \(x+y\)), the entire edge between them is optimal
No — the maximum is uniquely \(15\) at \((9,6)\) alone, since it is listed after \((0,15)\) in the corner-point search
No — although two corners tie, only single points can ever be optimal in an LPP, never a whole edge
questions.explanation: \(Z(0,0)=0\), \(Z(0,15)=15\), \(Z(9,6)=15\), \(Z(9,0)=9\); the maximum is \(15\), achieved at BOTH \((0,15)\) and \((9,6)\). Since both of these lie on the same boundary line \(x+y=15\), and the objective \(Z=x+y\) has coefficients that exactly match that line's, every point along the entire edge between them also gives \(Z=15\) — confirming genuine multiple optimal solutions, not just a coincidental corner tie.
questions.hint: When a tie occurs at the actual maximum value, check whether both tied corners share the same boundary edge and whether the objective is parallel to it.
distractor_logic: Whether the region is bounded or unbounded affects whether an EXTRA verification step (the half-plane test) is needed before trusting a corner value; it has no bearing on whether a tie at the already-confirmed maximum counts as multiple optimal solutions, which this one does.

The order in which corner points happen to be listed or checked has no bearing on which one is optimal; both \((0,15)\) and \((9,6)\) give the identical maximum value \(15\), regardless of search order.

This is factually wrong: when the objective's direction exactly matches a binding edge, every point along that whole edge (infinitely many) genuinely IS optimal, not just isolated corner points; this is precisely what "multiple optimal solutions" means.

questions.topic: Special Cases: Multiple Optimal Solutions, Infeasible Problems, and Unbounded Optimal Values
questions.question: Three short business scenarios are described: (I) a factory must produce at least \(15\) units but can produce at most \(10\); (II) a shop must stock at least \(5\) units of an item, with no upper limit, while trying to maximise total stock value; (III) a bakery has oven-time and packaging limits (both \(\le\)) and wants to maximise profit. Which scenario is \(\textbf{infeasible}\)?
options: None of the three scenarios is infeasible
Scenario (I) — "at least 15" and "at most 10" directly contradict each other, so no feasible production level exists at all
Scenario (III) — having two separate \(\le\) constraints together always causes infeasibility
Scenario (II) — since it has no upper limit, it must be infeasible
questions.explanation: Scenario (I) requires production to be simultaneously at least \(15\) and at most \(10\), which is a direct numeric contradiction — no production level can satisfy both, so its feasible region is empty and it is infeasible. Scenario (II) is instead an example of a potentially unbounded optimal value (an unbounded region with a maximisation objective that could grow without limit), and Scenario (III), with two ordinary upper-limit constraints, is a completely standard bounded LPP with neither issue.
questions.hint: Infeasibility comes from constraints that flatly contradict each other on the same quantity — look for a "must be at least" paired with a smaller "must be at most".
distractor_logic: Scenario (I)'s two production requirements are mutually contradictory as explained, making the correct answer that Scenario (I) specifically IS infeasible, not that none of the three scenarios has an issue.

Two ordinary \(\le\)-type capacity constraints, as in Scenario (III), is the most standard and unremarkable setup for a bounded LPP; it does not cause infeasibility, and this describes a completely ordinary problem.

Having no upper limit (as in Scenario II) is the hallmark of an UNBOUNDED region, potentially leading to an unbounded optimal value under maximisation — a completely different special case from infeasibility, which requires an empty feasible region.

questions.question: For Minimise \(Z=5x+4y\) subject to \(x+2y\ge8,\ 2x+y\ge8,\ x,y\ge0\), the corner points are \((0,8)\), \(\left(\dfrac83,\dfrac83\right)\), \((8,0)\), giving \(Z=32,\ 24,\ 40\). The region is unbounded. Verify whether \(Z=24\) is genuinely the minimum, and state the correct special-case conclusion.
options: \(Z=40\) is the minimum, since it is the value obtained at the corner point with the largest \(x\)-coordinate, \((8,0)\)
Since the region is unbounded, this LPP automatically falls under the "unbounded optimal value" special case, regardless of what the verification shows

\(Z=24\) at \(\left(\dfrac83,\dfrac83\right)\) is genuinely the minimum — the region only extends where both constraints' left-hand sides keep growing, and along every such direction \(5x+4y\) also keeps growing rather than falling below \(24\); this is an ordinary LPP with a single unique optimum, not a special case
\(Z=24\) cannot be trusted at all, since it comes from a fractional corner point rather than an integer one
questions.explanation: The smallest corner value is \(24\), at the fractional corner \(\left(\dfrac83,\dfrac83\right)\). Since the region is unbounded, this needs checking: the region only stretches where \(x+2y\) and \(2x+y\) both keep growing, and along every such escape direction \(5x+4y\) grows too (never falling below \(24\)), confirming it as the genuine minimum. This is therefore an ordinary LPP with one unique, verified optimal solution — the region being unbounded did not, in the end, create any of the three special cases.
questions.hint: A fractional corner point is just as legitimate as an integer one and must be evaluated exactly like any other — what actually needs the extra check for an unbounded region is the escape-direction verification, not the corner's coordinates being whole numbers.
distractor_logic: "Largest \(x\)-coordinate" is not a valid rule for identifying the minimum (or maximum) in the corner point method; every corner's \(Z\)-value must be individually computed and compared, and \((8,0)\) in fact gives the LARGEST, not smallest, value here.

An unbounded region does not automatically mean the optimal value is itself unbounded; that conclusion must be earned by checking whether \(Z\) can actually be pushed further along the region's escape directions, which here it cannot.

A corner point having fractional coordinates makes it no less valid than any other — the corner point method treats every genuine corner identically, regardless of whether its coordinates happen to be whole numbers or fractions.
